articles.title: Elon Musk suggests US government was behind Starlink restrictions in Ukraine – Europe live
articles.body:
'Sanctions must not be lifted,' Zelenskyy says, as he says Russia's attacks come 'in response to signals from US'
Oh, and we have just heard from Zelenskyy again, doubling down on his criticism of Russia and attributing its latest attacks to “signals from the US.”
Responding to a “horrific” drone attack on a supermarket in Odesa, he said:
“Russia continues its bloody terror. The store was partially destroyed, and cars were damaged. Three people were injured. All necessary emergency services are working at the scene and providing assistance to those affected. It is important that our partners help us defend against this. Residential buildings, stores, energy and other critical infrastructure are under attack virtually nonstop. Not a single hour of peace.”
Crucially, he continued:
“What is happening is Russia’s pointed response to the signals it is receiving from America. Unfortunately, there are dangerous signals about the possibility of further sanctions relief. These sanctions were imposed by the world, by America, Europe, and our partners in response to Russia’s aggression against Ukraine and its war against us. Nothing has changed. The war has not stopped. The sanctions must not be lifted. Russia must end the slaughter it itself started and has continued for 1,695 days now. More money to fund the killing will not help bring this about. Strength is what is needed, and America is stronger than Russian terror.”
Zelenskyy claims Ukraine destroyed four Russian planes by striking airfield
A Ukrainian missile strike destroyed four fighter jets at an airfield in western Russia overnight, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said in a social media post.
Last night, Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck an airfield in the Voronezh region. Four Su-34 aircraft were destroyed and two more Su-34s were hit. Our Long Neptune missile was used to strike the target.
The claim has not been independently verified, and there has been no immediate comment from Russia’s defence ministry. The Voronezh region borders Ukraine.
Posting to social media, Nato’s secretary general Mark Rutte confirmed he met earlier with Bulgarian prime minister Rumen Radev and Romanian president Nicușor Dan to discuss security in the Black Sea and the latest attacks on commercial shipping (13:01).
The alliance leader said:
Nato will continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed.
Violent clashes have been taking place in Albania, where prime minister Edi Rama has today rejected calls to resign.
Protesters have voiced anger about perceived corruption, the cost and quality of education and a deal to sell off parts of its southern coastline to a luxury resort development backed by US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.
In a written statement to Reuters, Rama rejected calls to quit, saying:
My responsibility is to listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward. The alternative would be a betrayal of the Albanians who gave me a strong mandate to complete negotiations on EU membership.
EU leaders heading for mighty clash over EU's next long-term budget - snap analysis
Jennifer Rankin
in Brussels
One other thing that is clear from this morning’s doorstep statements: leaders are heading for a mighty clash over the EU’s next long-term budget.
Agreeing the EU seven-year budget is always a fraught negotiating exercise, which pits a group of “frugals”, such as Germany, Sweden, the Netherlands, who oppose a bigger budget, against a larger group in southern and eastern Europe, who want to maintain the EU’s traditional spending on agriculture and regional funding.
European Council president António Costa wanted a deal by the end of the year to ensure that the next long-term budget (2028-35) would be ready on time – and avoid getting caught in the crossfire of major elections next year in France, Poland and Italy.
That timing is in doubt, as the EU’s frugals (who prefer to be called “modernisers”) reiterated this morning they are in no hurry.
Sweden’s prime minister Ulf Kristersson said he expected tense talks today.
“We are not reaching agreement this month, not next month. I don’t know even if it’s possible to reach an agreement before the end of the year. I think we are not in a hurry, honestly. We need to have a budget that could combine the modernisation, the resources for Ukraine and of course the traditional things as well. But all the titles [areas of spending] need to be decreased to be able to reach an agreement.”
Friedrich Merz said he expected the “very, very difficult” talks to run into December (11:05) but privately Germany has made it clear it is ready to see the talks go into next year unless there are massive cuts to the current proposal.
In the other camp is Spain’s Pedro Sánchez, who described the current proposal as “insufficient” to face the bloc’s challenges, adding that his government would fight to expand it. But with Spain due to hold elections in November, the Socialist leader may not be around to make that argument.
The latest draft summit conclusions call for only a “timely agreement” rather than setting a deadline “by the end of the year”, as in an earlier version.
The European Commission’s €2tn (£1.7tn) budget proposal, which aims to increase spending on defence, border security and research, has already been trimmed by €140bn by Ireland, who as holders of the rotating presidency were tasked with finding a common ground by October.
But almost nobody is happy. The frugal camp thinks the cuts, which target defence and research, are in the wrong places, while the self-styled “friends of cohesion” think there is too much scrimping on the EU’s traditional priorities, such as regional development funds.
France, which does not belong in either camp, but faces acute budget pressures, wants to see the EU agree to new common taxes in order to fund a budget that allows increased spending on new priorities such as defence and maintain the traditional ones, such as farm subsidies.
While the Commission has floated EU taxes on big companies, tobacco and e-waste, member states cannot agree on any of the options.
And the whole budget has to be agreed … by unanimity.
Two drones hit ships in Romanian territorial waters, president Dan says ahead of urgent talks with Nato
Back to Romania, the country’s president Nicușor Dan confirmed that two aerial drone hit ships which caught fire in Romanian territorial waters overnight (12:03).
Dan also said the Romanian state will offer “a reaction” to the incident, without speculating on what it could be. He also suggested that the issue should be added to tomorrow’s agenda on Ukraine-related issues.
Later today, Dan and Bulgaria’s PM Rumen Radev will meet with Nato’s secretary general Mark Rutte to discuss the recent incidents in their respective territorial waters.
Swedish parliament rejects Andersson's PM candidacy
A quick update from Sweden, wherethe country’s parliament rejected Social Democrats leader Magdalena Andersson’s candidacy to form a single-party minority government.
Only 99 lawmakers voted in favour, with 248 against. Two people were absent.
The vote, forced by the parliament’s speaker Andreas Norlén, was widely expected to fail, but is intended to put more pressure on parties as they continue discussions on who could form the next government.
Four centre-left opposition parties, which have all said they favour Andersson as prime minister, won last month a majority of seats in Sweden’s parliament, the Riksdag, but do not agree on who should be part of a new government.
Norlén will now have to appoint a new candidate to hold further exploratory talks on the new government.
'Sanctions must not be lifted,' Zelenskyy says, as he says Russia's attacks come 'in response to signals from US'
Oh, and we have just heard from Zelenskyy again, doubling down on his criticism of Russia and attributing its latest attacks to “signals from the US.”
Responding to a “horrific” drone attack on a supermarket in Odesa, he said:
“Russia continues its bloody terror. The store was partially destroyed, and cars were damaged. Three people were injured. All necessary emergency services are working at the scene and providing assistance to those affected. It is important that our partners help us defend against this. Residential buildings, stores, energy and other critical infrastructure are under attack virtually nonstop. Not a single hour of peace.”
Crucially, he continued:
“What is happening is Russia’s pointed response to the signals it is receiving from America. Unfortunately, there are dangerous signals about the possibility of further sanctions relief. These sanctions were imposed by the world, by America, Europe, and our partners in response to Russia’s aggression against Ukraine and its war against us. Nothing has changed. The war has not stopped. The sanctions must not be lifted. Russia must end the slaughter it itself started and has continued for 1,695 days now. More money to fund the killing will not help bring this about. Strength is what is needed, and America is stronger than Russian terror.”
US effort to get Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire collapses
Andrew Roth
in Kyiv
The White House’s unilateral effort to negotiate an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine has collapsed as Moscow sent a record swarm of drones overnight to attack infrastructure in central Ukraine and Kyiv appeared to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries – despite warnings from Donald Trump.
Zelenskyy said on Wednesday that he would resume strikes on Russian oil refineries after halting those attacks to show that Ukraine was ready for peace talks. “The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” he told the Financial Times. He also attacked the gap in US intelligence sharing as “dangerous”.
Images from Ryazan showed flames at the refinery, which regional officials said had been targeted by 69 drones and four Flamingo cruise missiles. Debris from a drone struck by anti-aircraft fire had hit the refinery and sparked the fire, the ministry claimed.
In Ukraine, more than 360 Russian drones targeted Kirovohrad, a central region that has been hit less hard than others closer to Russia, in attacks that killed three and injured six.
“The enemy deliberately hit critical infrastructure, transport enterprises, logistics facilities and residential homes,” the regional governor, Andriy Raikovych, said in a statement.
'We need honesty from our partners about this war,' Zelenskyy says
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy offered an update on last night’s Russian attacks on Ukraine.
“Emergency services are still providing assistance in dozens of our cities and communities. Repair crews and rescuers are working to deal with the aftermath of Russian attacks. For practically all of yesterday and throughout last night, a massive shahed attack was under way. The drones kept coming in waves, and there was not a single hour when our skies were clear of them.”
He said “more than 850” drones were sent against Ukraine, “at a time when the speed of our defence capabilities is being artificially restricted.”
He added:
“It is obvious that Russia deliberately chose to escalate its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine. Russia exploits every such opportunity and must be held accountable for what it does. Strong decisions are needed to end this war. Ukraine needs steady support, above all in defending our skies.
We need HONESTY from our partners about this war: It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war, and guarantee security.”
Seven people missing after fire on vessel in Black Sea off Romania
Just as the leaders sit down at the big table in Brussels, Romania has said that seven people are still missing after a fire on a vessel in Romanian territorial waters of the Black Sea.
Suspected Russian drones have hit several ships off Romania and neighbouring Bulgaria since last week in a spillover from the Ukraine war, AFP reported.
Romanian authorities did not say whether a drone caused the fire on the vessel, named as the Wine Trader, which reported a blaze at around 7am, approximately 13 nautical miles southeast of the Romanian city of Sulina.
“Whether it was struck by a drone or not, an investigation is currently underway,” defence minister Radu Miruță told the Digi24 television channel.
The Romanian Naval Authority said in a statement there were 12 people on board the vessel, AFP reported.
Eight crew were initially reported as missing.
“Five of the sailors on board the Wine Trader have been rescued, a further seven people are still missing,” the Naval Authority said in an update.
EU will voice dismay and 'regret' over the US diesel deal with Russia
Jennifer Rankin
in Brussels
EU leaders will voice dismay over Donald Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel.
“The European Council regrets the United States’ decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel,” states a draft statement seen by the Guardian to be issued by the 27 leaders when the two-day summit concludes on Friday.
Other leaders, such as Sweden’s Ulf Kristersson, were blunter in their assessment of the deal (9.36).
But EU leaders tread a fine line between their obvious dislike of Trump’s actions towards Russia and dependence on US military support.
That balancing act was epitomised by comments from Estonia’s prime minister, Kristen Michal.
He recalled that the US was one of three Nato nuclear-armed partners supporting his country and described the US as “strong allies” (the others are the UK and France).
He referenced Nato’s help when Estonia faced hybrid attacks and other threats, such as the cutting of cables, Russian fighter jet incursions and drones.
“This kind of help came from Nato and we still have Nato ships on the sea guarding our critical infrastructure. So, [based] on that I must say that Nato is working well and the US is a partner in Nato. And Trump has assured us and everybody else last time in Ankara that he is following Nato and also Article 5 [on collective defence]. So we rely on them – and also sometimes even good friends need a reminder what is right.”
We should put pressure on Russia, not Ukraine, EU's foreign policy chief says
EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas acknowledged that the EU and the US had “definitely different approach to this war,” as she said Europeans believe “we should squeeze Russia, not Ukraine, to surrender and end this war.”
Responding to the US diesel deal with Russia, she said:
“The majority of Russia’s funding for the war comes from oil revenues. Clearly, Ukraine wants this war to stop, and that’s why … cutting off the funding for the war is the way to do it.
We see that we should squeeze … Russia, not Ukraine, to surrender to end this war.”
She added that the EU has adopted a new round of sanction listings earlier this week, as “this is the only way to put pressure on Russia.”
She also said that it’s important to send a clear message to Russia that “all these things they are interested in – [unfreezing] frozen assets, lifting the sanctions – are actually up to Europeans to decide.”
“And these things are not given for free for them,” she said.
Germany's Merz calls for stronger support for Ukraine, but warns of 'very, very difficult' budget talks
Germany’s Friedrich Merz also focused on the budget talks, saying they remain “very, very difficult” and expecting them to run well into December.
On Ukraine, he warned that “we are witnessing an increasingly ruthless wave of attacks by Russia,” and said that “we must do everything possible to support Ukraine not just through the winter, but into next year as well.”
“It remains my firm conviction that we are not merely defending Ukraine’s territorial integrity; we are defending the political order of Europe, which is being subjected to intense pressure by Russia in every respect.”
Hungary’s Péter Magyar focused on other issues in his doorstep statement, particularly on migration and the next EU budget.
But he welcomed the much-awaited law reform in Ukraine that could resolve a longstanding dispute over the rights of the Hungarian minority in western Ukraine, which until now threatened to bloc Kyiv’s accession path.
Magyar will hold a one-on-one with Ukraine’s Zelenskyy tomorrow, his first since ousting Viktor Orbán and coming into power earlier this year.
Ireland's Martin urges Europe to 're-engage' with US, but also calls for 'practical' support for Ukraine with EU accession prospects
Ireland’s Micheál Martin urged Europe to “re-engage” with the US and figure out the best way forward, despite tensions over Ukraine.
“We have had moments in the past when there were challenges and difficulties in respect of this, and it was retrieved by good outreach and engagement from Europe with the US, and I have no doubt that will continue.”
But he said the focus should also be on what the EU can do itself, and that’s primarily to do with advancing Ukraine’s accession process to the bloc.
“I would say to my colleagues across Europe that now is the time to be ambitious over the next number of months to open all clusters in respect of Ukraine and Moldova. The people of Ukraine need that as a very strong signal, given the extraordinary pressure they are under from the Russian attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure.”
He said “the most fundamental thing we can do in Europe now is to recommit to opening all clusters in respect of Ukraine’s application.” “That would send a powerful signal to the people of Ukraine that Europe is really progressing its pathway to accession,” he said.
The recent attacks are “appalling and horrific, and it illustrates that Putin is not interested in peace.”
“That’s why we must manifest our support for Ukraine in the practical ways … and certainly the membership agenda is one of those.”
'We very much regret this agreement on diesel,' Sweden's Kristersson says
Sweden’s Ulf Kristersson also offered his backing for Ukraine, as he criticised Donald Trump’s diesel deal with Russia.
“We very much regret this agreement on diesel. It’s obviously not a very big part, but still, it’s in the wrong direction. And every step now to help the Russians to increase their the financing of the war is a bad sign.
So we very much stick to Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s view on this.”
This 'senseless war of aggression' only continues because of Putin, Dutch PM says
EU leaders are now arriving for the European Council summit in Brussels and understandably they get asked about the latest situation in Ukraine.
Dutch PM Rob Jetten offered his strong backing for Ukraine and president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, saying “there is only one reason why this senseless war of aggression is continuing, and that’s because Putin chooses to do so.”
“He is the one that can end this war by starting negotiations for just and lasting peace. And as long as he doesn’t, the Ukrainians will have to defend themselves and defend European values, and we stand shoulder to shoulder with the Ukrainians.”
He urged other leaders “to do more financially, militarily, and non-militarily, because a lot of European countries are lagging behind in the support for Ukraine.”
“So let’s step up our game and make sure that they can win this senseless war.”
Starlink satellite restrictions highlight Europe's dependency on US technology
As Ukraine reported problems with Starlink satellite internet terminals and US data that warns of Russian ballistic missile attacks, Kyiv also faced the harsh reality that its European allies cannot offer any ready-made alternatives, Reuters reported.
European countries have voiced strong support for Ukraine and Zelenskyy. But the problems with vital data highlighted that Ukraine and Europe depend heavily on US systems for both low-orbit satellite communications – provided by SpaceX via Starlink – and space-based infrared sensing that feeds into early-warning systems.
A US satellite constellation called the Space-Based Infrared System provides early missile warnings.
As for Starlink, Europe does not have a ready-made alternative that Ukrainian soldiers could attach to their drones, although European governments and companies are working on long-term options.
Shares in European satellite operator Eutelsat soared on Wednesday following news of Ukraine’s difficulties with Starshield, fuelled by investor bets that European providers could benefit from growing strains between Washington and Kyiv.
Morning opening: Musk suggests US government was behind Starlink restrictions
Billionaire tech mogul Elon Musk has suggested that the US government could be behind the decision to restrict the speed of SpaceX’s satellite-technology used by Ukraine’s military.
In a post of X, he appeared to suggest the Trump administration was behind the move, which Ukraine says restricts its ability to use key defensive weapons.
Musk said:
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.
Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”
In further posts overnight, reacting to Zelenskyy’s comments on his relationship with Donald Trump, Musk went further and appeared to suggest Zelenskyy should leave the post, saying it’s “time to go.”
In a TV interview with Piers Morgan, Zelenskyy said he felt “betrayed” by Trump’s decisions and worried about “losing a strong partner,” playing a critical role across Ukraine’s defence.
For what it’s worth, Trump denied that his administration had cut intelligence sharing on Tuesday, but Zelenskyy said in an interview with US broadcaster NPR, aired on Wednesday, that military advisers had received threats from the US that intelligence sharing could be limited in the future.
The issue is likely to come up again today and tomorrow as EU leaders meet in Brussels for key political talks on the future.
With today’s discussions focused on the bloc’s internal matters, including the EU’s next budget, Ukraine is expected to come up on Friday when Zelenskyy joins other leaders in Brussels. But the ongoing crisis in Ukraine’s relations with the US risks overshadowing the entire meeting.
I will bring you all the updates throughout the day.
It’s Thursday, 15 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia’s billions in arms fail to buy security
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia’s billions in arms fail to buy security
TEHRAN - Saudi Arabia spends tens of billions of dollars on arms every year, but is struggling to protect key assets such as airports, refineries and pipelines from missiles and drones fired by Ansarallah, also called the Yemeni Armed Forces (YAF).
Despite acquiring state-of-the-art weapons systems from the United States and Europe and possessing multi-layered air defenses, the kingdom has seen deadly attacks on the main airport serving the capital, Riyadh, over the past week.
Saudi Arabia spent $83 billion on defense last year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, putting it firmly among the top ten military spenders worldwide. It has acquired U.S. fighter jets as well as Patriot and THAAD air defense systems, and a range of advanced weaponry from France and the United Kingdom.
Ansarallah have learned to combine ballistic and cruise missiles with long-range drones to overwhelm Saudi defenses. The approach resembles Russia’s playbook: Moscow has frequently used a mass of drones along with cruise and ballistic missiles in barrages against Ukraine.
Cruise missiles fly at lower altitudes, making them harder to identify and track. Ansarallah have also introduced a new generation of ballistic missiles that are maneuverable.
No single air defense system can guarantee that every incoming threat will be intercepted.
Experts note that the latest Ansarallah missiles, such as the Hatem-2 and the Palestine-2, are fast and accurate.
Last year, an Ansarallah missile evaded Israel’s vaunted air defenses and impacted near Ben Gurion airport. Analyst Amir Bar Shalom told CNN at the time: “They were very accurate, and to be very accurate if you’re launching from 2,000 kilometers, it’s impressive.”
Pandora’s box opened in March 2015
Saudi Arabia’s de facto leader, Mohammed bin Salman, opened Pandora’s box in March 2015 when he ordered an attack on Ansarallah in support of Yemen’s government, which was aligned with Riyadh. At the time, he vowed that Saudi Arabia would crush Ansarallah within weeks. Despite receiving logistical and intelligence support from the United States, the war against Ansarallah turned into a humiliating ordeal for the Saudi kingdom.
Seven years of conflict with Saudi Arabia -- from 2015 to 2022 -- caused immense suffering in Ansarallah-controlled parts of Yemen, and an economic and transport embargo has continued since.
Ultimately, that led Ansarallah in July to declare they would attack Saudi shipping in the Red Sea – and the campaign of missile strikes began soon afterwards, initially targeting an Aramco oil refinery on the Red Sea coast and Saudi airbases.
Ansarallah are demanding an end to Saudi airstrikes in support of its proxies in Yemen, as well as billions of dollars in compensation from Saudi Arabia.
Iran has offered to mediate between Riyadh and Ansarallah. On Monday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran was ready to provide “any assistance necessary to facilitate the start of talks between Saudi Arabia and Yemen.”
Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of Ansarallah’s political bureau, said on Monday that Riyadh had accepted mediation but Ansarallah had rejected truce proposals of two weeks and of one month.
“The battle this time is not like its predecessors; the arena is no longer the same arena,” al-Bukhaiti said. “Every day that passes in this battle will expand its scope and deepen its losses, and the settlement that is possible today may become difficult or impossible tomorrow.”
Escalation, through even more intense airstrikes, would bring the risk of further missile attacks that would undermine the goal of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to make Saudi Arabia a world-class destination for investment, technology and tourism.
The stakes extend beyond the oil industry. Data centers, desalination plants and airports underpin the kingdom’s technology ambitions, water supply and tourism economy. The crown prince’s marquee investment event in Riyadh later this month will put his pitch to international investors in the spotlight.
But major corporations shied away this week from the World Petroleum Congress in Riyadh.
Defeating Ansarallah forces through a ground offensive involving Saudi-backed Yemeni forces seems highly unlikely. Ansarallah forces are entrenched, battle-hardened and know the mountainous terrain. They have inflicted heavy losses on the Saudi-backed forces in the last month.
Last year, the U.S. spent more than $1 billion on a seven-week campaign of air-strikes against them. They eventually agreed not to attack U.S. shipping in the Red Sea but remained very much in place – and in the meantime shot down a number of highly advanced U.S. Reaper drones.
If anything, Ansarallah, who may have as many as 350,000 men under arms, are on the front foot. They have now encircled the city of Taiz, Yemen’s third largest and a vital logistical hub, the Institute for the Study of War said on Monday.
The Saudis are seeking to mobilize an international coalition against Ansarallah. Regional allies have offered help in the way of defensive systems. Pakistan has sent thousands of troops to help defend the kingdom. Egypt has offered whatever support is asked for.
The Saudis may also be able to procure more air defense systems from Europe and the U.S., after running down shipments delivered at the start of the war against Iran.
But the U.S. itself is short of such systems. A report by the U.S. Defense Department’s Inspector-General said the campaign against Iran had “resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply.”
And with mid-term elections three weeks away, Donald Trump is wary of yet another entanglement in the Middle East. He has been non-committal about direct U.S. strikes against Ansarallah, while not ruling them out.
“U.S. reluctance to get involved stokes the perception that the United States has abandoned a partner at its moment of greatest need,” according to Michael Ratney at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington.
Writing before the airport strikes, Ratney – a former ambassador in Riyadh – added: “The kingdom is under attack, and as a political matter, it has to retaliate. But ultimately, we should expect a return to diplomacy – imperfect, unsatisfying diplomacy that nonetheless deescalates the conflict.”
Analysts believe that wealthy Saudi Arabia should swallow its pride and engage in serious dialogue with Ansarallah, whose power has grown despite years of hardship and conflict. Riyadh should have realized by now that security cannot be bought through alliances with Western powers or the purchase of billions of dollars’ worth of advanced Western weaponry, particularly from the United States.

articles.title: ‘Putin Is Laughing’ – Zelensky Calls Trump’s Russian Diesel Deal a Victory for Moscow
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky described US President Donald Trump’s Russian diesel deal as a victory for Vladimir Putin, warning that Moscow was exploiting Washington’s decisions to pressure Ukraine into concessions.
In a wide-ranging interview with British broadcaster Piers Morgan on Wednesday, Oct. 14, Zelensky criticized Starlink restrictions that he said had cost Ukrainian lives.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Morgan ended the interview with a direct appeal to Trump, comparing Putin to Adolf Hitler and warning against appeasement.
The interview took place during Zelensky’s visit to Britain for meetings with Prime Minister Andy Burnham and King Charles III, amid renewed Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and growing tensions between Kyiv and Washington.
‘Putin is laughing’ – Trump’s diesel deal hands Moscow a victory
Morgan questioned Trump’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel amid rising energy prices linked to the war involving Iran, arguing that the deal would have little impact on US fuel prices.
Zelensky agreed, describing the arrangement as a tactical victory for Putin.
“Now Putin is laughing,” he said, suggesting that the Kremlin was gaining concessions from Washington even as Russia struggled on the battlefield.
Zelensky said the diesel agreement and restrictions affecting Starlink had handed Putin victories without requiring Russian forces to achieve military breakthroughs.
Morgan suggested Trump might be seeking to deflect public anger over rising gasoline prices ahead of the US midterm elections.
King Charles Welcomes Zelensky as Britain Steps Up Military Support for Ukraine
Zelensky acknowledged that domestic political pressures could be influencing Washington, but said Russia was also trying to exploit the situation to force Ukraine into concessions.
He warned that Moscow was looking for ways to force Ukrainian troops out of Donbas without defeating them militarily.
Zelensky also suggested that Russia was offering Washington potential business ventures and economic projects to influence its decisions.
He insisted that the real cause of rising fuel prices was the conflict in the Middle East and disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, not Ukraine’s strikes against Russian energy infrastructure.
‘We’re losing America – but not because of us’
Asked how he reacted to Trump’s diesel agreement, Zelensky expressed deep disappointment.
“It’s a pity that we are losing. We are losing a strong partner,” he said.
“You think you’re losing America?” Morgan asked.
“Yeah. But not because of us,” Zelensky replied.
The Ukrainian president stressed that Kyiv could not sacrifice its sovereignty to maintain Washington’s support.
“We can’t be weak. Otherwise we can’t survive… We are not selling our country. Look, guys. It’s not about business for us. It’s just our life, and this is our country.”
He described Ukraine as the home of its people and children, rather than something that could be traded in negotiations.
“That’s why it’s painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side,” Zelensky said.
He argued that Trump could remain a neutral mediator, but should not move toward Moscow.
“We are okay that he’s in the middle. But if you’re in the middle, you have to stay in the middle, not on the wrong side.”
Zelensky questioned the advice Trump was receiving.
“I think his advisors are wrong. I don’t know who is pushing him not to the right side… This is not the right side of history.”
Morgan also quoted Trump supporter Laura Loomer, who questioned why Moscow was not being held accountable for violating the energy ceasefire.
Loomer had described Putin as the “Hitler of our time.”
Asked whether he agreed, Zelensky replied: “Absolutely.”
But he challenged the perception that Putin was overwhelmingly powerful.
“He’s not so strong as [he is] evil, I think. But people are afraid of him,” Zelensky said.
He argued that the United States was stronger than Russia and had the power to stop Moscow’s aggression.
“The United States is stronger... and they have to be on our side.”
Zelensky said Putin’s strength depended on how far other countries allowed him to go.
“He’s strong till the world will stop him.”
‘Russia wants Trump to be weak’
Asked what message he would send directly to the US president, Zelensky began by thanking Trump and the American people for their support.
But he warned that Russia was deliberately undermining Trump’s authority.
“He has to understand that Russia wants him to be weak,” Zelensky said.
He characterized Moscow’s continued bombardment of Ukrainian energy infrastructure after Trump’s ceasefire announcement as an act directed against the American president himself.
Morgan suggested Russia was openly mocking Trump.
“They’re mocking him, aren’t they?”
“Absolutely,” Zelensky replied.
Morgan argued that Russia was demonstrating its disregard for Trump’s demands by continuing to launch missiles and drones against Ukraine.
Zelensky said the Kremlin cared far more about destroying Ukraine than about American political considerations.
“They hate Americans. It’s absolutely clear,” he said.
Zelensky said Ukraine supported Trump’s proposed energy ceasefire even though Kyiv had not been informed before the US president announced it.
“We need our people to live, to go through this winter and to stop the war,” he explained.
According to Zelensky, Ukraine refrained from striking Russian energy infrastructure for three days and did not immediately retaliate when Moscow resumed attacks.
“We didn’t attack during three days any kind of energy objects,” he said. “We didn’t respond.”
He recalled warning American officials that Russia would take advantage of the arrangement.
“They will attack energy. They will do it.”
Russia subsequently launched another massive barrage, including approximately 40 ballistic missiles aimed at Ukrainian energy infrastructure, Zelensky said.
Morgan noted that Ukrainian defenses intercepted only four of the ballistic missiles, leaving dozens to penetrate the country’s defenses.
Zelensky argued that Moscow was exploiting the ceasefire rather than honoring it.
Starlink restrictions – ‘We are professionals, we know what’s going on’
Zelensky also criticized restrictions affecting Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite communications system during Russian attacks.
He said Ukrainian forces lost connectivity around 1 a.m., affecting interceptor drones used to destroy incoming Russian Shaheds.
Morgan asked whether the restrictions had been imposed deliberately.
“I’m sure that they knew what they did. Absolutely. Because it was 1 a.m.,” Zelensky replied.
He said Ukrainian soldiers attempted to contact SpaceX, American generals and other US partners after discovering the disruption.
“We are professionals. We understand what’s going on. If you are losing the speed of Starlink, we understand what’s going on. So they switched off. That’s their decision,” Zelensky said.
The Ukrainian president stressed that Starlink was not used solely for offensive missions.
“It’s not just about attack. As I said, we didn’t attack their energy. It’s also about defending the lives.”
Asked whether he was angry with Musk, Zelensky described the restrictions as a serious mistake.
“I don’t know, him or somebody pushed him to... I don’t know really,” he said.
But he warned that disruptions to air defenses were already having deadly consequences.
“People are dying because of his decision.”
Zelensky urged the restoration of full connectivity, while acknowledging that a major technical problem remained a possibility.
“I hope that it’s a mistake, maybe huge technical problem, I don’t know,” he said.
He also emphasized that European countries, including Poland, had paid for the Starlink services used by Ukraine.
The operational restrictions have been confirmed by Ukrainian officials, although responsibility for ordering them remains disputed.
US missile warnings also disrupted
Zelensky said Ukraine was facing another serious problem: interruptions in intelligence warnings from the US about incoming Russian ballistic missiles.
“It’s two big problems,” he said, distinguishing between Starlink connectivity and advance missile intelligence.
American officials had attributed the intelligence disruptions to technical difficulties, Zelensky said, but the problems continued during Russian attacks.
Without timely warnings, Ukrainian civilians have less opportunity to reach shelters before ballistic missiles strike.
Trump has denied suspending American intelligence-sharing with Ukraine.
Despite Russia’s continued strikes against Ukrainian cities, Zelensky said Putin was suffering enormous military losses.
“Putin, he’s losing at the battlefield.”
He estimated that Russia was suffering approximately 43,000 casualties each month. Of those, Zelensky said approximately 20,000 to 25,000 were being killed monthly.
Asked how Ukrainian losses compared, he described a casualty ratio of approximately one Ukrainian for every seven to ten Russians.
Zelensky also said Ukraine had approximately five or six wounded soldiers for every soldier killed, while Russia’s casualty ratio was closer to 50–50 between killed and wounded.
“For them it’s nothing, for us it’s important,” he said.
Zelensky maintained that Ukrainian forces had stabilized the front despite continued Russian offensives and argued that Moscow was seeking political victories because it was struggling to achieve decisive battlefield gains.
Trump wants Zelensky replaced – ‘No Trump, no Musk can choose our president’
Morgan played a recording of Trump calling for Ukraine to replace Zelensky with someone willing to negotiate a deal with Russia.
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal,” Trump said. “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
Morgan asked whether Trump was attempting to force Zelensky from office.
Zelensky recalled that Russia had already occupied Crimea and parts of Donbas before he became president in 2019.
He argued that replacing Ukraine’s leader would not resolve Russia’s aggression.
“No Trump, no Musk, nobody in the world can choose the president… in other countries,” he said.
Zelensky stressed that only Ukrainians could choose their president and expressed confidence that whoever succeeded him would continue defending the country.
“I’m sure the new man or woman will defend our country. This is our home.”
‘I will never accept Ukrainian land as Russian land’
Morgan pressed Zelensky on whether a peace agreement could involve Ukraine formally surrendering territory to Russia.
Zelensky suggested that his refusal to recognize Russian sovereignty over occupied Ukrainian territory was one reason powerful figures might want him replaced.
“Some big guys want to change me, because I will never accept Ukrainian land as Russian land,” he said.
He nevertheless acknowledged that avoiding further loss of life was essential.
“I’m a realist, and I understand that people are more important than one kilometer or two kilometers.”
“It’s not about kilometers. I mean, this is about land and homes.”
He distinguished between acknowledging Russian occupation and legally recognizing the territory as Russian.
“Yes, it’s occupied, but this territory is occupied. It’s temporary.”
“These territories are Ukraine.”
Zelensky expressed confidence that Ukraine would eventually recover its occupied regions, potentially through diplomacy rather than further military offensives.
“In any way it will come back, but without weapon,” he said.
‘I’m not resigning’ – elections impossible during Russian attacks
Asked whether he intended to resign, Zelensky rejected the suggestion.
“No, of course. It’s my responsibility.”
He also said Ukraine could not hold a secure presidential election while Russian missiles and drones continued attacking the country.
“From the point of security, you can’t do elections.”
Zelensky stressed that Ukrainian service members on the front lines must be able to participate in any national vote.
“We can’t choose the president without soldiers, because they give and gave their lives.”
“They are first who have to vote, and I think it’s fair.”
Asked whether Ukrainian citizens supported him, Zelensky emphasized national unity.
“We are all Ukrainian people, and we are all on one side.”
“We have only one enemy: it’s Russia.” ‘We will not lose our independent country’ – even without America
Morgan asked whether Ukraine could prevail without US support.
Zelensky distinguished between preserving Ukraine’s independence and forcing Putin into negotiations.
“We will not in any way lose our independent country,” he said.
But he acknowledged that a diplomatic settlement would become much more difficult without Washington.
“We will have huge problems with how to push Putin to diplomatic way of ending this war – to negotiations.”
He praised European leaders, including Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and French President Emmanuel Macron, for their continued support.
Zelensky said Ukraine needed clear commitments from its partners on weapons, sanctions and funding.
“Putin will not win, will not prevail, 100%,” he declared.
‘Putin’s goal is total occupation of Ukraine’
Toward the end of the interview, Morgan asked whether Zelensky genuinely believed Ukraine could achieve victory.
Zelensky returned to what he described as Putin’s original objective.
“Putin’s goal is total occupation of Ukraine,” he said.
Asked what Ukraine wanted, Zelensky replied: “To stop this war, make peace, stay where we stay.”
He maintained that occupied Ukrainian territories remained Ukrainian and would eventually return.
“Everything will come back because we are a real country.”
He said that Russian political circumstances would eventually change and could create opportunities for the peaceful return of occupied land.
Morgan’s final warning to Trump: ‘Don’t appease Hitler’
Morgan concluded the interview by addressing Trump directly, telling him that siding with Putin against Ukraine would place Washington on the wrong side of history.
“It’s what we called in World War II appeasement to Hitler. Don’t be that guy,” Morgan warned. “Give this guy the support he needs to defeat the modern-day Hitler.”
Zelensky thanked Morgan and the British public, praising the United Kingdom for supporting Ukraine since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
He described Britain as a friend that had stood on the right side of history.
You can also highlight the text and press Ctrl + Enter

articles.title: North Korea fires two types of submarine-launched missiles
articles.body:
- North Korea said it test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles on Oct. 14, without Kim Jong Un attending.
- South Korean experts believe the missiles came from Hero Kim Kun Ok, marking the submarine’s first public missile launch since 2023.
North Korea test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles in the sea east of the Korean Peninsula on Oct. 14, state media said, in what South Korean analysts believe was the first missile launch from the Hero Kim Kun Ok, the submarine Pyongyang unveiled three years ago as its first “tactical nuclear attack submarine.”
The Korean Central News Agency reported on Oct. 15 that the country’s Missile Administration carried out the launches. It did not give flight times, distances or missile names, but released photographs of a submarine and of missiles climbing away on trails of flame. Based on those images, South Korean experts concluded the launch platform was the 3,000-ton-class Hero Kim Kun Ok.
“The test-fire aimed to examine the current mobilized posture of the underwater combat systems and contributed to getting the Navy skilled in performing its strategic missions,” KCNA said.
Kim Jong Un did not attend. Senior Workers’ Party official Kim Jong Sik and Missile Administration chief Jang Chang Ha oversaw the launches together with navy underwater weapons engineers, KCNA said, adding that the test had no adverse impact on the security of neighboring countries.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff did not announce the launches on Wednesday but said the next day that it had tracked the missiles from before launch through the end of their flights, using assets it declined to identify because of confidentiality arrangements with the United States. A JCS spokesperson said one missile was fired from a vertical launch tube and the other from a torpedo tube, Yonhap reported.
North Korea launched Hero Kim Kun Ok, hull number 841, on Sept. 6, 2023, with Kim Jong Un saying at the ceremony that arming the navy with nuclear weapons could not be delayed further. Despite its label, the boat is a diesel-electric submarine rebuilt from an old Soviet-designed Romeo-class hull; the “nuclear” designation refers to the nuclear-capable missiles it is meant to carry. Until this week, the submarine had not been publicly seen firing a weapon.
Some South Korean analysts told Korea JoongAng Daily that the two weapons may have been a longer-range Hwasal-2 and a shorter-range Pulhwasal-3-31, a missile with a reported range of up to 2,000 km (1,240 miles) that North Korea says can carry its Hwasan-31 tactical nuclear warhead. At that range, the missile could reach all of South Korea and U.S. military bases in Japan. One analyst quoted by the newspaper said firing two missile types with different speeds and approach paths at staggered times would make them harder for air defenses to intercept.
Cruise missiles fly low, often around 100 meters (330 feet) above the surface, which makes them harder to spot on radar than ballistic missiles. Unlike ballistic missile launches, cruise missile tests are not banned under United Nations Security Council sanctions on North Korea.
The previous submarine-launched cruise missile test North Korea reported came in January 2024, when Pulhwasal-3-31 missiles were fired from the smaller 2,000-ton-class experimental submarine 8.24 Yongung with Kim Jong Un watching. Earlier this week, North Korea also fired tactical ballistic missiles from the Pyongyang area toward the same sea.

articles.title: Volodymyr Zelenskyy feels ‘betrayed’ by Donald Trump over Starlink access
articles.body:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he feels personally betrayed by Donald Trump after it emerged that Ukraine’s military has had its access to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite squeezed, raising doubts about long-term US support for Kyiv.
The Ukrainian president, on a visit to London, accused Trump of picking the other side after more than four years of war, risking a breakdown in relations already strained by the US agreeing to buy diesel from Moscow.
Ahead of a meeting with prime minister Andy Burnham in Downing Street, Zelenskyy appeared in a TV interview where he was asked whether the sudden restriction of Starlink was deliberate and if he felt betrayed by Trump.
“Really, yes … but it’s a little bit more complicated than just my emotions or my feelings,” the Ukrainian president replied, adding: “It’s a pity that we are losing, we are losing a strong partner.”
Overnight, Ukraine’s military reported that, without explanation, the Starlink satellite communications system, produced by Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, was no longer working at speeds greater than 100mph.
That effectively rendered most of the drones used by Ukraine to strike behind the frontlines inoperable – and, it later emerged, affected the most effective air defence system to stop Russian jet-powered attack drones bombing Kyiv.
“I am sure they knew what they did, absolutely. Because it was 1am at night, Starlink was blocked by SpaceX and the United States,” Zelenskyy said in an interview with Piers Morgan. “This decision will bring a lot of human losses … of course, people will die.”
The sudden outage came as Russia launched ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US for a second night. For years, the US has provided Ukraine with intelligence when strikes were about to take place.
Trump denied that his administration had cut intelligence sharing on Tuesday, but Zelenskyy said in an interview with US broadcaster NPR, aired on Wednesday, that military advisers had received threats from the US that intelligence sharing could be limited in the future.
The US president has demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries, which he has blamed for the high cost of diesel, although most analysts say the closure of the strait of Hormuz after the US-Israel attack on Iran has had a far larger impact on global energy prices.
The two leaders fell out in the spring of 2025 during a disastrous visit by Zelenskyy to the Oval Office, where the US president said: “You don’t have the cards” to win the war. The row was followed by a brief pause in intelligence sharing and a desperate scramble by European allies to calm the row.
Burnham met Zelenskyy in Downing Street on Wednesday, hours after he promised MPs that the Ukrainian president “would not leave empty-handed” and that he had tasked officials with drawing up further sanctions and options for speeding up military aid.
As the pair met at No 10, he promised that Britain’s support for Ukraine would remain constant. “You have seen the solidarity and the support you have got from everybody here in Britain. We are behind you and that will not change,” he said.
Zelenskyy had met King Charles in Buckingham Palace earlier on Wednesday.
In brief remarks to reporters, Zelenskyy said he hoped to raise access to Starlink and intelligence sharing in his meeting with the British prime minister.
Burnham pledged that he would accelerate the supply of British lightweight multi-role missiles to Ukraine, which the country uses to counter Russian drone strikes and said they were looking for “all possible avenues” of further support.
The prime minister also said he was prepared to discuss the ceasefire proposed by Trump on attacks on energy infrastructure but acknowledged that Moscow had not abided by it.
“Sadly, what we have seen from Russia is further attacks on critical national infrastructure in Ukraine,” he said.
Earlier Burnham told MPs at PMQs that he wanted to be “careful” about potential criticism of Trump that might risk exacerbating tensions, saying he was “laying the ground” for a reconciliation: “I will listen to President Zelenskyy carefully, but he won’t be going away from Britain today empty-handed.”
The UK is also set to give £17m in funding towards repairs to the protective roof over the destroyed Chornobyl nuclear power plant which was damaged by Russian drone strike last year.
The meeting, which lasted just over an hour, began as Burnham greeted Zelenskyy with a hug on Downing Street, before the pair walked to the door of No 10 and posed for photographs, flanked by Irish Guards in full ceremonial uniform.
Musk said the decision to curtail Starlink was not one made by him. The communications system is not directly licensed to clients who are using weapons, and the Ukrainian military was linked to a related network called Starshield, which is operated by the US government.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk said, referring to Trump.
Terminals travelling at more than 100mph and using a version of Starlink for the military and other national security agencies suddenly lost connectivity, said Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser on military technology to Zelenskyy, in what appeared to be a targeted outage meant to disrupt military operations.
“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” said Beskrestnov, who is also a popular military blogger. “It’s clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation.”
Limiting Starlink’s access speeds would have a significant effect on Ukraine’s air defences because it is being used, according to Beskrestnov, in “the most current effective solution”: interceptors that target the jet-powered Shahed drones now deployed in large numbers to bomb Ukraine.
“With their actions, our partners are depriving us of one of the few chances we have to defend ourselves,” he added in a follow-up post. Shahed interception rates had already dropped from more than 90% to about 60% when Russia upgraded its engines to jet power in the early summer.
It also complicates Ukraine’s use of medium-range, mid-strike drones for hitting targets in its territories occupied by Russia. But, ironically, it would have no impact on Ukraine’s deep strike bombing of oil refineries because Kyiv is banned from using Starlink to hit targets inside of Russia.
Russia carried out a massive strike against Ukrainian energy infrastructure late on Tuesday evening, Zelenskyy said, launching 39 ballistic missiles and 120 attack drones against Kyiv and Kharkiv. The strikes hit five big power plants, key substations and other infrastructure that sustains major cities including Kyiv.
At least 600,000 people were now without power, he said, adding that outages could become more widespread.
Trump last week announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine that has not been confirmed. Zelenskyy said he had not heard of the deal until Trump announced it on his Truth Social site, and the Kremlin on Wednesday claimed it was abiding by the ceasefire because Trump had not specified which energy infrastructure it included.
Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin’s spokesperson, told reporters: “The energy truce proposed by Trump was not specified in detail, so it cannot be claimed that Russia is failing to observe it.”

articles.title: Could Israeli technology aid Saudi Arabia's struggles to stop Houthi missile attacks? - analysis
articles.body:
Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on October 8, 10, and 11 killed at least 16 people. The deadliest strike, on October 10, killed 12 people and injured 309 others. On October 13, another attack damaged an administrative building at Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran. Saudi forces have intercepted numerous incoming weapons, but others have reached their targets despite the billions of dollars the kingdom has spent on air defenses.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Why are missiles and drones still getting through, and could Israeli technology help Saudi Arabia stop them?
Israel has spent decades developing defenses against different types of aerial threats. Some have already been supplied to the United Arab Emirates. In May, US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee confirmed that Israel had sent Iron Dome batteries and personnel to help defend the UAE against Iranian attacks.
There have also been reports of Saudi-Israeli discussions about sharing intelligence through American military channels. Neither government has confirmed such an arrangement, but it raises the possibility of cooperation that would have been politically difficult to imagine only a few years ago.
Why are Saudi defenses struggling?
Saudi Arabia operates American-made Patriot missile batteries and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD), which is designed to intercept ballistic missiles at high altitude. The kingdom’s first THAAD battery became operational in July 2025, according to the Saudi Press Agency.
These systems provide substantial protection, but the Houthis have weapons designed to exploit different weaknesses.
Ballistic missiles climb high into the atmosphere before descending at high speed toward their targets. Cruise missiles fly more like pilotless aircraft, sometimes close enough to the ground to escape radar detection until late in their flight. Drones can be smaller, slower, and much less expensive than the missiles used to shoot them down.
A defender facing multiple weapon types at once must identify each threat, choose the right interceptor, and respond before the weapons reach their targets.
A 2020 study by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, The Missile War in Yemen, documented the Houthis’ growing arsenal of missiles and drones, developed with Iranian assistance, and their repeated attacks on Saudi territory.
The Houthis have since improved their capabilities. Regional officials told the Associated Press that investigators believe drones were launched ahead of cruise and ballistic missiles during the recent attack on Riyadh’s airport. If confirmed, the sequence would suggest an attempt to stretch Saudi defenses by presenting several threats in quick succession.
The kingdom has faced similar problems before.
After the September 2019 attacks on the Abqaiq and Khurais oil facilities, Washington Institute for Near East Policy researchers Michael Knights and Conor Hiney examined gaps in Saudi radar coverage and weaknesses in the coordination of its defenses.
The weapons appeared to approach from the north, while much of Saudi Arabia’s defensive posture was oriented toward threats from the east. Low-flying missiles and drones could take advantage of radar blind spots created by terrain, the curvature of the Earth, and the limitations of individual sensors.
The researchers recommended better coordination among existing radars, command systems, and interceptors, rather than relying solely on additional missile batteries.
Saudi Arabia’s geography presents another problem. The kingdom covers nearly 2.15 million square kilometers, approximately 78 times the combined land area of Israel and the West Bank. Its cities, airports, refineries, oil fields, military bases, and ports are scattered across enormous distances.
Israel’s much smaller geographic area lets some defensive systems cover several population centers or installations. Saudi Arabia needs far more widely distributed equipment, even though large stretches of sparsely populated desert do not require the same protection as major cities or oil facilities.
Cost is another concern. An inexpensive drone can force defenders to fire an interceptor worth hundreds of thousands or even millions of dollars.
Dr. Sidharth Kaushal of Britain’s Royal United Services Institute discussed the depletion of Gulf interceptor stocks and the difficulty of replacing them quickly in an April 2026 BBC interview. The Financial Times reported this week that Saudi Arabia was struggling with interceptor shortages and ongoing gaps in radar coverage.
Interception does not always prevent casualties. On October 13, debris from intercepted cruise missiles injured four people and damaged 15 homes in Riyadh, according to Saudi Civil Defense.
Which Israeli systems could help?
Israel’s air defenses rely on several systems that operate at different ranges and altitudes. Iron Dome is the best known, but other Israeli weapons may be better suited to some of the threats Saudi Arabia faces.
Iron Dome was developed to intercept short-range rockets. Its radar tracks incoming projectiles and calculates where they are likely to land, allowing the system to focus on threats to populated areas or key installations.
Upgrades have expanded its ability to engage drones and cruise missiles. Iron Dome batteries could protect individual Saudi sites, but their coverage is too limited to defend much of the kingdom’s territory.
David’s Sling, developed jointly by Israel and the United States, is designed to intercept cruise missiles, certain ballistic missiles, aircraft, and drones. Tests conducted in February 2026 included improvements intended to address newer aerial threats.
Arrow 2 and Arrow 3 are intended mainly for ballistic missiles. Arrow 3 can intercept suitable targets outside the atmosphere, before they descend toward the ground. Israel has used Arrow-family defenses against missiles launched from Iran and Yemen.
Such systems could strengthen Saudi Arabia’s ballistic-missile defenses, but they would not solve the problem of detecting and intercepting a small drone approaching an airport at low altitude.
Two less familiar Israeli products could be especially useful for defending individual installations.
Rafael’s mobile SPYDER system is designed to engage aircraft, drones, and cruise missiles. Israel Aerospace Industries manufactures Barak MX, which uses different interceptors against aircraft, drones, cruise missiles, and some ballistic threats.
Either could potentially complement Saudi Arabia’s existing defenses around oil facilities, airports, or military bases, provided the equipment could be integrated into the kingdom’s command and radar networks.
Iron Beam offers a different approach. Instead of firing an interceptor missile, it uses a powerful laser to destroy certain short-range threats. Israel delivered its first operational system to the military in December 2025.
The attraction is partly financial: Firing a laser can cost far less than using a missile against a relatively inexpensive drone.
Its limitations are substantial, particularly in Saudi Arabia. Lasers need a clear line of sight, and dust, haze, clouds, and distance can reduce their effectiveness. They cannot replace longer-range defenses against ballistic missiles.
Israel also operates C-Dome, a naval adaptation of Iron Dome that could help protect ships and offshore installations.
Which systems would be most useful to Saudi Arabia would depend on the targets it wanted to protect, the weapons it expected to face, and the equipment it already possessed.
How has Israel helped defend the UAE?
The United Arab Emirates offers the clearest example of Israeli air defense technology being used by an Arab country.
After Houthi attacks on Abu Dhabi in early 2022, Israeli defense sources told Breaking Defense that an agreement to supply Rafael’s SPYDER system was nearing completion. The publication subsequently reported that an Israeli-made Barak air defense system had been deployed in the UAE, although the precise model was not identified.
The two countries had established diplomatic relations under the 2020 Abraham Accords, removing a major obstacle to military purchases.
Their cooperation reportedly expanded during the 2026 war involving Iran.
On May 12, Huckabee publicly confirmed that Israel had sent Iron Dome batteries and personnel to help operate them in the Emirates, according to the defense publication Janes.
The Financial Times reported that Israel had supplied additional equipment, including a version of Iron Beam, surveillance technology, and real-time intelligence about Iranian missile launches.
Those details have not all been independently confirmed. An October study by the International Institute for Strategic Studies discussed the reported laser and surveillance deployments but did not independently verify that they took place. Janes also noted that Huckabee’s remarks did not confirm those specific transfers.
There is no public accounting of how many incoming weapons were intercepted by Israeli systems operating in the UAE.
Still, the deployment of Iron Dome batteries and personnel establishes that the Israeli-Emirati defense relationship has moved beyond ordinary equipment sales. That experience may offer lessons for Saudi Arabia, although Riyadh has not normalized relations with Israel.
Could Saudi Arabia obtain Israeli assistance without normalizing relations?
Intelligence sharing would probably be easier to arrange than a weapons sale.
Information about missile launches and flight paths could potentially be relayed through American military channels, giving Saudi crews more time to prepare an interception without requiring Israeli launchers or personnel on Saudi territory.
Regional arrangements already support this kind of cooperation. In January 2026, US Central Command announced the establishment of a multinational air- and missile-defense coordination cell at Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar. It aims to improve information sharing, joint planning, and coordination among regional military partners.
Israeli media reports suggest that Saudi-Israeli intelligence cooperation may already be taking place.
In September, The Jerusalem Post reported, citing a regional diplomat, that the two countries had discussed intelligence assistance through US Central Command. Ynet and Israel Hayom also reported, citing diplomatic and security sources, that Israeli intelligence was reaching Saudi Arabia through American channels.
Neither government has publicly confirmed those accounts, and it is unclear what information, if any, is being shared.
The Media Line reported in September that senior military commanders from Israel, Saudi Arabia, and six other Middle Eastern countries had attended a US-organized security meeting in Germany. US Central Command confirmed the gathering, but it did not establish a formal military alliance.
Saudi political analyst Abdulaziz Alshaabani warned against assuming that such contacts would lead to open military cooperation.
“Any intelligence coordination would likely remain limited and pragmatic, while Riyadh continues to rely primarily on its own security mechanisms and broader regional frameworks,” Alshaabani told The Media Line.
Purchasing Israeli missile defenses would raise additional problems.
Israel would have to authorize the export, and Saudi Arabia would need arrangements for training, maintenance, software, spare parts, and replacement interceptors. Some Israeli systems would also require American approval because of US involvement in their development.
Germany’s purchase of Arrow 3, for example, required Washington’s consent.
Political considerations could be harder to overcome than the technical requirements.
Saudi Arabia has repeatedly insisted that diplomatic relations with Israel depend on the establishment of a Palestinian state. Its Foreign Ministry reiterated in February 2025 that it would not normalize relations without an independent Palestinian state with east Jerusalem as its capital.
A publicly acknowledged purchase of Israeli weapons would be considerably more difficult for Riyadh to explain than intelligence cooperation conducted through American military channels.
Saudi Arabia has not publicly announced an agreement to purchase Israeli missile defense systems, nor has it officially confirmed that negotiations for such a deal are underway.
Would Israeli technology solve the problem?
Israeli missile defense systems could strengthen Saudi Arabia’s defenses, but acquiring and deploying them would take time.
Saudi Arabia would need its own launchers, radars, trained crews, and interceptor supplies. Iron Dome batteries stationed in Israel are too far away to protect Riyadh. Any new equipment would also have to operate alongside the kingdom’s existing Patriot and THAAD systems.
Israel has its own shortages to consider after prolonged fighting with Iran and the Houthis. Its military needs to replenish interceptor stocks, which could limit the equipment available for export.
Saudi Arabia is also seeking assistance from established defense partners, including the US, Britain, France, Turkey, and Pakistan. Those relationships offer alternatives without the political complications of buying weapons from Israel.
Protecting civilians remains important even when interception fails. Reuters reported that Saudi Arabia stopped issuing public warnings of imminent attacks after September 29, leaving residents without official alerts before the deadly airport strikes. Warnings later resumed, including alerts issued by Saudi Civil Defense for Riyadh and Al-Kharj on October 14.
For Saudi Arabia, earlier warning of incoming attacks may be more immediately useful than new missile batteries. Better intelligence could help its existing defenses respond sooner, while new equipment would require procurement, deployment, and training.
A Saudi purchase of Israeli missile defenses would be a much bigger step, requiring decisions in Riyadh, Jerusalem, and possibly Washington. In the meantime, Saudi forces must defend widely separated cities and installations against missiles and drones that can approach from different directions, often with little warning.

articles.title: Hypersonic missiles highlight arms race on Korean Peninsula
articles.body:
Hypersonic missiles highlight arms race on Korean Peninsula
October 15, 2026
North Korea announced that it had tested two types of submarine-launched cruise missiles off its east coast on Wednesday — a day after the state-run Korean Central News Agency reported that leader Kim Jong Un had visited a new defense industry museum, where he admired an intercontinental ballistic missile reportedly capable of hitting targets in the continental United States.
The visit came five days after South Korean President Lee Jae-myung observed the test launch of his country's first domestically developed hypersonic missile.
South Korea's breakthrough came after Pyongyang announced a test on October 3 of what it described as a hypersonic intermediate-range missile that traveled 350 kilometers (220 miles) before striking its target.
"Comrade Kim Jong Un expressed the expectation and belief that all the nation's missile forces would remain faithful to their missions of defending the sovereignty and security of the republic in a responsible combat posture," the KCNA reported.
'Advanced conventional weapons'
Both North and South Korea are primarily racing to develop hypersonic technology because it offers a step-up in offensive capabilities at a time of worsening tensions in the Indo-Pacific region.
Hypersonic missiles are weapons that can travel at velocities of at least five times the speed of sound (Mach 5) or over 6,100 kilometers per hour.
Their speed makes it far harder for defenders to identify, track and destroy inbound missiles, which can carry conventional or nuclear warheads. Their additional advantage over previous generations of missiles is their ability to suddenly change course, dip or weave in flight, making interception significantly more difficult.
"There has been an arms race on the Korean Peninsula for many years and hypersonic weapons are just the latest manifestation of that," said Chris Green, Korea Peninsula analyst for Crisis Group International.
Hypersonic weapons have become a "priority for the South" as the North has ramped up its capabilities and forged military and economic ties with Russia, he said.
"And North Korea has nuclear weapons, but it would not be viable to use them as the threat has always been that doing so would mean that the US would turn the country to glass," he told DW.
"For the North, it is unsurprising that the geopolitics of the region have encouraged them to pursue advanced conventional weapons as they try to have dominance on the peninsula."
Pyongyang 'should not be underestimated'
And while it is impossible to confirm with any certainty that the weapons the North says it has developed have the capabilities they claim, Green said it would be a mistake to underestimate Pyongyang.
"We do not know their capabilities and it is possible this is all propaganda, but there is a long list of times the North's capabilities have been underestimated only to be shown that they can, in fact, do what they say."
Chun In-bum, a retired general in the South Korean army and now a senior fellow with the National Institute for Deterrence Studies, shares that assessment of the threat.
"It's anybody's guess whether they're telling the truth on this, but any prudent military planner should always assume the worst," he said.
The North's mastery of the advanced technology required to operate hypersonic missiles appears to have been sudden, although it remains unclear how it acquired the capability.
"They probably obtained the technology through illegal means," Chun said. "They snoop around firms in the US, South Korea and Japan for this sort of information, but they also do it to their 'friends.'"
Wherever the data came from, the fact that North Korea's hypersonic missiles appear to have performed as required should be cause for deep concern.
"A greater offensive capability increases the overall danger posed by the North, and if they have weapons that are harder to shoot down, then it is possible there are greater temptations to use them," Chun said.
"I'm speculating, of course, but I'm sure that we are looking at ways to neutralize this particular threat, but as I understand it there is no good answer right now," Chun added.
Canceling each other out?
Green, however, believes that both sides developing viable systems means that they may cancel each other out as a potent battlefield advantage.
"I do not think this changes the balance of power," he said. "The North still has its nuclear deterrent and this 'porcupine strategy' of being sharp and prickly in order to keep everyone else at arm's length. And it's not a game changer south of the Demilitarized Zone either," the expert added.
"It is clear, however, that if the North continues to develop its offensive systems and is able to deploy them in huge numbers, then there will have to be a conversation about greater missile defense not only in the South but also in Japan, and that will then raise some very difficult questions."
Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

articles.title: Musk Says US Government Controls Ukraine’s Starshield Limits as Zelensky Accuses Russia of Exploiting Outage
articles.body:
Elon Musk said on Wednesday, Oct. 14, that the US military – including US President Donald Trump himself, not SpaceX – decides speed limits on Ukraine’s military Starshield terminals.
His remarks came after restrictions imposed overnight on Oct. 13-14 disrupted Kyiv’s drone operations, particularly interceptor drones – among Ukraine’s few effective tools against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones, which are significantly harder to intercept due to their speed.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“It is clear that the Russians are trying to exploit problems with Starlink’s operation in Ukraine, as interceptor drones rely significantly on this connection,” President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a statement on Wednesday, after meeting with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham in London.
Speaking during an interview on “Piers Morgan Uncensored,” released on Wednesday, Zelensky said he feels betrayed by Trump and warned that SpaceX’s new Starlink restrictions will cost lives. “I’m sure they knew what they did,” he said regarding the outage.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said Starlink’s connectivity at speeds of up to 160 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour) is being restored. “Removing Starshield’s speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine’s defense,” he said in a post on X, thanking Musk for his “continued support.”
General Staff Reports 222 Clashes on Wednesday as Russia Continues Pressing Pokrovsk Axis
According to the latest estimates by Zelensky, Russia launched 124 drones overnight and another 145 during the day, with more than 40 Shaheds still in Ukraine’s airspace as he wrote.
UK fast-tracks missiles against jet-powered drones
Zelensky said he and Burnham agreed to speed up deliveries of British air defense systems to counter the jet-powered drones, which fly faster and higher than older Shahed models.
Earlier on Wednesday, The British government said it would accelerate deliveries of Lightweight Multirole Missiles (LMMs), under a £45 million (approximately $60 million) surface-to-air missile package, bringing forward £10 million (approximately $13 million) to meet Ukraine’s urgent winter needs.
“My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer, we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace in Europe” Burnham said ahead of the meeting.
He has also tasked ministers with preparing new sanctions and further military and financial aid.
According to the BBC, Burnham greeted Zelensky at Downing Street with a military ceremonial guard – the first such honor for a foreign leader.
The visit followed a massive overnight strike in which Russia fired at least 39 missiles and 128 drones, cutting power to at least 600,000 people, according to Zelensky earlier in the day.
Questions over US intelligence sharing
The recent strains with Washington deepened after Ukraine received no early warning from Western partners about incoming Russian ballistic missiles for two nights in a row.
Zelensky said Kyiv’s systems detected the missiles only as they approached the capital.
Although NATO and EU, as well as Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said they had seen no sign that sharing had stopped, recent reports by other senior Ukrainian authorities appeared to suggest otherwise.
The lapse followed reports that Washington had threatened to cut intelligence sharing for Kyiv during roughly eight hours of talks in Miami on Friday, Oct. 9.
Reportedly, senior US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner warned Ukraine’s delegation that it could lose access to US intelligence if it kept striking Russian oil refineries.
Several US media separately reported that Trump’s administration also warned it could suspend the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) – a mechanism that enables European purchases of US weapons for Ukraine, the main channel for buying Patriot interceptors.
US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker denied the claims, saying that no change has been made.
On Oct. 9, Trump struck a diesel deal with Putin that eased US sanctions on Russian fuel, which 12 senators from both parties called “a betrayal of Ukraine” in a joint letter, urging the US President to rescind the diesel deal and enforce the new Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.
Around the same time, Trump criticized Zelensky and said it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
The US President then announced an energy truce on Oct. 11 that neither Kyiv nor Moscow confirmed, insisting the two sides agreed “because I said, ‘You agree.’”
