Although Ukraine abided by the abrupt ceasefire announcement, Russia continued striking Ukraine nationwide. On Wednesday, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that Trump’s energy truce was never defined, so Russia cannot be accused of breaking it.

articles.title: Why South Korea has fallen out with Ukraine but seeks reconciliation with North Korea: Korean expert explains
articles.body:
Why South Korea has fallen out with Ukraine but seeks reconciliation with North Korea: Korean expert explains
Just two weeks ago, relations between Ukraine and South Korea seemed almost trouble-free. Russia and North Korea were deepening their military cooperation, North Korean soldiers were fighting against Ukraine, and Kyiv and Seoul appeared to have an increasing number of shared security interests.
On 23 September, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha met his South Korean counterpart Cho Hyun in New York. They discussed strengthening political dialogue, trade, investment, Ukraine's reconstruction, and the common threats posed by military cooperation between Russia and North Korea.
The meeting was a continuation of an eventful year in bilateral relations. In July, Volodymyr Zelenskyy met South Korean President Lee Jae-myung for the first time. Seoul announced an additional US$100 million in non-military assistance to Ukraine. Economic cooperation also held considerable potential: a framework agreement between the two countries provided for up to US$2.1 billion in preferential South Korean loans for Ukraine's reconstruction by 2029.
But on that very same day, 23 September, relations between the two countries began to deteriorate rapidly.
During his address to the UN General Assembly, Zelenskyy announced that Ukraine had transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea. Both soldiers had been captured by Ukrainian forces in Russia's Kursk Oblast in January 2025.
On the face of it, this should have been seen as an example of successful cooperation between Kyiv and Seoul. After all, South Korea had previously advocated the transfer of prisoners to its territory, where they could live in safety.
Instead, on 24 September, President Lee Jae-myung publicly accused Ukraine of violating a confidentiality agreement. According to Seoul, the transfer was supposed to remain undisclosed to protect the prisoners themselves and their families still living in North Korea. Ukraine denied that any such agreement existed.
South Korea demanded an official explanation and an apology. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described the situation as a diplomatic misunderstanding. His South Korean counterpart, Cho Hyun, later confirmed that he had received a letter of apology but said it fell short of Seoul's expectations.
On 2 October, Lee Jae-myung threatened Ukraine with further measures unless Kyiv acknowledged its breach of the agreement and issued a public apology. He also criticised Ukrainian statements about the threat of a military conflict between North and South Korea, accusing Kyiv of using rhetoric that could push the Korean Peninsula towards war.
On 8 October, the diplomatic crisis escalated to the recall of an ambassador: South Korea's Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced its decision to bring its ambassador to Ukraine, Park Ki-chang, back to Seoul.
Ukrainian–South Korean relations had thus entered one of their most serious political crises since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion.
All this is happening as President Lee Jae-myung seeks to ease tensions with North Korea and restore inter-Korean dialogue. Pyongyang, however, has shown little interest in reciprocating.
Quite the opposite. On 7 October, Kim Jong Un sent Vladimir Putin a birthday message in which he called the Russian president his "dearest friend", reaffirmed his commitment to developing the strategic alliance with Moscow, and once again expressed support for Russia's "sacred war".
While Seoul is looking for ways to reconcile with Pyongyang, North Korean troops are gaining combat experience in Russia's war against Ukraine, and Moscow is helping North Korea develop its military technologies.
Why did the transfer of two prisoners of war provoke such a strong reaction from South Korea? Does Seoul's policy of reconciliation with Pyongyang stand any chance of success? What is North Korea gaining from its involvement in Russia's war against Ukraine, and how could this change the balance of power on the Korean Peninsula?
Ukrainska Pravda spoke about these issues with Sangmin Shim, Senior Research Fellow at the Center for Foreign Policy and National Security at the Asan Institute for Policy Studies, who specialises in international law and security affairs. His analytical articles and commentary on security and environmental issues in East Asia have appeared in international publications, including the American magazine The National Interest, as well as leading South Korean newspapers such as Chosun Ilbo and JoongAng Ilbo.
Although Shim is critical of certain policies and approaches pursued by the current South Korean administration, he is not a political opposition figure. His perspective is primarily that of an independent policy expert, shaped by his background in international law, diplomacy and national security. He previously taught international law at the Korea National Diplomatic Academy and has advised the government on legal and foreign policy issues.
The crisis in Ukrainian-South Korean relations
Ukrainian-South Korean relations are experiencing their first political crisis since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion. South Korea recently even recalled its ambassador from Ukraine. Why has the issue of the two North Korean prisoners become so sensitive for President Lee Jae-Myung's administration?
Well, this is my personal take, but I believe the South Korean government is so pro-Russian that anything potentially sensitive for bilateral relations between North Korea and the Russian Federation is largely discounted. That is what we are seeing today. Even though Ukraine has graciously sent those North Korean prisoners to South Korea, the South Korean government is not really appreciative of it. South Korea is so preoccupied with normalising relations with the Russian Federation that the many gestures the Ukrainian government approaches us with do not really count from the South Korean perspective. This is a truly sad matter, in my view.
Did the situation with those two North Korean prisoners create any domestic debate in South Korea?
In the general public's view, it is great that these prisoners have been transferred to South Korean territory to live in a free state. But the current South Korean government is extremely worried about the consequences of having these North Korean prisoners on its territory.
They fear the possible negative effects of holding them in South Korean custody, which makes them highly sensitive about their presence. This is completely irrational from my perspective. South Korea has always strongly argued for the transfer of Korean prisoners of war to its territory, as the government deems these POWs to be its own citizens.
There is a total inconsistency in logic between the South Korean government's general policy and what they are doing in this specific situation.
Inter-Korean tensions
What we see in the news now is that the South Korean president wants to ease tensions and restore inter-Korean relations and dialogue. But how realistic is this when there appears to be very little interest in dialogue from North Korea?
This might be my personal judgement, but looking at the South Korean government's attempts to ease tensions with North Korea, I don't think it is going to happen. The North Korean government is completely focused on differentiating the two regimes. Pyongyang believes that any ties it might have with South Korea will not bring any real benefit to the prosperity of the North Korean regime. Therefore, the North Korean regime has decided to totally sever ties with South Korea, and that is exactly what they are doing. Unfortunately, the South Korean government is not ready to give up its hope for reconciliation with North Korea. This is where the real tragedy begins.
We also see that North Korea has physically reinforced the separation. They are building barriers, laying mines, and fortifying the border with South Korea. From your point of view, is this just another period of rising tension, or has Kim's "two hostile states" policy changed these relations?
From what I can see, North Korea is highly focused on differentiating between the South Korean and North Korean regimes. They started by laying mines to prevent South Korean troops from crossing into North Korean territory. This is extremely unfortunate, and as you know, it has led to unnecessary casualties among South Korean soldiers. I do not know how this issue can be resolved between the governments of South Korea and North Korea, but I really hope it will be smoothed over. I hope we can find common ground to talk to each other, with the understanding that this issue should not destroy us. There are still many factors that can influence a hopeful outcome in the future.
President Lee's opponents accuse him of being overly cautious about provoking North Korea. How strong is this criticism inside South Korea, and does it explain the unusually sharp reaction to Ukraine?
There is a deep political divide between the progressive and conservative fronts. The conservative front argues that any engagement with North Korea is basically a concession. Meanwhile, the progressive front believes it is a necessary step toward reconciliation. So, there is a huge divide regarding how they want to move forward in the current situation.
President Lee also criticised Ukraine's statement regarding a possible future conflict between North and South Korea, saying such rhetoric could push the peninsula towards war. Why is this topic particularly sensitive for him?
This is anyone's guess, but as I perceive it, a high-ranking official from the Ukrainian Presidential Office stated that ignoring the ties between North Korea and the rest of the world would have a ripple effect on South Korea's security. But is South Korea ready to accept that?
They believe that through peaceful inter-Korean relations, we will have better relations with every country south of the Korean peninsula. But this is unproven. So we will continue to have contentious relations with both the Ukrainian and North Korean governments.
The role of the North Korean military in the war in Ukraine
North Korea has already sent roughly 15,000 troops to Russia, and thousands of them have reportedly been killed or wounded. Before this, North Korea lacked military experience in such a large-scale war. How different is the North Korean army today because of its experience in Ukraine?
After sending their forces to defend or take over the Kursk region, those North Korean troops have gained valuable battlefield experience in modern warfare — particularly combining drone warfare with conventional warfare. From a South Korean perspective, this is not something we can easily discount. South Korea now needs to prepare for potential provocations from North Korea. However, the current government is not taking this seriously. Because this administration leans pro-Russia, pro-China, and pro-North Korea, they do not see these signs of provocation as something to truly worry about. I am sorry to criticise my government, but this appears to be the reality.
And have you already seen evidence that the lessons learned by North Korean soldiers have been incorporated into North Korean training or doctrine at home?
What I can see from the collaboration between North Korean and Russian forces is that the Russians have been sharing technical advice to further develop North Korea's military expertise — particularly in military tactics and drone warfare. Because of this, North Korean forces are in a better position. I do not know how else to put it, but those North Korean forces are now superior to South Korean forces in terms of dealing with drone warfare and other non-conventional forces involvement.
So, could you say that soldiers returning from Russia will eventually form a new, combat-experienced elite within the North Korean military?
First of all, the initial group sent to Russian territory consisted of combat troops from their special operations forces. They sent about 10,000 of their best elite troops, and the results speak for themselves. The involvement of these forces has genuinely contributed to retaking territories crucial to the Russians from Ukrainian control. This has had a major effect. I do not know if this trend can continue, because the North Korean government will also face difficulties with the continuous mobilisation of its armed forces. We do not know how the next stage will play out.
Let us look at the evidence the North Korean government is presenting. They are doing everything they can not to reveal the presence of their personnel on the battlefield. They want to limit their manpower to factories and other workforces – helping Russian forces and industries build stronger weapon systems. So, from what I perceive, North Korean personnel are not going to be seen anywhere near the front lines. But what I really want to emphasise in this case is that North Korea is collaborating with the Russian government and military to build up Russian stockpiles, ensuring the Russian military is prepared for incoming attacks from Ukraine or other countries.
We have a fairly good picture of what is moving from North Korea to Russia: soldiers, ammunition, and missiles. But we know much less about what is moving in the opposite direction and so from your point of view, what's North Korea actually getting in return from Russia?
I mean, what North Korea really hopes to gain from the collaboration with the Russian regime is that they will get military expertise in terms of ballistic missiles development and other top-notch military development. And in turn those current regimes will provide war forces in the form of manual labour and everything to provide the help necessary for the Russian Federation to rebuild their drone systems. So, then they will be able to compete with Ukraine in terms of non-conventional forces engagement.
The Russian government is seeing that the Ukrainian government will not be able to provide all the necessary supplies for all the necessary equipment for forever. And then this is going to be a kind of a war of attrition between Russia and Ukraine in which both will be subject to having to pay the highest consequences from this military conflict. This is so sad but this is also a fact.
If North Korea is developing the capacity to mass produce Shahed-type drones with Russian assistance, how would that change the threat facing South Korea and is South Korea prepared for the kind of mass drone warfare we have seen in Ukraine?
I mean, we have heard the most recent report from the National Security Advisor of the Korean Republic that if North Korea has been engaging too much in this Russia-Ukraine conflict, this would be the best opportunity for Korea to start taking over the northern part of the Korean Peninsula and making the whole Korean Peninsula as a unified nation. But this is not going to be the case that I have been seeing because this is not going to involve the political discussions between the major powers and basically the military aspect will not resolve the matters as we see it.
So what I perceive to be the case is that whatever happens in the territories between Ukraine and Russia will not have any consequences for the inter-Korean relations.
Inter-Korean relations will have to be dealt with by their own dynamics. Meaning that Russia, the United States, Japan, Korea and both North and South Korea will have to be sitting at the same table to negotiate away the differences. This is not going to be a short-term matter but it has to include the case of negotiations.
How Ukraine іs perceived in North Korea
Maybe you know how North Korean propaganda explains Ukraine to its own population? What have North Koreans been told about why their soldiers are fighting and dying thousands of kilometres from home?
I mean the North Korean government is ready to just decorate their lost lives as their national heroes. But this is not going to be the case if the loss of the lives and casualties continues to accrue for the North Korean regime. We have a report that records those current casualties at around 3,000 soldiers who have lost their lives and then another 33,000 soldiers who have basically lost their capability to re-engage in the world.
But with the intensification of the war and tensions within Russia and Ukraine, this will lead to more casualties for North Koreans. And I don't know if the North Korean government will be able to continue to persuade their general public with this loss of life as an unavoidable matter.
I don't know, but the North Korean government is not a democratic nation but they will not be subject to national approval or to answering the questions of the people but they will still feel the pressure from the North Korean populace about the loss of life that has been the consequence of the involvement of North Korean troops in the Ukrainian military conflict.
Is Ukraine portrayed as an enemy in its own right or is it simply as part of a larger confrontation with the United States and the West?
This is a really interesting question. Between the US and Ukraine, they don't seem to have much differences. But by just looking at the recent episode between the Ukraine and Republic of Korea, they seem to have some impending conditions to be dealt with between these two nations.
But from my perspective, these would be only diplomatic matters and if these matters were to be entrusted with both countries' foreign ministers, these differences will be easily negotiated away. What matters to Korea for now is that the current president of the administration. He's so active in voicing criticism about the Ukrainian government. This is not going to be helpful for settling the battle between Ukraine and South Korea. I really hope that the South Korean president will stay silent for at least for the next two weeks for the two ministers to be able to reach a mutually satisfactory agreement.
And from your point of view, how much do the average North Koreans actually know about the scale of their country's involvement in Russia's war?
From the conservative people's point of view, this government is so pro-North Korea and they suspect that North Korea has a huge influence over the matters of the South Korean government, but I don't believe this. But whatever is the case with the North Korean and the South Korean government, I suspect that the South Korean government needs to be in a better position to fight away the incoming threats from North Korea.
Basically in terms of cybersecurity and maritime security. But without those concerns, we have to see that the South Korean government is going to live their lives as if nothing has happened. This is not going to be a very positive case for the South Korean population.
And what happened with thousands of soldiers who return home with direct experience of Russia, of modern warfare, of modern technologies which are most likely not represented in North Korea?
I mean, these North Korean soldiers who have been sent back to the North Korean territories have returned with better experience with drone warfare and better experience with modern warfare. So they may have something to say to their military leadership. But what are considered to be the barricades with these North Koreans, they have been so exhausted with the too-stressful battlefield conditions. So, they may be the key. I mean, this is my hopeful suggestion, but these people will be the driving forces for asking for more changes regarding the South Korea and North Korea territories. And then, if the current administration fails to address these questions then there will be more political decisions, moving forward.
And could these people potentially be a problem for the regime now?
This is another matter that we don't really know the answer to. Military and civilian society have been in co-existence for a long time. But what I perceive in that case is that the military, they are taking the upper hand with the civilian structures. So whatever situation may arrive, it's going to be down to the hands of the military that will take the final decisions.
How South Korea іs helping Russia and what the consequences could be
What we see in the recent investigation by Reuters is that South Korean petroleum product experts have reportedly helped Russia with fuel shortages caused partly by Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries. How is this issue perceived in South Korea or is it even discussed there?
There are two different opinions about this matter. For conservative people, this is a really serious matter because it seems to be the case that the South Korean government is basically just looking away in the case of helping the Russian economy by support with petrochemical fuels.
But at the same time, from a purely technical perspective, the South Korean government is not prohibited from providing petrochemical products to the Russian Federation because this is not going to be subject to any country's sanctions regimes. So this is kind of revealing a kind of difference between many different countries' sanctions regimes.
From my perspective, it should be right to tighten the grip upon the differences in the different countries' sanction regimes. But at the same time, we have to hold our countries to settle out the differences between many unlike-minded nations to achieve the core missions of these sanctions which is to weaken the fighting ability of the Russian Federation in terms of the battlefield between the Russian Federation and Ukraine.
From the Ukrainian perspective this trade could be the next major source of tension between Seoul and Kyiv. From your perspective, how could these South Korean-Ukrainian relations be mended?
I mean, we have current issues between Ukraine and the Republic of Korea, but I strongly believe that this case will be settled away between the diplomatic negotiations between these countries.
What I perceive to be the more worrisome outcome is if the South Korean president Lee Jae-myung continues to press hard on the relations between Ukraine and the Korean Republic. And if that would be the case, then there's not going to be a case for these two bilateral regimes to be reconciled pretty much soon. Because as long as the president's mandate is not going to be met, there's not much that the South Korean foreign minister will do proactively to settle the differences. So all it might come down to is the president changing his position between Ukraine and the Republic of Korea.
In a way, the revealing of the identity of the prisoners, those North Korean soldiers, would not be so much to disrupt the bilateral relations between these countries. It's really important that the South Korean government is so aware of this importance and also about the importance of not being too far away from these two government's positions.

articles.title: Ukraine accuses Elon Musk’s SpaceX of throttling Starlink terminals
articles.body:
Musk says US military controls Starlink’s limits after Ukraine outcry
Officials say ability to block Russian drones restricted as Kyiv reels from second night of ballistic missile attacks.
Ukrainian officials have accused SpaceX of throttling Starlink satellite services, disrupting its ability to carry out military operations and leaving Kyiv vulnerable to deadly attacks.
An adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that without warning, services had been limited for terminals travelling over 100mph overnight on Wednesday – effectively limiting Ukraine’s ability to launch drones, which use satellite internet to pilot the craft.
Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, which operates Starlink and its military version, Starshield, has since claimed on X that the United States government and military control all Starshield speeds.
“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately [President of the United States],” wrote Musk, a major US defence contractor and former top adviser to US President Donald Trump, after receiving criticism for the disruptions.
The White House has not confirmed or denied Musk’s assertion. The Pentagon did not immediately respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
Writing on Telegram, Ukrainian defence technology adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said Ukraine was “deprived of one of the few chances to defend itself from Shahed drones”.
He added that frontline logistics and long-distance missions were also disrupted.
Asked about the restriction on the military version of Starlink, Zelenskyy told Piers Morgan Uncensored it was “a big mistake” that “will bring a lot of human losses”.
US Senator Jeanne Shaheen, a member of the armed services and foreign relations committees, wrote on X: “These restrictions on Ukraine’s access to Starshield must stop immediately. Lives are at stake.
“The Pentagon is also required to notify Congress if it pauses or downgrades intelligence sharing with Ukraine. If that happens, Secretary of War [Pete Hegseth] must provide that immediately.”
The suggestion that Musk’s company had throttled Starlink services drew the ire of Poland, which pays for Ukrainian Starlink subscriptions on Kyiv’s behalf.
“Hey Elon Musk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?” wrote Radoslaw Sikorski, Poland’s foreign minister. “As your European customers, we are watching you.”
The “big man” gibe refers to a public dispute on social media between Musk, Sikorski and United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio in 2025, when the SpaceX boss told Sikorski to “be quiet, small man” on his X platform.
Starlink is a sensitive topic between Sikorski and Musk. The two previously clashed over the technology after the trillionaire said Ukraine’s “entire frontline could collapse” if he switched off Starlink.
Following the dispute in 2025, Musk said “no matter how much I disagree with the Ukraine policy, Starlink will never turn off its terminals.”
At the time he added, “We would never do such a thing or use it as a bargaining chip.”
‘Cannot be a coincidence’
The slowdown comes after Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv for the second night in a row, killing at least nine people and damaging electricity and heating infrastructure. Zelenskyy said Ukraine did not receive its usual warnings from Western allies for a second day, without specifying which partners.
Sources have told Reuters and other media that the US has threatened to cut off intelligence for early warning of missile strikes on Ukraine, pressing Kyiv to suspend attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Trump said on Tuesday the US has not stopped sharing intelligence.
Beskrestnov warned that the slowdown “cannot be a coincidence” after Trump struck a deal with President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel – despite international sanctions to isolate Moscow.
Speaking to AFP, another Ukrainian official accused Washington of throttling Starlink and helping Russia.
On Saturday, Trump suggested Zelenskyy had not done enough to end the war with Russia, blaming him for high diesel prices in the US.
Last week, Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel under pressure to curb fuel prices that have soared since the US war with Iran began as the midterms rapidly approach. He told Kyiv to stop attacking Russian refineries and urged Ukrainians to replace Zelenskyy.
“It’s painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side,” Zelenskyy said in the interview with Morgan.
The Ukrainian leader explained he was fine with Trump being in the middle between Ukraine and Russia, but “if you are in the middle, you have to stay in the middle.”

articles.title: Ukrainians fear US intelligence cuts as Russian strikes intensify
articles.body:
Ukrainians fear US intelligence cuts as Russian strikes intensify
Reduced missile warnings increase threat to civilians as Trump pushes an ‘energy ceasefire’ and peace negotiations.
Kyiv, Ukraine – The supernova-like blasts of exploding Russian ballistic missiles are followed by thunderous thumps, shockwaves, fires and deaths – and the staccato of Ukrainian air defence systems.
This week’s nightly attacks on Ukraine that killed at least 15 and wounded dozens resembled hundreds of previous raids – with one exception.
The air raid sirens began howling just seconds before or after yet another wave of missiles struck apartment buildings, power plants and warehouses.
But Ukraine’s partners did not provide the country with intelligence data from NATO’s early-warning satellites, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday, as tensions between Washington and Kyiv rise.
He did not name the United States and President Donald Trump has denied that Washington has stopped sharing intelligence.
The constellation of military satellites detects Russian ballistic missile attacks by the rockets’ thermal flames seconds after launch.
The warnings give Ukrainians up to 10 minutes – precious, life-saving time to sound air raid sirens and send emergency text messages to prompt evacuations to bomb shelters.
“That’s what helps prevent the killings,” Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine’s ground radars can only detect the incoming missiles as their speed ranges from 6,000 to 12,000km/h (3,730 – 7,260 miles per hour).
‘Trump pressures our president’
Despite Trump’s denial, Ukrainian observers have a simple yet harrowing explanation – the US president wants to help Republicans win more congressional seats in upcoming midterm elections by pressuring Kyiv into declaring an “energy ceasefire” with Moscow that would drive global oil prices down.
“Trump pressures our president, pressures Ukraine” as he strives to “get advantage by any means necessary in the election campaign,” Lieutenant-General Ihor Romanenko, former deputy head of Ukraine’s general staff of armed forces, told Al Jazeera.
The lack of intelligence data “significantly affects the effectiveness of air defence, we don’t have time to respond,” he said.
Without the satellite data, Ukrainian drones and missiles also “lose precision when striking targets deep in Russia,” he said.
On Sunday, Trump announced the ceasefire that envisages no mutual strikes on energy infrastructure – from Russian oil refineries and fuel depots to Ukrainian power and heating stations.
“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” Trump wrote on social media.
Kyiv said the announcement was a surprise, while Moscow declined to say whether it backs the idea – and kept on hitting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
The pressure goes beyond the refineries as Trump wants to quickly reopen, arbitrate and complete peace talks between Kyiv and Moscow – even if they benefit the Kremlin.
“He needs peace talks to succeed. Ideally, it is a certain unblocking of the peace settlement process, when Kyiv shows more willingness to agree with Russia’s demands,” Kyiv-based analyst Igar Tyshkevych told Al Jazeera.
The pressure will continue until “Kyiv shows readiness for a compromise and concessions towards Russia,” he said.
Moscow “simply abuses” the pressure and the suspension of air raid warnings to escalate attacks on Ukraine, he said.
Kyiv’s ‘priority’: The destruction of oil refineries
The suspension of data-sharing was especially shocking, given that Kyiv did stop hitting Russian refineries for three days.
It was only on Wednesday that its drones attacked refineries in Saratov and Ryazan regions, said Russia’s Deputy Prime Minister, Aleksander Novak.
However, Kyiv’s focus on striking oil refineries is ineffective and counterproductive, another observer said.
“Kyiv’s strategic priority is still the destruction of oil refineries,” Nikolay Mitrokhin of Germany’s Bremen University, who has penned hundreds of authoritative analyses of the hostilities, told Al Jazeera.
However, Russia overcame the initial shock by transporting gas from refineries in Siberia and exporting it from neighbouring Belarus and Kazakhstan.
No economic collapse, massive joblessness or public protests followed the strikes, while Moscow continued its air raids, adding jet-powered drones that resemble cruise missiles and are hard to down with Ukraine’s existing air defence system, he said.
“What is the basis for Kyiv’s and its backers’ conviction that strikes on oil refineries and depots will lead to Russia’s strategic defeat before Ukraine is defeated? I don’t understand,” he said.
However, Ukrainian attacks on data centres, bridges and factories where drones are assembled are far more effective, he said.
Recent strikes on data centres of Russian online giant Yandex and the state-run Sberbank resulted in disruptions of services in Russia and even former Soviet republics where Yandex operates its online payment, food delivery and taxi services.
Trump “didn’t ask him to stop the war, to give away cities or stop striking Russian rears in general,” Mitrokhin said.
Kyiv has repeatedly reiterated that it was ready to start peace talks if they are preceded by a ceasefire, but Moscow wanted to continue ground assaults and air raids until the peace terms were finalised – which could take months or even years.
‘We’re ready for any turn of events’
On Wednesday, Ukraine’s drone czar accused Elon Musk’s SpaceX of throttling Starlink satellite terminals that are part of the military-grade Starshield system.
Serhiy Beskrestnov said that SpaceX abruptly and without any warning limited services for terminals placed on drones flying over 160km/h (100mph).
The limit affected crucially-important interceptor drones and followed Trump’s request, presidential adviser Serhii Sternenko said.
Musk said that the White House owns and controls the Starshield systems and that any limits on speed are decided by Trump.
Some military analysts warn that the limit may be followed by a total shutdown of Starlink for Ukraine that could damage the quality of all military communications.
“But we were getting ready for everything,” Andriy Pronin told Al Jazeera. “We already know it may happen, that’s why we’re ready for any turn of events.”
In September 2022, Musk secretly ordered engineers to switch off Starlink coverage in the Russia-occupied Kherson region, effectively thwarting Kyiv’s push to retake it, Reuters reported.
In 2023, Musk threatened to cut off Ukrainian military access to Starlink unless the US defence department took over the costs.
Later, the Pentagon, Poland and other European allies took over the costs.

articles.title: Ukraine accuses US of helping Russia as Starlink restrictions disrupt drone attacks
articles.body:
Senior Ukrainian officials accused the United States on Wednesday of imposing restrictions on Kyiv's ability to use the Starlink satellite network, owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX, for military operations in its defense against Russia's invasion. The satellite communications network is critical to the Ukrainian military, and officials in Kyiv now report restrictions on its use at high speeds, disrupting drone attacks against Russian forces, among other operations.
Musk and his company have not commented on the allegations, which come amid intense pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump, a close ally of Musk, on Kyiv to halt its attacks on oil facilities deep inside Russia. According to reports, Trump has even threatened to suspend intelligence assistance or weapons deliveries to Ukraine.
Musk allowed Ukrainian forces to use Starlink's internet satellites in the early days of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Since then, the communications and navigation capabilities they provide have become critical on the battlefield.
Starlink is also considered more resistant to electronic jamming, making it useful for drone attacks carried out by Kyiv, particularly in Russian-held areas of eastern and southern Ukraine. According to Reuters, Ukrainian drones do not use Starlink when entering Russian territory, relying instead on other communications systems.
But senior Ukrainian officials now say restrictions on military use of Starlink are severely hampering Ukrainian operations, particularly along the front lines. The New York Times reported that officials in Kyiv were stunned by the restrictions.
Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky, said Wednesday morning that no advance warning was given before the restrictions were imposed, disrupting several "missions."
According to Beskrestnov, the restrictions cut off access to the military version of the service at speeds exceeding 160 kilometers per hour (100 mph). He added that Starlink is also crucial to air defense systems Kyiv is using to intercept the fast jet-powered drones Russia has begun deploying in attacks on Ukrainian cities in recent months. These faster drones are more difficult to intercept.
Beskrestnov suggested the move was deliberate. "It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," he said.
Ukraine's military said the restrictions had also caused disconnections during drone flights at lower speeds of 110 to 120 kilometers per hour (68 to 75 mph).
"The drones kept moving, but these interruptions made them harder to control," said the 7th Rapid Response Corps, a Ukrainian air force unit operating in the country's southeast.
A source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry also told Reuters that the restrictions significantly complicate logistics and the operation of several types of drones.
The Starlink restrictions come alongside allegations made in recent days by Zelensky and his aides that Kyiv had, on several occasions, failed to receive advance warnings from Western allies about Russian missile attacks.
Western intelligence is also critical to Kyiv's preparations for such attacks, and no warnings were issued in the Ukrainian capital on either of the past two nights when Russian missiles were launched toward the city.
According to the Ukrainian air force, Russia launched another 39 ballistic and cruise missiles overnight Tuesday into Wednesday, along with 128 drones. Only four missiles and 115 drones were intercepted.
At least four people were killed and about 20 others wounded in the overnight attack on Kyiv. Two other civilians were killed in the Dnipropetrovsk region and a third was killed in the Zaporizhzhia region.
"A Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. Once again, no early warning from our partners," Zelensky said Wednesday morning.
A U.S. official told Agence France-Presse that Washington "has not changed its policy on intel-sharing" with Ukraine. However, a senior official in Kyiv told the news agency that the United States had threatened to suspend intelligence assistance unless Ukraine stopped attacking Russian oil refineries.
According to the Ukrainian official, Washington had in fact failed to warn Kyiv about ballistic missile launches on two occasions.
"And on top of that they've throttled Starlink speeds," the Ukrainian official said on condition of anonymity. "It's obvious they [the United States] are helping Russia for some reason."
Trump has demanded that Ukraine halt its attacks on Russian oil refineries, arguing that they have caused a surge in global diesel prices. Experts, however, say the war in Iran is the main reason for the increase, which is hurting Republicans' chances of retaining control of Congress in the U.S. midterm elections.
After stunning Kyiv and its European allies by lifting sanctions on Russia late last week to allow it to export diesel to global markets, Trump also announced an "energy ceasefire" on Sunday, supposedly with the agreement of both sides. In reality, however, no such agreement had been reached.
Zelensky revealed Tuesday that Ukraine had indeed suspended its attacks on Russian oil facilities for two days, but said Russia had continued attacking energy facilities in Ukraine throughout that period.
He said the latest overnight strikes also targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, particularly in the Kyiv and Kharkiv regions, leaving 600,000 people without electricity.
"We ask America and everyone in the world who does not close their eyes to reality to react and react harshly. Russia missed the opportunity for de-escalation and clearly chose to continue its insane war of destruction," Zelenskyy said following the overnight Russian attack.
Zelenskyy called on Trump to renew pressure on Moscow, invoking the approach of former Republican President Ronald Reagan. "Peace can only come through strength, and we ask America to remember this principle of Reagan's," he said.

articles.title: Ukrainian officers warn Starlink slowdown ‘comparable to a nuclear strike against us’
articles.body:
Ukrainian frontline soldiers are alarmed that Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service is reportedly being restricted on fast-moving military platforms, warning of severe operational consequences.
“This is comparable to a nuclear strike against us. All operations are on hold. This will cost many of us our lives,” an experienced Ukrainian officer told POLITICO and the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network.
The officer commands a medium-range drone strike unit in southeastern Ukraine. The unit relies heavily on Starlink for the operation and navigation of its American-made Hornet drones, used to strike targets at a range of up to 150 kilometers.
Advertisement
“Since last night, all Starlink and Starshield terminals used by our forces have been subject to a speed limit of 100 kilometers per hour,” the officer said.
POLITICO talked to three frontline soldiers, who all spoke on condition of being granted anonymity, as well as a Ukrainian defense ministry spokesperson and the EU's top defense official.
The reported restrictions have revived a question Ukrainian commanders have worried about for years: how much of the country’s battlefield communications can rely on a service controlled by a U.S. company.
Ukrainian soldiers say the restrictions have halted some medium-range drone strikes over Ukraine, disrupting attacks on Russian logistics and leaving frontline Ukrainian troops with less support. The scale of the disruption — and whether it was deliberate — remains unclear.
In a comment on X, Musk said: "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," referring to the Starshield division of Starlink that is used for military purposes.
"Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX," he added. "Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company."
Advertisement
Mykhailo Fedorov, Ukraine's former defense minister who has good contacts in Silicon Valley, said late Wednesday: "Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 km/h is being restored. Removing Starshield’s speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine’s defense."
The White House and the Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The restrictions have brought “all medium-range strike operations to a complete halt,” the officer said, including those using mesh-based systems. These rely on a single Starlink-equipped UAV to receive and relay signals to other drones connected through a mesh network, allowing them to strike targets deep inside Russian-held territory or in areas heavily protected by Russian electronic warfare systems.
Such targets include the Donetsk region, the strategically important Novorossiya highway linking Russia to Crimea, the Crimean Peninsula itself, the Kerch area and the Black Sea.
“We can no longer fight effectively to support our infantry on the battlefield. We can no longer strike multiple-launch rocket systems, North Korean-supplied heavy self-propelled artillery positioned deep behind enemy lines, ammunition depots, command centers and other targets,” the officer said.
"The Ukrainian frontline is very much dependent on Starlink-operated mid-strike drones," Iryna Terekh, CEO of Ukrainian missile-maker Fire Point told POLITICO.
Advertisement
Ukraine's devastating campaign
For months, Ukrainian medium-range strike drones have inflicted significant damage on Russian logistics in frontline regions. They have disrupted the supply of fuel, ammunition and other military equipment, slowing Russia's advance.
Members of a special operations unit pilot a reconnaissance drone in the Kharkiv region on Feb. 27, 2026. | Chris McGrath/Getty Images
The officer said he feared that the Starlink restrictions will give Russian troops a critical opportunity to strengthen their positions.
“Starting today, the enemy will build up its logistics routes to Crimea to reinforce its forces there,” he warned.
Two other Ukrainian frontline soldiers operating ground robots and conventional first-person-view drones in the Donbas confirmed to POLITICO that Starlink services for Ukrainian units were abruptly restricted on Wednesday.
“On the night of October 14, without prior notice to the Defense Forces, SpaceX unilaterally restricted the operation of Starshield terminals while in motion,” a Ukrainian defense ministry official told reporters in Kyiv.
The official added that the problems occur at speeds varying from 72 kph to 161 kph, "depending on the specific vehicle and unit."
Advertisement
The slowdown in Starlink terminals comes as U.S. President Donald Trump exerts fierce pressure on Ukraine to stop attacking Russian refineries. That follows his deal with Russian leader Vladimir Putin to release diesel onto global markets — part of Trump’s effort to reduce fuel prices ahead of next month’s U.S. midterm elections.
"Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is associated with the current political situation," Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said in a Facebook post.
Asked about the rising American pressure on Ukraine, EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said at a POLITICO event on Wednesday: "Political development sometimes makes strange influence. Elections are coming."
“We are quite dependent on American space capabilities,” Kubilius acknowledged. “The answer to that situation is to develop our own capabilities.”
The Starlink slowdown was condemned by one of Ukraine’s key European allies.
“Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again? As your European customers, we are watching you,” wrote Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski.
Advertisement
Ukraine depends on Starlink
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Starlink has become central to Kyiv's war effort. In the spring of 2022, Ukrainian defenders trapped in the besieged city of Mariupol used satellites operated by SpaceX to send messages to the outside world. Ukrainian units relied on the system to coordinate operations during the fierce urban fighting around Bakhmut in 2023.
To this day, soldiers use Starlink to rapidly adjust artillery fire and navigate naval drones during attacks on Russia's Black Sea Fleet. Ukraine's former army chief, Valerii Zaluzhnyi, once praised the terminals for their "extraordinary utility."
That reliance always carried risk. In the early months of the war, Starlink reportedly shut off terminals that were going to be used in a naval attack on the Russian fleet.
But SpaceX has also acted to favor Ukraine. In February, SpaceX shut down access to Starlink terminals being used illegally by Russia, causing immediate chaos. Ukraine then ramped its own use of the terminals.
Kyiv's armed forces began widely equipping medium-range strike drones with Starlink terminals. Without them, operations would become considerably more complex. The military would, for example, have to calculate terrain elevations and antenna availability itself and install additional communications equipment.
"Starlink allows you not to have to deal with radio physics," a Ukrainian officer with the call sign Jura said in August. "Starlink allows operators to maintain a live video connection with a drone until shortly before impact."
Advertisement
Starlink can also provide so-called "synthetic GPS coordinates," which can help drones navigate when conventional GPS signals are jammed.
A Ukrainian serviceman assembles a drone ahead of a combat mission in the Kharkiv region on May 22, 2026. | Diego Fedele/Getty Images
But Ukrainian officers feared that decisions made in Washington or in the executive offices of American companies could suddenly weaken Ukraine.
"Many of my colleagues and I myself are very nervous about the question of how we would operate without Starlink," Jura said. "We have discussed this question several times among our officers: 'What if Elon Musk or someone at SpaceX switches it off?'"
As Trump has ramped up pressure on Kyiv in recent weeks, Ukrainian officers reported growing problems with Starlink.
One Ukrainian drone pilot, who operates medium-range strike drones, reported severe connectivity problems on Sept. 11 and 12, as well as further disruptions on Sept. 17. He said soldiers from several Ukrainian units had experienced similar problems.
The incidents occurred shortly after U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner had concluded visits to Kyiv and Moscow. "After few days, the normal work with Starlink come back. But I believe that was the signal," the pilot said.
Advertisement
He argued that Russian jamming equipment could not plausibly have produced such geographically consistent disruptions across multiple sectors of the front.
"So that was, I guess, administered from some office," he said. POLITICO could not independently establish whether the disruptions resulted from deliberate restrictions imposed by the American satellite provider or another technical cause.
The incidents have reinforced concerns among Ukrainian military personnel about their dependence on American-controlled technology.
"The reason is politics and the American option to 'switch off' or critically decrease” U.S. systems, the pilot said.
Veronika Melkozerova reported from Kyiv.Daniella Cheslow and Audrey Decker contributed reporting.

articles.title: Ukrainian drone attack causes fire at Russian oil refinery (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Ukrainian drone attack causes fire at Russian oil refinery (VIDEO)
A blaze has broken out at an oil refinery in Russia’s Ryazan Region as a result of a major overnight Ukrainian drone attack, local governor Pavel Malkov has written on Telegram.
In recent days, Kiev has continued its strikes on Russian energy infrastructure despite US President Donald Trump’s attempts to broker an “energy truce.”
A warehouse and several vehicles belonging to another local enterprise were also damaged during the raid, Malkov said.
However, there were no casualties, according to preliminary information, the governor stressed. The extent of damage is currently being assessed, with emergency services working in the affected areas, he added.
The Russian Defense Ministry said in a later statement that the Ukrainian attack on an oil refinery in Ryazan Region occurred between 4 AM and 7 AM local time.
A total of four long-range Flamingo cruise missiles and 69 fixed-wing UAVs, fired by Kiev, had been shot down by air defenses and military aircraft, the statement read.
The fire at the facility had been caused by the debris of an intercepted drone, the ministry said.
US President Donald Trump demanded last week that Ukraine halt its attacks on oil refineries in Russia, saying that they were the reason for surging energy prices. On Sunday, the US president claimed that Moscow and Kiev had agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire.
Vladimir Zelensky reacted by saying that the announcement “was news” to him, but expressed a readiness to stop the strikes if Russia does the same.
Zelensky also said that Kiev would introduce a three-day pause in attacks on Russian energy infrastructure. However, the pledge was violated on Wednesday, with Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak saying that two oil refineries – in Ryazan and Saratov Regions – were targeted by Ukrainian drones.
In order to alleviate the situation, Trump eased restrictions on Russia’s diesel exports following a phone call with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, last week.
The US president accused Zelensky of seeking to “make problems” for the US and the whole world by attacking Russian oil refineries and suggested that Ukraine needed a “new president.”
“He goes and hits the diesel fuel. He can do whatever he wants, but he can’t do that. He’d better damn well stop,” the US president said.
On Tuesday, Zelensky confirmed reports that the US had threatened to stop sharing intelligence with Kiev if it kept ignoring Trump’s demands. This week, Ukrainian officials also complained about receiving no advance warning from the Americans before Russian missile strikes as well as about problems with Starlink; the satellite internet service is used by Kiev’s troops for communications and controlling drones.
Zelensky blamed Trump for “betrayal” of Ukraine and suggested that the actual reason for the global energy shortage was the US war on Iran.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Thursday in the day that “in fact, there was no moratorium on the part of Ukraine. Strikes on our oil refineries and energy facilities continued throughout this whole period. Therefore, there is nothing new here.”
The Trump administration’s “active attempts” to settle the Ukraine conflict “are being crushed by the unwillingness of the Kiev regime and Zelensky, in particular, to agree to peace,” Peskov added.
Russian officials have said repeatedly that Moscow seeks a long-term settlement of the Ukraine conflict rather than a temporary truce, which would be used by Zelensky’s government to rearm and regroup its forces.

articles.title: Ukraine is going back to hitting Russian oil after its Trump-pressured pause, during which Kyiv got no US warnings of incoming ballistic missiles
articles.body:
Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries, ending a three-day pause it held at Washington’s request, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the Financial Times in an interview published on 15 October. Russia kept bombing Ukraine’s energy system throughout the pause, while Kyiv lost US missile warnings and its Starlink service slowed. Zelenskyy said Ukraine would halt energy strikes again only in exchange for more US air defense.
Ukraine's deep-strike campaign targets the Russian oil industry, which fuels Russia's army in Ukraine and earns the export revenue funding the war. Striking the plants that turn Russian crude into fuel, 12 of them hit in September alone, is one of the few levers Kyiv controls on Moscow’s war income. US President Donald Trump has blamed those strikes for higher US fuel prices, which most analysts attribute to the Iran war, and Washington has threatened to withhold intelligence, and reportedly weapons, unless Kyiv gives it up. Each step Washington takes toward Moscow, from fuel waivers to talk of frozen assets, widens the gap Europe and Ukraine must fill, while Russia gains revenue and time to keep striking.
A pause that bought nothing
Zelenskyy said he stopped the refinery strikes for three days to meet US wishes, but Russia kept hitting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and killing civilians. During the pause, Ukraine received no US warnings of ballistic missile launches, he said. Starlink also slowed across the country, hampering front-line operations and mid-range strikes on Russian military targets, he added.
Russia used those days to fire 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones at Ukraine’s grid overnight into 14 October, leaving at least 600,000 people without power. “We hold energy ceasefire from our side,” Zelenskyy told Piers Morgan on 14 October. Of the Starlink slowdown, he added: “I’m sure that they knew what they did.”
The price of another pause
Ukraine could again stop hitting Russian energy only if it receives more US interceptors for its Patriot systems, Zelenskyy told the FT. He warned that a halt could simply invite more US-Russia deals that feed Russia’s war machine, and predicted the next one would involve gas.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government”: Musk says Trump, not SpaceX, is behind cut hitting Ukraine
US intelligence officials had warned Ukraine’s embassy in Washington that a new strike on Russia’s energy facilities would end all intelligence sharing at once, The Washington Post reported, citing a person familiar with the matter. Washington has not fully cut it off, but the threat stands, the person said. Trump said on 13 October that the US was still sharing intelligence.
Washington’s other moves toward Moscow
A senior US official told Axios the administration had nothing to do with the Starlink limits, which Elon Musk had blamed on the US military. The administration is also considering easing sanctions on shadow fleet tankers, which have carried oil from Russia, Iran, and Venezuela, so the blacklisted vessels could haul non-sanctioned cargo, a US official told Reuters. The US Energy Department said the move would not help Russia ship its oil or fuel.
Washington eased sanctions on Russian oil this spring, after which Russia’s oil income jumped $890 million in a week, and it extended that waiver despite telling allies it would not. US envoys also proposed unfreezing part of Russia’s frozen assets to lure Moscow back to talks, an idea European officials rejected, the Financial Times reported.

articles.title: US effort to get Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire collapses
articles.body:
The White House’s unilateral effort to negotiate an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine has collapsed as Moscow sent a record swarm of drones overnight to attack infrastructure in central Ukraine and Kyiv appeared to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries – despite warnings from Donald Trump.
Moscow accused Ukraine of launching a strike against a Russian oil refinery in the Ryazan region, its first since Trump abruptly declared an “energy ceasefire” that neither Russia nor Ukraine said they had agreed to.
Trump has demanded that Volodymyr Zelenskyy stop attacking Russian oil refineries, claiming it was the cause of a global rise in the price of diesel fuel.
Zelenskyy said on Wednesday he would resume strikes on Russian oil refineries, after briefly halting them to demonstrate that Ukraine was ready for peace talks. “The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” he told the Financial Times. He also attacked the gap in US intelligence sharing as “dangerous”.
Images from Ryazan showed flames at the refinery, which regional officials said had been targeted by 69 drones and four Flamingo cruise missiles. Debris from a drone struck by anti-aircraft fire had hit the refinery and sparked the fire, the ministry claimed.
In Ukraine, more than 360 Russian drones targeted Kirovohrad, a central region that has been hit less hard than others closer to Russia, in attacks that killed three and injured six.
“The enemy deliberately hit critical infrastructure, transport enterprises, logistics facilities and residential homes,” the regional governor, Andriy Raikovych, said in a statement.
Zelenskyy said Russia had attacked Ukraine with more than 850 Shahed drones at a time when the speed of Ukraine’s defensive capabilities was being “artificially restricted”, a reference to the sudden limitations on Ukraine’s use of the Starlink and Starshield mobile internet terminals.
“It is obvious that Russia deliberately chose to escalate its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said in his social media post on X, referring to a growing quarrel with the Trump administration. “Ukraine needs steady support, above all in defending our skies. We need HONESTY from our partners about this war: It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war, and guarantee security.”
Trump suddenly declared an “energy ceasefire” last week, writing on TruthSocial: “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!”
Despite Trump’s claims, however, Russia continued to launch heavy strikes on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure, using hypersonic and ballistic missiles to target key Ukrainian power plants, leaving cities including Kyiv without power and water for hours. Ukraine said it would not strike Russian oil refineries in the interim in order to show that it was ready for negotiations.
But the White House piled pressure on Zelenskyy to capitulate to Russia by threatening to cut programmes to deliver arms to Ukraine and to stop sharing US battlefield intelligence with Ukraine.
The US appeared to make good on some threats. Ukraine said it had not received advance warning from Washington of Russian missile strikes for several days this week. And on Wednesday, Ukrainian soldiers also complained that their access to Starshield programmes controlled by the US military had been restricted, scuppering drone missions on the frontlines.
The feud between Zelenskyy and Trump has spun out of control over the last week. Trump, who believes that his support for Ukraine should come with a degree of control over the country’s leadership, has said that Ukraine should “get a new president”.
Asked on Thursday by Piers Morgan whether he felt betrayed, Zelenskyy said yes. “It’s a pity that we are losing, we are losing a strong partner,” he said.
Musk, the powerful head of SpaceX, which produces the Starlink terminals used by Ukraine’s military, has emerged as a top critic of Zelenskyy in the US.
On Thursday, Musk denied throttling the Starlink systems and said they were controlled by the US government. But in a social media post commenting on a Zelenskyy statement that Ukraine would continue to fight until Russia’s defeat, he wrote: “And so the slaughter continues … Time for Zelensky to go.”

articles.title: Russia’s largest drone attack on Kirovohrad Oblast since the full-scale invasion kills three in Kropyvnytskyi
articles.body:
Russia hit central Ukraine’s Kirovohrad Oblast with its largest attack since the full-scale invasion, killing residents of the oblast capital, Kropyvnytskyi, the oblast’s head said. Russian strikes hit more than a dozen oblasts, and Ukraine’s president said Moscow escalated deliberately after sanctions relief.
Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine continues on the front line and behind it, where its drones, missiles, and glide bombs strike towns daily. Kyiv is drafting winter crisis plans as Russia targets the biggest cities, and logistics is hit too: Russia struck one retailer’s warehouse hub 10 times in a day.
Three dead in Kropyvnytskyi
Oblast head Andrii Raikovych counted almost 360 Russian drones over Kirovohrad Oblast and hits on 26 locations, mostly in Kropyvnytskyi. In his words, “the enemy deliberately struck critical infrastructure, transport enterprises, logistics facilities, and residential buildings.” In a post after midnight, he reported a third death and six injured, five of them in hospital.
Air-raid alerts around the city ran from 15:20 on 14 October to 05:33, and Suspilne correspondents heard more than 20 explosions in Kropyvnytskyi, the public broadcaster reported. The national emergency service counted 25 struck locations, and rescuers were still putting out fires in the morning, the service’s spokesperson in the oblast said.
A wave Kyiv ties to sanctions relief
Nationwide, Russia launched 580 drones and two Kh-59 guided missiles from 18:00 on 14 October, and air defenses downed or suppressed 536 drones by 08:00, the Air Force reported. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia killed three people in Kropyvnytskyi and three in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, where oblast head Oleksandr Hanzha reported two dead.
Ukraine is going back to hitting Russian oil after its Trump-pressured pause, during which Kyiv got no US warnings of incoming ballistic missiles
Zelenskyy counted more than 850 Iranian-designed Shahed attack drones between the start of 14 October and 09:00 the next day, “precisely at the time of an artificial speed limitation for our defensive capabilities.” Overnight into 14 October, SpaceX capped speeds on its military Starshield satellite service, disrupting Ukrainian missions. He added that Russia escalated “deliberately, having received a relaxation of sanctions and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine.” Last week, Washington cleared Russian diesel trade after a call between US President Donald Trump and Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin.
Strikes from Kyiv to Odesa Oblast
In Kyiv, a drone fell into a residential yard, Mayor Vitali Klitschko wrote, later putting the injured at six. Drones hit two industrial enterprises in Poltava Oblast, its head Vitalii Diakivnych wrote, and a later strike on Poltava injured three people, rescuers said in a preliminary count. Ukraine’s state gas company Naftogaz said a drone set one of its gas production facilities in the oblast on fire, halting its work.
Russian guided aerial bombs injured two women and a man in Izium, Kharkiv Oblast, on 15 October, according to preliminary data from oblast head Oleh Syniehubov, who had counted nine injured in the oblast over the previous day. Over that day, Russian attacks killed three people in Donetsk Oblast, the oblast police said, and one in Kherson Oblast, where oblast head Oleksandr Prokudin reported five more injured. In Kherson city, a drone injured a man, the oblast administration said. In Sumy Oblast, a drone hit a house and left two people in acute stress, its administration said.
In Odesa Oblast, strikes damaged two apartment blocks, a company, and a bank office without casualties, oblast head Oleh Kiper said. Later, a jet-powered Shahed hit a store in the oblast, Zelenskyy wrote, and Kiper counted four injured in a preliminary tally. Drones also hit an enterprise in Ternopil Oblast, and five people sought medical help, rescuers said, while drones damaged two homes in Rivne, oblast head Oleksandr Koval said.
