articles.title: Ukraine live: Romania probes possible drone attack on tanker
articles.body:
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky on Thursday asked the United States not to stand with Russia and called for "honesty" after Kyiv said it had been betrayed by Washington's intelligence sharing gaps. Earlier, Moscow struck Ukraine's Izmail port and two cargo ships en route to Odesa, the Russian Defence Ministry said. Follow our liveblog for the latest updates.
Ukraine destroyed four fighter jets at Russian airfield, Zelensky says
A Ukrainian missile strike destroyed four fighter jets at an airfield in western Russia overnight, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a post on X.
He shared what appeared to be a satellite image showing a charred airfield strewn with debris.
Zelensky says meeting NATO chief, EU leaders in push for 'real pressure' on Russia
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in Brussels seeking to rally support from Europe at meetings with NATO chief Mark Rutte and a summit with EU leaders, as his country fights off a Russian invasion.
"All of us in Europe want this war to end. And for that to happen, strong signals are needed – more real pressure on Russia and more defense support for Ukraine. It is especially important now to act together to protect lives," Zelensky posted online.
Russia detains independent outlet Novaya Gazeta editor Sergei Sokolov
The chief editor at Russia's independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta, Sergei Sokolov, has been detained and taken to Moscow's Investigative Committee, his newspaper said Thursday.
Click the link below to find out more ⬇️
EU will need to increase Ukraine funding to plug gap, says Germany's Merz
Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said the European Union will have to find more money to finance Ukraine, as Kyiv warns it faces a major budget shortfall next year.
"We must do everything we can to help Ukraine through the winter and also to help next year," Merz said at the start of a two-day summit of EU leaders in Brussels for crunch budget talks.
"We will have to increase the funds again here in order to really assist Ukraine on a lasting basis."
EU leaders to clash over long-term budget, Ukraine support
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky will join the EU leaders' budget summit in a bid to rally support amid fresh tension with US President Donald Trump.
FRANCE 24's Europe Editor Armen Georgian reports from Brussels, Belgium.
Kremlin says Ukraine derailing US peace efforts with refinery strikes
The Kremlin accused Ukraine of going against US President Donald Trump's peace efforts by striking Russian oil refineries, despite Moscow itself never publicly agreeing to Washington's "energy ceasefire".
Kyiv "continues to launch strikes against these facilities. In doing so, it is coming into serious conflict with the peace efforts of the United States and American negotiators, who are making vigorous efforts to initiate the peace process," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
Ukraine's Starshield functionality in motion has been restored, source says
Ukraine's Starshield satellite internet functionality while in motion has been restored, a source in Ukraine's defence ministry said a day after the crucial service was throttled at speeds of over 100 miles per hour.
The source said the defence ministry would continue to seek clarification on the reasons for Wednesday's disruption of the military-grade version of SpaceX's internet service, which affected drone missions across the front line.
📸 Russia builds major new drone attack base in six weeks, satellite images show
Russia has nearly finished building a major new base for launching jet-powered drones in just six weeks, according to defence experts and satellite imagery, in the latest expansion of its attack capability close to Ukraine.
The site in what was an empty field in Russia's southwestern Rostov region on August 31 had become a complex facility the size of around 126 soccer pitches by Wednesday, commercial imagery provided by Planet Labs and Airbus showed.
Mike Monnik, founder and CEO of private intelligence company DroneSec, said the site in the imagery would be capable of launching Russia's newest types of jet-powered drone, the Geran-4 and Geran-5 models.
He said the western edge of the facility showed eight platforms for launch rails capable of firing those drones, adding to an existing Russian network of at least 11 fixed launch sites used for drone attacks on Ukraine.
"The speed of construction ... demonstrates the ease with which Russia can bring now-established offensive capabilities to bear rapidly," Monnik said.
The site, he added, looked very close to completion and it will be "probably a matter of weeks before (it is) fully operational, if not earlier".
Zelensky asks US not to stand 'with the aggressor', calls for 'honesty'
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky urged the United States not to stand with the aggressor, calling for "honesty" after Kyiv said it had been blindsided by Washington's intelligence sharing gaps and Starlink restrictions.
"We need HONESTY from our partners about this war: It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war, and guarantee security," Zelensky said on social media.
Russia says Ukraine attacked oil refinery in Ryazan, south of Moscow
Russia said Ukraine targeted an oil refinery in Ryazan (📍), around 180 kilometres (110 miles) south of Moscow, causing a fire.
"The Kyiv regime attempted a large-scale attack on an oil refinery in Ryazan," Moscow's defence ministry said in a statement, adding that a "fire broke out after drone debris fell onto the refinery site."
📸 Aftermath of a Russian drone attack in Kropyvnytskyi
Firefighters worked at the site of an enterprise hit by a Russian drone strike in Kropyvnytskyi, Ukraine.
Ukraine says it destroyed six Russian military jets in missile strike on airfield
Ukraine's navy said it had destroyed six Russian Su-34M military aircraft in an overnight strike on the Borisoglebsk airfield in Russia's Voronezh region.
The navy said on Telegram it used its Neptune coastal missile system in the attack.
FRANCE 24 could not independently verify the battlefield reports.
All EU leaders need to step up support for Ukraine, Dutch PM says
All European leaders need to do more to support Ukraine in its war against Russia, Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said ahead of a summit of EU leaders
"I call upon all the European leaders to do more financially, militarily and non military, because a lot of European countries are lagging behind in the support of Ukraine," Jetten told reporters in Brussels.
"Let's step up our game and make sure that they can win this senseless war."
Russia hits Ukraine's Naftogaz gas extraction facility in Poltava
Russia hit Ukraine's Naftogaz gas extraction facility in the central Poltava region overnight, the
company said.
It said in a statement on the Telegram app that the attack suspended the operations, damaged equipment and caused a fire.
Russia says it detained a Swedish citizen for illegally crossing the border
Russia's FSB security service said that it had detained a Swedish national for illegally crossing the border, the TASS state news agency reported.
Romania says eight people missing after fire on vessel in Black Sea
Romania said eight people were missing after a fire broke out on a vessel flying the San Marino flag, the latest incident in the Black Sea, which has seen a series of drone attacks.
"There were 12 people on board the vessel. Four of them are safe, whilst eight are currently missing," the Romanian Naval Authority said in a press release.
France 'can no longer finance' Ukraine, far-right candidate Marine Le Pen says
Far-right leader and presidential candidate Marine Le Pen said on Wednesday that France could no longer afford to fund Ukraine, citing the country's high deficit and weak economic growth.
Click the link below to learn more ⬇️
Germany's Klingbeil says support for Ukraine comes with reform expectations
German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said his country's support for Ukraine was
clear but comes with clear expectations for political reforms.
Klingbeil was speaking to reporters on the sidelines of IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok.
Lawyers for a Ukrainian ex-military officer accused of leading the bombing of Russia's Nord Stream pipeline in September 2022 argued at the start of his trial in Germany that "an aggressor's infrastructure" may have been a lawful target.

articles.title: Houthis look to build ballistic missiles with Chinese supplies
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Yemen's Houthis look to build ballistic missiles with more Chinese supplies, report says
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels are attempting to build a new advanced medium-range ballistic missile system with the help of Chinese parts, according to a new report released Wednesday by a group that tracks the use of weapons in conflict zones.
The report by the U.K.-based Conflict Armament Research group came as the Houthis, in their ongoing war with Saudi Arabia, are demonstrating remarkable ability to wreak havoc on one of the Middle East’s best equipped militaries.
The weaponry under development could help the group more precisely target the Saudis and Israel. By turning to China, it also appears to be a sign of increasing independence.
The rebels expand their ambition 
The Houthis have tried to acquire key parts from Chinese suppliers that could be used to make a version of Iran’s Kheibar Shekan precision-guided missile, according to the report. The Kheibar Shekan has a range of roughly 1,200 miles (2,000 kilometers).
"The local ambition of the Houthis for manufacturing is beyond what was previously assumed," said Fabian Hinz, a senior analyst at Conflict Armament Research, a research outfit specializing in tracing the flow of arms in war zones around the globe. "These types of parts are very specific, and producing them would have required design information related to the missile."
They're "not goods that can be used for a variety of civilian applications," Hinz said.
The Chinese Embassy in Washington didn't respond to a request for comment.
China is a major purchaser of both Iranian and Saudi oil and leveraged its ties with both countries to broker a rapprochement in 2023. It has condemned a series of attacks on Saudi airports by the Houthis and called for a de-escalation in the fighting.
Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s government launched a military campaign last month aimed at driving back the Houthis from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical Middle East trade route for oil and other goods.
Yemen interdicted key components to building missiles 
The Conflict Armament report was based on information released by Yemeni government authorities in July after officials interdicted two shipments that included suspicious equipment.
The shipments originated from China and were intended to be delivered to Hodeidah, a Yemeni port that Israeli officials say has been commonly used by the Iranians as a weapons transfer point. China accounts for the largest share of seized shipments destined for the Houthis, according to U.N. reports.
Components integral to the functioning of a missile were among the parts found in the cargo. They included stabilizing fin cores, rocket motor aft closures with nozzle attachments, and rocket motor igniters.
The cargo also contained phenolic resin, a material used in creating ablative heat shields. These shields protect ballistic missiles from the intense heat associated with atmospheric flight at high supersonic speeds, the report said.
Hinz said that the combination of materials made clear that the Houthis intended to assemble that specific type of Iranian-designed missile.
"This particular type of system is very difficult to smuggle. And you can’t just disassemble and reassemble them," he said.
Houthi weaponry has grown more sophisticated over time 
The Houthis rose to prominence more than 20 years ago as an insurgent group armed with Soviet-era and North Korean weapons seized from the Yemeni government's military.
But over the years, the group's access to advanced weaponry has expanded and so has its ability to menace neighbors.
In the current weekslong conflict with Saudi Arabia, the Houthis have fired ballistic missiles and utilized maneuverable warheads and long-range drones. They previously have fired scores of drones and missiles at Israel, more than 1,000 miles (1,600 kilometers) away.
Over the past week, they managed to puncture the kingdom’s stout air defense system with strikes on Riyadh’s international airport that killed at least 18 people.
Iran could find value in redundancy 
Iran has been an important supplier of blueprints and components for the Houthis. But procuring parts from beyond Tehran could be crucial for the group.
"Redundancy is an asset, not a liability in military planning," said Benham Ben Taleblu, a senior director of the Iran Program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a hawkish Washington think tank. "With a blockade of Iran in place, the Houthis are diversifying."
The rebels had long received weapons and materials smuggled from Iran. But the shipments have changed and now more often contain components rather than intact weapons.
The group’s arms program has been "increasingly backstopped by a hybrid, global supply chain serviced by a web of participants — including tribally connected smugglers across Yemen and businessmen working from export hubs in eastern China," according to research published earlier this year by The Century Foundation, a Washington think tank.
Security forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government have repeatedly intercepted missile components and launch equipment at the port of Aden, according to Yemen’s Aden Counter Terrorism Unit.
Yemen experts believe that the Houthis still rely on Iran for more sophisticated components needed to manufacture guided missiles, including navigation and control systems. But the group has expanded its capacity to manufacture and assemble weapons domestically at facilities deep inside territory under their control.
"The Houthis cannot yet manufacture highly complex weapons systems, and … they still rely heavily on Iran for technology and many critical items," The Century Foundation report said. "The group has reached a capability tipping point and can build a significant proportion of some weapons systems using imported components."
Yehoshua Kalisky, a senior researcher at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies, said that the Houthis’ supply chain historically mirrored that of other Iranian proxies, including Hamas and Hezbollah.
Iran is among the world’s most advanced in ballistic missile development. And both in Gaza and Lebanon, Iran-backed militant groups have smuggled in raw materials, and relied on Iran for more sophisticated components and assembled weapons themselves, he said.
Kristian Ulrichsen, a Middle East fellow at the Baker Institute, said that the Houthis’ growing reliance on Chinese components could have broader implications for politics in the Gulf.
"Now that the situation has really escalated and seen these attacks on infrastructure and airports, we could see more pressure from the Saudis," he said, noting that China is Saudi Arabia’s largest trading partner.

articles.title: Musk pointed at the US military over Ukraine’s satellite limits. Now a US official says the administration had nothing to do with them
articles.body:
Ukrainian officials contacted the White House, CIA, and Pentagon after the restrictions, which Ukraine says affected both Starlink and Starshield, Axios reported on 14 October. A senior US official told Axios the Trump administration had nothing to do with the restrictions. On the same day, Elon Musk said on X that Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government, and that any speed or usage limits are decided by the US military and ultimately the president.
The restrictions could affect Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian attack drones and carry out mid-range strikes against Russian forces and military targets in occupied Ukrainian territories. A speed cap of 160 km/h was insufficient to intercept some jet-powered drones, an unnamed Ukrainian official told Axios. Ukrainian officials told Axios they suspect SpaceX imposed the restrictions to pressure Kyiv to accept US President Donald Trump’s demand to stop striking Russian oil refineries, though the motive remains unconfirmed. But Starlink does not work inside Russia, and the drones attacking Russian oil facilities use other communications systems, according to Reuters.
What Musk and the White House said
Musk did not directly address the throttling, Axios noted. Starlink, he wrote, “is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX,” limited to civilian or defensive use.
White House officials told the Ukrainians they don’t have control over SpaceX, two sources told Axios. One said the administration would reach out to SpaceX to figure out what happened. The White House did not immediately respond to Axios’s request for comment.
How the cap disrupted drone missions
Presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said on 14 October that SpaceX had imposed a 160 km/h limit on Starshield’s “military package” overnight without warning. Ukraine’s 7th Rapid Reaction Corps said mid-range strike drones must reach high speed quickly and that an unstable connection “will make it impossible to launch such aircraft or use them as intended.” One unit on the Huliaipole front had to cancel some missions, the corps told Novynarnia.
Ukraine is going back to hitting Russian oil after its Trump-pressured pause, during which Kyiv got no US warnings of incoming ballistic missiles
Ukrainian officials told Axios the system turned off when drones exceeded 160 km/h, and sometimes 80 km/h, before service was partially restored on 14 October. The Defense Ministry said SpaceX continues to restrict Starlink to 160 km/h and that it remains in communication “with partners and SpaceX regarding stable service conditions and the prevention of sudden restrictions,” Axios reported.
A diesel deal
The restrictions followed Trump’s 9 October deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin easing sanctions on Russian diesel. A day later, Trump told reporters: “We said you could do whatever you want to Russia, don’t hit the refineries,” the Kyiv Independent reported.
Read also
- NATO country that pays for Kyiv’s Starlink warns Musk as his cap breaks Ukraine’s drone missions: “As your European customers, we are watching you”
- “Trump and Musk must be held accountable”: US senator warns Starlink network failing over Ukraine could cripple its shield against Russian missiles and drones
- US continues sharing intelligence with Ukraine, Trump says amid Russia deal backlash. Questions remain over missed warning for latest attack

articles.title: North Korea test-fires submarine-launched cruise missiles amid rising tensions
articles.body:
North Korea test-fires submarine-launched cruise missiles amid rising tensions
North Korea test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles on Wednesday, state media KCNA reported Thursday, saying the launches posed no threat to neighbouring countries. The tests follow heightened tensions with South Korea after a September 21 landmine explosion in the Demilitarised Zone injured three South Korean soldiers.
North Korea has test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles, state news agency KCNA said Thursday.
The agency said the missiles were fired Wednesday into the East Sea, also known as the Sea of Japan, without "any adverse impact on the security of neighbouring countries".
The reported launch came after weeks of mounting friction over a landmine explosion along the heavily fortified border between North and South Korea.
Three South Korean soldiers were injured in the September 21 blast in the Seoul-controlled area of the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ), with both countries testing upgraded missile technology in the aftermath.
The latest testing "aimed to examine the current mobilised posture of the underwater combat systems" and served as a Navy training exercise, KCNA said.
The tests showed the "high reliability, trustworthiness and ability of the war deterrents of the DPRK", the agency reported, referring to North Korea by the abbreviation of the country's official name.
Photos released by KCNA showed one missile blasting vertically out of the sea trailed by a thick plume of smoke. Another photo appeared to show a projectile erupting from the water at a 45-degree angle.
Read moreNorth Korea launches ballistic missile as tensions with Seoul grow over border mine blasts
Other images showed a missile flying horizontally over the sea, as well as a submarine traveling on the water's surface.
The North's ability to launch missiles from submarines at two different angles carries "tactical significance", Hong Min of the Korea Institute for National Unification told AFP, as the two launch methods serve different purposes.
"Vertical launches allow missiles to climb steeply before descending towards their targets, potentially extending their range," he said.
"Angled launches, on the other hand, allow missiles to fly at lower altitudes from the outset, making them harder for missile defence systems to detect and intercept."
North Korea has carried out several missile launches from submarines in recent years, although its sea-based launch capabilities remain unclear.
Cruise missiles tend to be jet-propelled and fly at a lower altitude than more sophisticated ballistic missiles, making them harder to detect and intercept.
Proven submarine-launched ballistic missile capability would take North Korea's arsenal to a new level, allowing deployment far beyond the Korean peninsula and a second-strike capability in the event of an attack.
North Korea has carried out multiple ballistic missile tests in October, most recently on Monday.
The two Koreas have engaged in a tit-for-tat series of missile tests this month, with both sides test-firing hypersonic weapons.
South Korea test-fired its first homegrown hypersonic missile last week, days after Pyongyang said it had launched an AI-assisted intermediate-range hypersonic missile.
Seoul and Pyongyang remain technically at war as the Korean conflict ended in 1953 with a truce rather than a peace treaty.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Donald Trump claims ‘Iran war will end very soon’ as midterm rallies heat up – US politics live
articles.body:
Trump returns to White House amid weak polls ahead of midterms
Donald Trump is returning from the campaign trail to Washington DC this morning amid weak polls that could point to trouble for the Republican Party in the midterm elections.
According to an exclusive new poll for the Guardian, voting groups that are key to winning votes in the midterms – including independents, rural voters and even some Republicans – are increasingly disenchanted with the economy. Three in four Americans are now concerned about the potential for a recession.
In another poll conducted by the Associated Press, about 8 in 10 voters overall say the economy or the cost of living is among their top issues for the upcoming election, while about two-thirds say this about healthcare and the war in Iran. Other issues that are stronger for Trump – like immigration or crime – are lower priorities.
US officials considering ad campaign to urge South African Afrikaners to emigrate
Joseph Gedeon
The US government could spend hundreds of thousands of dollars on a media campaign in South Africa to figure out why more white Afrikaners are not applying to become refugees to the US, as Donald Trump had hoped.
State department officials, according to an August proposal seen by the Guardian, outlined a roughly $335,000 research and advertising effort after applications to the refugee program “trended lower than expected” since Afrikaners were allowed to apply directly online in November 2025. The document, written by the US mission in South Africa with a department research unit for the embassy in Pretoria, admits officials know little about why.
“There’s currently little research about why Afrikaners are not applying to request referral into the US Refugee Admissions Program,” the proposal reads.
The focus on Afrikaners flows from a February 2025 executive order directing officials to put Afrikaner resettlement first while the broader refugee program stayed suspended. Administration officials had said Afrikaners face racial discrimination and “white genocide”. The South African government has rejected the genocide claims, and experts have widely dismissed the idea that Afrikaners face targeted violence or genocide.
While Trump is in DC today, vice-president JD Vance will be in Monroe, Michigan, for a rally in support of Mike Rogers, the former Republican congressman vying to flip the open Senate seat against progressive Democrat, Abdul El-Sayed.
After back to back rallies in Arizona and Montana, Donald Trump’s day in Washington will consist of closed-door meetings, a private Rose Garden lunch and two tele- rallies. None of his scheduled events today are open to the press, but we’ll let you know if anything changes.
Tomorrow, the president will be back on the trail to campaign in Dalton, Georgia.
Key US voters say economy is getting worse ahead of midterms, new Harris poll finds
Lauren Aratani
The majority of those surveyed were pessimistic about the economy, with three quarters of Americans saying they are concerned about a recession while 61% wrongly believe that the US is already experiencing one. By its typical definition, the US is not currently experiencing a recession.
The poll shows growing weariness across the political spectrum over high prices.
Republicans, fighting to keep control of Congress, are losing support with independent voters, who are expected to be the deciding factor in key swing races. Nearly two-thirds (65%) of independents said the economy is worse, up from 48% who said the same in September 2024 in the heat of the 2024 presidential election.
Even within the Republican ranks, optimism has waned. In February 2025, just a few weeks after Trump was inaugurated, 39% of Republicans said the economy was getting better. By February 2026, just before the US launched attacks against Iran, that optimism was up to 49%. In the latest poll, just 28% of Republicans said the economy is getting better.
In the new poll, a vast majority of Americans agreed that there is an affordability crisis, including 96% of Republicans. But Americans still remain divided over who has a solution.
Democrats (71%) were more likely than Republicans (59%) to say that their own party had a solution.
Republicans were more likely (26%) to say neither party has a solution compared with Democrats (17%)
Half of independents said neither party has a solution, while 14% sided with Democrats and 10% with Republicans.
Trump returns to White House amid weak polls ahead of midterms
Donald Trump is returning from the campaign trail to Washington DC this morning amid weak polls that could point to trouble for the Republican Party in the midterm elections.
According to an exclusive new poll for the Guardian, voting groups that are key to winning votes in the midterms – including independents, rural voters and even some Republicans – are increasingly disenchanted with the economy. Three in four Americans are now concerned about the potential for a recession.
In another poll conducted by the Associated Press, about 8 in 10 voters overall say the economy or the cost of living is among their top issues for the upcoming election, while about two-thirds say this about healthcare and the war in Iran. Other issues that are stronger for Trump – like immigration or crime – are lower priorities.
US voters overwhelmingly want change in Washington, new poll finds
A strong majority of voters believe president Donald Trump is falling short at home and abroad, and they want significant change in the upcoming midterm elections, according to a new AP-NORC poll.
The survey, which was conducted less than four weeks before Election Day, finds that registered voters who identify as Democrats are more enthusiastic than Republican voters about casting a ballot.
More voters want Democrats to win control of Congress and have a more negative view of Republicans.
The poll’s findings paint a difficult picture for Republicans, who are clinging to control of Congress under the weight of an unpopular war with Iran and surging prices in the US.
About 8 in 10 voters overall say the economy or the cost of living is among their top issues for the upcoming election, while about two-thirds say this about healthcare and the war in Iran. Other issues that are stronger for Trump — like immigration or crime — are lower priorities.
James Talarico, the Texas Democratic nominee for Senate, sat face to face with several undecided voters who grilled him on a slew of contentious issues including Israel’s military campaign in Gaza, abortion and foreign aid, during a CNN town hall on Wednesday evening.
Jodi Hunt, a self-described single-issue voter, probed Talarico’s pro-choice stance, asking: “How would you convince me as a Catholic voter that I can trust you would protect the most innocent among us?”
Talarico described the Bible as being silent on abortion, to which Hunt countered quoting “Thou shalt not kill”.
“We may have different, moral conclusions when it comes to this particular ethical question, but we actually have the same public policy goal,” Talarico said, framing abortion as a public health issue that could be solved with a reduction in unplanned pregnancies.
During the night, Talarico cast himself as a moderate, who would put the needs of Texans over party allegiances. He railed against the ultra-wealthy, framing them as the common enemy.
Turning to James Talarico, the Democratic candidate fighting for a Texas US Senate seat might not have sparred with his Republican rival Ken Paxton last night but that doesn’t mean he was spared from attacks.
At a rally in Texas on Wednesday, JD Vance responded to an audience member who shouted his praise by responding: “I love you too sir.” He then added: “In a totally platonic way, to be clear. I’m the vice president, not James Talarico.”
It’s part of the Republican strategy to cast doubt down on Talarico’s Texan credentials and whether he’s “man enough,” according to the New York Times.
Recent polls have shown that the Democratic candidate is leading against his Republican counterpart.
Meanwhile Paxton, who declined an invitation to meet voters with Talarico last night, has focused his efforts in an ad blitz. Already more than $500m has been spent on television ads for the Texas race, according to CNN.
The White House’s unilateral effort to negotiate an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine has collapsed as Moscow sent a record swarm of drones overnight to attack infrastructure in central Ukraine and Kyiv appeared to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries – despite warnings from Donald Trump.
Zelenskyy said on Wednesday that he would resume strikes on Russian oil refineries after halting those attacks to show that Ukraine was ready for peace talks. “The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” he told the Financial Times. He also attacked the gap in US intelligence sharing as “dangerous”.
Images from Ryazan showed flames at the refinery, which regional officials said had been targeted by 69 drones and four Flamingo cruise missiles. Debris from a drone struck by anti-aircraft fire had hit the refinery and sparked the fire, the ministry claimed.
In Ukraine, more than 360 Russian drones targeted Kirovohrad, a central region that has been hit less hard than others closer to Russia, in attacks that killed three and injured six.
US president Donald Trump claimed the Iran war “will end very soon,” as voters consider their options ahead of midterm elections that are taking place amid economic uncertainty and ongoing global conflict.
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday evening, Trump said: “The Iran war will end very soon. It’s going to end very soon, as soon as I want it to end, it’ll end.” He added that Iran would “never have a nuclear weapon” and that oil prices would “drop like a rock”.
The US president has in recent weeks attempted to shift focus towards Ukraine, and has suggested that its attack on Russian refineries are responsible for rising fuel prices. His renewed messaging on Iran suggests that the price of daily goods – and gas at the tank – are having an impact at the polls.
Voting groups that are key to winning votes in the midterms are increasingly disenchanted with the economy, according to an exclusive Harris poll for the Guardian. Three in four Americans are now concerned about the potential for a recession.
Elsewhere:
James Talarico, the Texas Democratic nominee for Senate, faced a grilling from undecided voters on a range of issues from Gaza to his faith at a town hall. Something he emphasized was his aspiration to put residents above party allegiance.
Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he felt ‘betrayed’ by the US after Ukraine’s military access to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite was restricted. The US president has denied that the administration has cut intelligence sharing but Musk suggested on X that the US government was behind the restrictions.
Trump’s new press secretary Katie Zacharia is facing scrutiny over her claims that she’s a lawyer. Zacharia has clarified some of the questions but the big one remains: has she ever passed the bar?

This live blog has now ended. Make sure to follow us for the latest news on Facebook, X, and Instagram.
Breadcrumb
Welcome to our continuing coverage of events in the Middle East and beyond.
Here are the updates of the day:
The former head of Israel's Shin Bet domestic security agency on Wednesday sued Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for defamation weeks before elections in a row over responsibility for Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack.
Netanyahu, who polls show in a tight race to stay in power in the October 27 election, has been hammered by the opposition for failing to prevent the attack, the deadliest day in Israeli history.
Netanyahu, who has cast himself as a guarantor of Israel's security over his decades-long career, has insisted that he could have stopped the attack had the Shin Bet's then director, Ronen Bar, or military leaders called to wake him up the day of the early-morning attack.
In the 134-page court document, Bar accused Netanyahu of "lying to cover himself" and said it was slanderous to accuse him of "criminal failures" over the attack.
Netanyahu made accusations against Bar "that he knew to be false, with the aim of diverting the debate from his own responsibility for the events of October 7", the lawsuit said.
Instead it was Netanyahu's policies over several years that had "increased the dangers posed by terrorist organisations in Gaza", it said.
Bar resigned in June 2025, saying at the time that "all the systems collapsed" in the security agency and that Shin Bet "failed to sound the alarm".
New Zealand has issued new "Do Not Travel" warnings for the entirety of Saudi Arabia amid escalating regional tensions with Yemen's Houthis.
The NGO Human Rights Watch said Wednesday that military authorities in eastern Libya executed at least 31 people earlier this year, the first reported death sentences to be carried out in the country since 2010, according to the group.
Forces under the control of military leader Khalifa Haftar and his clan executed the people between late August and September 10 "following grossly unfair military trials", HRW said in a statement, adding another 50 people in detention were "at imminent risk of execution".
Read the full story here.
US tech firm Palantir and London mayor Sadiq Khan's office have settled Palantir's lawsuit over a decision to block a £50 million ($66 million) contract with London police, both parties said on Wednesday.
Palantir had agreed a two-year contract with the Metropolitan Police to use its artificial intelligence systems to automate certain tasks and for analysing evidence.
But the mayor's office refused to approve the deal, telling the Met Police it had failed to have an open competition for the contract, with reports also quoting a spokesperson for Khan citing concerns Palantir did not align with "London's values".
Federal authorities investigating Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar seized the Democratic lawmaker's phone and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, according to a person briefed on the probe.
The subpoenas were issued for a grand jury collecting evidence in Minnesota as federal authorities probe potential fraud in Omar's immigration paperwork, said the person, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation. The investigation led to federal agents searching Omar's Washington, D.C. home on Monday just weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking reelection.
The scope of the investigation into Omar is unclear, though Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has suggested that authorities were examining potential crimes related to her family’s immigration paperwork.
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels are attempting to build a new advanced medium-range ballistic missile system with the help of Chinese parts, according to a new report released Wednesday by a group that tracks the use of weapons in conflict zones.
The report by the U.K.-based Conflict Armament Research group came as the Houthis, in their ongoing war with Saudi Arabia, are demonstrating remarkable ability to wreak havoc on one of the Middle East’s best equipped militaries.
The weaponry under development could help the group more precisely target the Saudis and Israel. By turning to China, it also appears to be a sign of increasing independence.
Palestinian officials said Israeli strikes killed four people in Gaza on Wednesday, days after the anniversary of the declaration of a US-mediated ceasefire.
Two young men died when Israeli forces struck a vehicle near Khan Yunis in the southern Gaza Strip, civil defence spokesman Mahmoud Bassal and Nasser Hospital said.
Two other people, including a woman, were killed when an Israeli aircraft struck an apartment building in Gaza City, according to Bassal and Al-Shifa hospital.
Israel's army chief said on Wednesday that the military was reinforcing troop levels "across all fronts", citing an increased risk of escalation as the country heads into elections this later month.
On a visit to the occupied West Bank, Lieutenant General Eyal Zamir said the potential for incidents on Israel's borders had grown because of the election period, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu facing a tight race to stay in power in the October 27 poll.
"In light of the increased number of alerts across all fronts and the sensitivity of this period, the potential for escalation has grown," he said, according to an Israeli military statement.
"We have reinforced our forces across all areas."
He added that the military had raised its level of readiness as it prepares "for scenarios in which attempts may be made to catch us by surprise".
Citing the need for "vigilance", Zamir said the military was "at a high level of readiness to launch extensive offensive operations against anyone who attempts to harm Israeli civilians".
A visiting senior United Nations official on Wednesday reaffirmed the body's commitment to stability in Lebanon as the mandate of its peacekeeping force in the country is set to expire this year.
Under-Secretary-General for Peace Operations Jean-Pierre Lacroix met officials as well as representatives of countries contributing to the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL), which counts some 7,500 personnel from nearly 50 countries.
"I thanked them for their critical support to UNIFIL and reiterated the UN's strong commitment to supporting peace and stability in Lebanon," Lacroix said.
The Istanbul governor’s office declared schools closed, placed some public sector workers on leave and urged people to stay at home after heavy rainfall caused floods across the city on Wednesday.
Media reports said that the downpour flooded homes and businesses and inundated roads and underpasses, stranding vehicles and causing traffic chaos in the city of around 16 million people. There were no reports of any serious injuries.
In one district, bystanders rescued a woman who was being swept down a street by the floodwaters, footage obtained by NTV television showed. Firefighters rescued another person who was trapped inside a flooded basement, the report said.
Images showed several parked cars being swept by the floods in another neighborhood.
The governor’s office said that education would be suspended for a day on Thursday, and state employees with disabilities and mothers with young children would be placed on leave. It advised residents to stay home unless travel was absolutely necessary and for people living in basement apartments to spend the night elsewhere.
Motorcycles, meanwhile, were barred from traffic.
Israeli forces are using tear gas during an incurrsion into al-Mughayyir near Ramallah, in the occupied West Bank, according to Palestinian media.
Saudi Arabia plans to move ahead with a major investment conference in Riyadh despite Houthi attacks on the kingdom, offering on-site and virtual attendance as well as alternative air and land travel routes, diplomatic sources told AFP.
Riyadh usually hosts a packed calendar of events, but it has recently seen escalating military tensions with the Iran-backed Yemeni group, which has intensified attacks on the kingdom's airports and oil facilities.
Saudi Arabia's Future Investment Initiative (FII) Institute hosts an annual forum dubbed "Davos in the desert", which usually draws foreign leaders and business titans, and this year it is scheduled to be held in Riyadh from October 26 to 29.
Diplomatic sources said that to prevent cancellation, organisers reached out to embassies and foreign companies to explore "hybrid" participation options, allowing officials and business executives to attend either in person or virtually.
They have even discussed arrangements for participants to fly by private jet to Dhahran airport in eastern Saudi Arabia before travelling by road to Riyadh.
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis said Wednesday that they targeted Riyadh's international airport with a ballistic missile, hours after the Saudi-led coalition reported an interception of one fired towards the capital.
"The Yemeni Armed Forces... were able to target King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi enemy's capital, Riyadh, with a ballistic missile, and the hit was accurate," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree posted on X.
French President Emmanuel Macron will travel to Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Qatar to meet the leaders of these countries from October 19 to October 21, his office said on Wednesday.
He plans to discuss the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and its impact on energy prices, the statement said.
At least ten vessels have been attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz since Sunday, a high since war broke out between the United States, Israel and Iran, security data showed Wednesday.
Four vessels were struck on Tuesday and six on Sunday -- the highest number of attacks in a single day since the start of the conflict -- according to data from security firm Vanguard, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) and the British maritime agency UKMTO.
Two seafarers have been reported missing and a container ship reportedly sank as a result of recent attacks, according to the maritime sources.
Israel’s defence minister has threatened to seize more territory in southern Lebanon and forcibly displace residents of Beirut’s southern suburbs if Hezbollah joins Iran in an attack on Israel.
Israel Katz’s comments on Wednesday come amid reports that Hezbollah is preparing for a new round of fighting with Israel, while Israel is also reported to be considering an escalation of its offensive in Lebanon in the coming weeks.
Hezbollah and Israel began exchanging fire in October 2023, with the conflict dramatically escalating into a full-scale war in September 2024. Fighting resumed on 2 March this year, alongside the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Thousands of people have attended demonstrations across southern Yemen in response to a call from exiled separatist leader Aidarous al-Zubaidi for a "popular mobilisation" to halt the ongoing Houthi advance.
In his first address since fleeing the country in January, the head of the Southern Transitional Council on Tuesday called on southern Yemenis to join the Saudi-backed government's efforts to turn the tide of the war.
Videos published by pro-separatist media showed mass protests in several cities - including Aden, Mukalla, Seiyun and Al-Ghaydah - which coincided with the anniversary of the 14 October revolution, the South Yemeni rebellion against British rule in 1963.
The Antigua and Barbuda-flagged Cape Dao sank close to the Strait of Hormuz after being struck by a projectile on September 23, data from UN shipping agency the International Maritime Organization showed on Wednesday.
The loss was reported less than 24 hours after the sinking of the Singapore flagged GFS Pride, which was struck by a projectile in a separate incident, maritime security sources said earlier on Wednesday.
Israeli forces are using live ammunition and tear gas during a military raid in the West Bank town of Salfit, according to Palestinian media reports.
Spanish humanitarian rescue charity SMH has postponed its next mission in the central Mediterranean until 2027 due to soaring fuel costs, the group said on Wednesday, highlighting the financial pressures facing humanitarian efforts along one of the world's deadliest migration routes.
SMH, which operates the Aita Mari, a former fishing vessel converted into a rescue ship in 2017, said on X the doubling of fuel prices had forced it to suspend operations in the central Mediterranean and shift activities to waters around Spain's Valencia coast, and the islands of Mallorca and Menorca.
It also launched a crowdfunding campaign to cover the extra costs.
The central Mediterranean crossing from North Africa to Italy and southern France is one of the world's most dangerous migrant routes, used by migrants from Africa and the Middle East seeking to reach Europe, often in overcrowded or unseaworthy boats.
Spanish NGO Open Arms said it had also scaled back its central Mediterranean missions in recent years because of rising fuel costs and Italy's policy of assigning rescue vessels ports in northern Italy. The practice can require ships to sail for two or three days from their operating area, increasing costs and reducing time available for search-and-rescue work.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's right-wing, anti-immigration government has repeatedly argued that humanitarian rescue vessels encourage migrants to attempt the crossing.
Turkish Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek on Wednesday agreed to let prosecutors open an investigation into the former head of Turkey's capital markets regulator, state news agency Anadolu said.
Turkey has been grappling with the fallout from an investment fund scandal which erupted a month ago, prompting an investigation into allegations of widespread market manipulation.
Simsek's green light came two weeks after prosecutors requested authorisation to investigate Ibrahim Omer Gonul, who chaired Turkey's Capital Markets Board (SPK) for four years until his mandate ended in April.
In their letter to the ministry, prosecutors said there were "clear and sufficient indications" that Gonul had failed to fulfil his responsibilities during his tenure in office.
The scandal has put pressure on President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's ruling AKP, with one senior party official resigning after allegations about her investment activities.
The crisis erupted when several funds were unable to satisfy investor redemption demands.
The SPK quickly placed seven companies that manage 131 investment funds with assets reportedly worth some $17 billion into liquidation.
More than 455,000 individual investors have been affected, it has said.
The chairman of Saudi Arabia's General Entertainment Authority on Wednesday said that the exhibition Six Kings Slam tennis tournament has been postponed for logistical reasons, after Yemen's Houthis carried out several deadly attacks on the kingdom.
"The Six Kings Slam tournament has been postponed due to logistical reasons and will now take place on December 27," wrote Turki Alalshikh on X, sharing a statement from the Riyadh Season entertainment programme.
Irish author Sally Rooney can no longer sell her books in the UK because of her support for the activist group Palestine Action, proscribed by London, her publisher Faber said Wednesday.
"Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work... As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format," Faber said in a statement on its website.
The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) said on Wednesday that it now recommends airlines take potential risks into account when flying in Jordanian airspace, easing earlier guidance that advised carriers to avoid the airspace altogether.
The conflict zone information bulletin on Jordan was however extended until November 16, it said on its website.

articles.title: Zelenskyy Vows Refinery Strikes, Expresses Anger At US Intel Disruption
articles.body:
KYIV -- Ukrainian forces have struck an oil refinery in Russia's Ryazan region, Russian officials said, hours after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine would resume attacks on Russian energy facilities and voiced anger over a "dangerous" disruption of satellite intelligence from the United States.
Defying an "energy cease-fire" announced unilaterally last week by US President Donald Trump, Zelenskyy told the Financial Times in an interview published on October 15 that "we're done" with holding off on launching attacks on Russia oil structures.
Hours later, Ryazan Governor Pavel Malkov said in a post on Telegram that "our region came under a massive drone attack," adding that "a fire broke out at the oil refinery."
Russia's Defense Ministry later said Ukraine had attempted a massive attack on the Ryazan oil refinery, adding that falling drone debris had sparked a fire at the facility.
The Ukrainian military has not immediately confirmed the attack, which would be the first by Kyiv since Trump announced the cease-fire on October 11. The Rosneft-owned Ryazan refinery has been targeted by drones several times in recent months and accounts for nearly 5 percent of Russia's total oil refining capacity.
Neither of the warring parties officially confirmed agreeing to the truce announced by Trump, and while Ukraine halted attacks on Russian refineries for three days, Russia continued to strike Ukrainian energy facilities and other installations.
"The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We're done," Zelenskyy told the Financial Times in the interview.
Zelenskyy had said Ukraine was willing to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries if Moscow agreed to stop striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
The Ukrainian leader's sharp tone continued when discussing a recent crisis involving a cut in the supply of US intelligence to Kyiv.
Zelenskyy told the FT that the suspension was presented to Kyiv as a technical glitch, an idea he dismissed while calling the disruption in the Starshield, the military version of the Starlink satellite communications system, "dangerous."
Pressure On The Pentagon
Pressure is mounting on the Pentagon to explain the reported restrictions on satellite communications used by Ukraine’s military, with Republican Senator Thom Tillis calling for an inspector-general investigation and warning that Ukrainian civilians and US personnel may have been put at unnecessary risk.
Tillis, a Republican, said on October 14 he would ask the Defense Department’s inspector-general to investigate what he described as a potentially dangerous breakdown involving Starshield, which is controlled by the US government.
“The latest reporting suggests this strategic snafu may have occurred more locally within DOD Starshield systems, not with Starlink or SpaceX,” Tillis wrote on social media.
He said Ukrainian civilians and US diplomatic and security personnel had been placed at unnecessary risk without warning.
“At best, this was an unacceptable error or lapse, and at worst a conscious decision to clear the field for a Russian attack,” Tillis added.
RFE/RL has learned from congressional sources that a group of lawmakers was circulating a letter on October 14 calling on the Defense Department’s inspector-general to investigate the episode. The letter was expected to be sent in the coming days.
The call for an investigation comes amid mounting bipartisan concern over reports that satellite connectivity restrictions have disrupted Ukrainian military operations. Some have also speculated that it could possibly be a move by the administration to pressure Kyiv into refraining from oil refinery attacks on Russia.
But it remains unclear who authorized the restrictions, whether they affected commercial Starlink or Starshield, and whether Washington also reduced intelligence support to Kyiv.
Axios, quoting sources, reported that the White House told Ukraine they do not control Elon Musk's SpaceX, the owner of Starlink.
Musk wrote on X, which he owns, that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
Dan Rice, president of American University Kyiv and a former special adviser to the commander in chief of Ukraine’s armed forces, warned that restrictions could have grave consequences if they prevented Ukrainian forces from directing interceptors against incoming Russian drones.
“When you have 500 inbound Shaheeds, jet-powered Shaheeds, and I was hit within 400 meters twice this week,” Rice told RFE/RL, “you need to have interceptors going out to protect Ukrainian civilians.”
He warned that if satellite connectivity prevented high-speed interceptors from reaching their targets, Russian drones could strike civilian locations, killing women, children and other noncombatants. He also noted that Russian forces had targeted universities, schools and children’s hospitals.
Retired Rear Admiral Mark Montgomery, senior director of the Center on Cyber and Technology Innovation and a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told RFE/RL that the reported limits impaired Ukraine’s ability to control medium-range drone strikes against Russian logistics routes and command-and-control facilities supporting Moscow’s forces in occupied Ukrainian territory.
He described the affected operations as involving targets roughly 150 to 250 kilometers behind Russian lines. He also distinguished the satellite-service issue from the reported failure to provide warnings of incoming attacks, saying the Pentagon inspector general should investigate both.
Meanwhile, Moscow continued its attacks on Ukraine on October 15, a day after Russian missile and drone strikes pounded civilian and energy infrastructure across the country, killing at least nine people and leaving hundreds of thousands without power.
Ukraine's Air Force reported on the morning of October 15 that Russia had launched 580 drones and two Kh-59 missiles at Ukraine overnight, adding that the attack was ongoing.

articles.title: North Korea tests two submarine-launched missiles, state media reports
articles.body:
North Korea tests two submarine-launched missiles, state media reports
The tests showcase North Korea’s war deterrent capabilities in the region, KCNA says.
North Korea has test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles in the sea off its east coast, state media KCNA reports.
The test-fire on Wednesday aimed to examine the reliability of war deterrents and improve the navy’s skill in performing strategic missions, the outlet said.
One of the missiles fired was a Pulhwasal-3-31, the same type of strategic cruise missile North Korea said it test-fired from land last week, according to KCNA.
Senior military officers observed the tests conducted at sea off the country’s east coast. KCNA added that the tests had no adverse impact on the security of neighbouring countries.
North Korea is not yet believed to have launched a modern missile submarine in full operation. This is a top military priority of the country’s leader Kim Jong Un, who has overseen the development of a range of strategic ballistic and cruise missiles.
Last year, Kim Jong Un criticised a nuclear submarine deal between the US and South Korea while he toured his country’s submarine production facility, where state media images showed an 8,700-tonne nuclear-powered missile submarine under construction. On his tour, he described the deal as a threat to the stability of the Korean Peninsula, KCNA reported.
Recent developments
Pyongyang has fired off a flurry of missiles in recent weeks.
Earlier this week, North Korea fired multiple ballistic missiles towards the sea off its east coast, adding to a series of tests as tensions between Seoul and Pyongyang are on the rise.
On October 3, North Korea also tested a hypersonic intermediate-range missile designed to evade missile defences in South Korea and Japan.
After the ballistic missile launch, Seoul’s Joint Chiefs of Staff spokesperson Jang Do-young said the move appeared to be a show of force as it came days after South Korea tested its own hypersonic weapon.
Last week, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung oversaw the country’s first test firing of a hypersonic missile, a rare public showcase of a missile test by a South Korean president.
Lee’s office said the hypersonic weapon, once fully developed, would enhance South Korea’s ability to strike key targets by surprise in the “Korean Peninsula theatre of operations”.
Inter-Korean relations have further soured as a landmine blast, which Seoul blamed on North Korea, wounded three soldiers in September in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) between the two countries.
A joint South Korean-United Nations investigation concluded that two landmines that exploded last month in the DMZ were planted by North Korean forces about a year ago, prompting Seoul to demand an official apology.
Pyongyang has sharply accelerated military fortification along the DMZ as part of leader Kim Jong Un’s “hostile-states” policy, launched in 2023, to permanently sever ties with South Korea.
Diplomatic efforts on the Korean Peninsula have stalled since the collapse of denuclearisation talks between Washington and Pyongyang in 2019 during the first Trump administration. While Trump has floated the possibility of meeting Kim Jong Un in his second term, no such meeting has materialised.

articles.title: FACTBOX: SpaceX restricts access to Starlink for Ukrainian military
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. SpaceX limited the speed of Starlink satellite internet terminals used by the Ukrainian army overnight, Sergey Beskrestnov, Vladimir Zelensky’s external adviser and expert in communications and unmanned systems, said.
Below are the main facts on the subject.
Restriction of access
- SpaceX imposed restrictions on the operation of Starlink terminals for the Ukrainian army overnight, disrupting its operations, Sergey Sternenko, a former adviser to Ukraine’s defense minister, wrote on Telegram.
- Sternenko speculated that SpaceX had acted at the request of US President Donald Trump’s administration.
- Zelensky’s external adviser Beskrestnov later confirmed the reports on Telegram.
- According to him, the restrictions currently apply to the ‘military package’ of Starshield services, with the speed limit set at 100 miles per hour (about 160 kilometers per hour - TASS).
- This "disrupted a number of missions," Beskrestnov said.
- In his view, "this action cannot be a coincidence and has to do with the current political situation."
- Ukraine once again received no intelligence warning from its Western partners last night, Vladimir Zelensky said.
- The US warned Ukraine that it could suspend intelligence sharing, Zelensky said in an interview with NPR. According to him, Ukrainian generals reported that they had been notified of this possibility at the military level.
- Ukraine received no intelligence warnings regarding the first wave of Russian ballistic missile launches overnight into October 14, but warnings about subsequent attacks did come in, RBC Ukraine quoted Ukrainian Air Force Spokesman Yury Ignat as saying.
Consequences
- A slowdown in Starlink service is making it virtually impossible to launch medium-range drones, and some missions involving them have already been cancelled since the start of the day, the 7th Corps of the Ukrainian airborne assault troops reported on Telegram.
- The Ukrainian armed forces rely entirely on Starlink satellite internet, so the Kiev authorities must travel to the US to negotiate the lifting of access restrictions, Verkhovna Rada lawmaker Alexey Goncharenko (listed in Russia as a terrorist and extremist) said.
- The Ukrainian army will no longer be able to counter Russian jet-powered drones due to the reduced speed of the US Starlink satellite Internet service, Zelensky’s external adviser on communications and unmanned systems, Beskrestnov, said.
- As the adviser pointed out, Kiev uses Starlink to counter jet-powered drones, but restrictions on its operation will now prevent the Ukrainian military from doing so.
- Beskrestnov said that through their actions Ukraine’s partners "actually deprive" Kiev of one of the few chances to intercept such drones.
- The slowdown of Starlink terminals caught the Ukrainian military by surprise, occurring entirely without warning, the British newspaper Financial Times (FT) wrote citing sources.
- The report says that Ukrainian drones relying on Starlink terminals are experiencing signal disruptions at speeds above 160 kmph.
- The reduction in intelligence-sharing from the United States, combined with Starlink's operational restrictions, is seriously hampering the Ukrainian military, unmanned aviation expert and CEO of the Center for Integrated Unmanned Solutions Dmitry Kuzyakin told TASS.
- According to him, the Kiev regime’s unchecked actions are irritating both the US president himself and a segment of the American establishment that has heavily invested in Ukraine.
- A number of cyber operations by the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) against Russia may be disrupted or delayed due to SpaceX restricting the speed of Starlink satellite Internet terminals used by Ukrainian security agencies, Sergey Trukhachev, a technical and digital security expert, told TASS.
- He also noted that the SpaceX restrictions would directly impact the Ukrainian armed forces as well.
- This would primarily affect Ukrainian operators of high-speed unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), the expert added.
Response
- Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski warned US entrepreneur and SpaceX owner Elon Musk on social media platform X, amid reports that connection speeds for Starlink satellite internet terminals used by the Ukrainian military have been throttled.

articles.title: US Threatened Immediate Intelligence Cutoff Unless Ukraine Halts Strikes
articles.body:
US intelligence officials warned Ukraine that Washington would immediately stop sharing intelligence if Kyiv continued attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.
The Washington Post reported, citing a person familiar with the matter, that the warning was conveyed to Ukraine’s embassy in Washington. It came amid disputes over an energy ceasefire announced by President Donald Trump and Ukrainian complaints that some Russian ballistic missile attacks had arrived without advance warning from partners.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Trump administration has previously warned that it could suspend intelligence sharing and halt European purchases of US weapons for Ukraine if Kyiv refused to stop deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
The newspaper’s source said the US had not completely halted intelligence sharing. The source also noted that the missiles used in recent attacks on Kyiv had previously evaded warning systems.
Earlier, Zelensky said that Ukrainian forces received no warnings from partners about Russian ballistic missile launches toward Kyiv for two consecutive nights, as attacks struck the capital’s energy infrastructure.
He subsequently disputed the Pentagon’s explanation that a technical problem was responsible, saying the failure to provide warnings reflected a deliberate decision, according to the Financial Times.
President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that military commanders had received warnings about a possible intelligence cutoff.
Trump Weighs Easing Shadow Fleet Sanctions to Lower Oil Shipping Costs
“They said this to my generals, not to me,” he said.
“My generals said they had received this information at the military level.”
Trump, however, said intelligence cooperation would continue.
“We are helping them, and we are sharing intel. We want the war to end,” he told reporters.
Trump announced an immediate energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on Oct. 11, saying both sides had agreed. He demanded that Ukraine refrain from attacking Russian oil refineries.
After several days of Russian attacks, Zelensky said he had lifted the prohibition on strikes against Russian refineries
Zelensky said Kyiv will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries after Washington pressured Ukraine to halt attacks, warning that the US has endangered Ukrainian lives by restricting access to intelligence and Starlink satellite communications.
“The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” Zelensky told the Financial Times in an interview in London.
Last week, Trump announced an agreement for Russia to supply diesel to US and global markets, drawing criticism from US lawmakers and European allies.
Zelensky described the deal as a “simple victory” for the Kremlin in an interview with British broadcaster Piers Morgan on Wednesday.
“It’s a pity that we are losing a strong partner,” Zelensky said.
He also accused Trump of taking Russia’s side in the war, arguing that Washington should remain neutral rather than favor Moscow.
“This is our country, our body, our home, our children,” Zelensky said. “That’s why it’s painful when Trump chooses one side.”
“If you’re in the middle, you have to stay in the middle. Not on the wrong side,” he added. “This is not the right side of history.”
The dispute comes as Russian forces continue attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities. Zelensky said Russian strikes had left more than 600,000 people without electricity.
Moscow has also intensified aerial attacks as battlefield advances remain limited, with both sides targeting energy infrastructure.
Zelensky has sought to strengthen European support amid uncertainty over Washington’s commitment. During his visit to London on Wednesday, he met British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and King Charles III.
You can also highlight the text and press Ctrl + Enter

articles.title: Zelensky Says US Deliberately Restricted Starlink as US Lawmakers Condemn Shutdown
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Starlink satellite communications were intentionally restricted during massive Russian attacks on Ukraine, questioning explanations that the disruption was caused by technical problems.
Speaking in an exclusive interview with British broadcaster Piers Morgan on Wednesday, Oct. 14, Zelensky said the restrictions undermined Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian drones, defend its energy infrastructure and protect civilians.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Ukrainian president said the disruption began around 1 a.m., as Russia launched another wave of missiles and drones against Ukraine.
“I’m sure that they knew what they did. Absolutely. Because it was 1 a.m.,” Zelensky said when Morgan asked whether the restrictions were deliberate.
“We are professionals. We understand what’s going on. If you are losing the speed of Starlink, we understand what’s going on. So they switched off. That’s their decision,” he added.
His remarks came as Ukrainian officials confirmed speed restrictions affecting military communications and US lawmakers from both parties condemned the disruption, warning that it could endanger Ukrainian civilians and benefit Russia.
‘People are dying because of his decision’
Zelensky said Ukrainian forces immediately contacted SpaceX, American military commanders and other US partners after discovering the overnight disruptions.
American officials had attributed the intelligence-sharing problems to technical difficulties, Zelensky said, but the disruptions reportedly continued during subsequent attacks.
‘Putin Is Laughing’ – Zelensky Calls Trump’s Russian Diesel Deal a Victory for Moscow
Starlink, meanwhile, plays a crucial role in Ukraine’s defense against Russian Shahed drones, including interceptor drones that use satellite communications to reach incoming targets.
“It’s not about just attack. As I said, we didn’t attack their energy. It’s not about attack. It’s also about defending the lives,” Zelensky told Morgan.
Asked whether he was angry with Musk, Zelensky described the decision as a serious mistake.
“I don’t know, him or somebody pushed him to... I don’t know really,” he said.
He nevertheless warned of the consequences.
“People are dying because of his decision,” Zelensky said, cautioning that further casualties could follow if Russian attacks continued while Starlink remained restricted.
He appealed directly for the restoration of normal service.
“I hope that it’s a mistake, maybe huge technical problem, I don’t know, but we are asking... to switch on,” he said.
US lawmakers condemn restrictions as potentially aiding Russia
The tightening of Ukraine’s satellite communications access drew bipartisan criticism in Washington, with lawmakers questioning the consequences of limiting critical defensive capabilities during active Russian attacks.
The Congressional Ukraine Caucus, whose co-chairs include Democratic Representatives Marcy Kaptur and Mike Quigley and Republican Representatives Brian Fitzpatrick and Joe Wilson, issued a joint warning.
“We are alarmed by reports from Ukraine that US intelligence and Starlink support are being withheld, putting innocent civilians and American citizens in Ukraine at the mercy of Russian attacks,” the lawmakers said.
The caucus said Washington must continue providing intelligence to protect civilians and stressed that US allies pay for Ukraine’s Starlink access.
“Restrictions that put civilians in harm’s way are unconscionable and will not be accepted by Congress,” the lawmakers declared.
Republican Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina also publicly challenged Musk, warning that intentionally degrading Ukraine’s ability to defend itself could be construed as helping a mass murderer.
Republican Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska criticized the administration’s handling of intelligence-sharing and Starlink access, arguing that reducing such support effectively aided Russia’s invasion and its attacks on Ukrainian cities.
Their objections underscored concern among Ukraine’s Republican supporters that the restrictions could weaken Kyiv’s defensive capabilities at a critical moment.
Democratic lawmakers also raised questions about the humanitarian and strategic consequences of restricting systems on which Ukrainian troops and civilians depend.
Democratic Congressman Steny Hoyer of Maryland issued one of the strongest statements, warning that the restrictions could leave more Ukrainian civilians exposed to Russian attacks.
In an official statement, Hoyer said that if Trump administration officials were involved, it would represent a “heinous act of betrayal” of Ukraine and a fellow democracy under attack.
He called for full Starlink access to be restored, arguing that Washington should help Ukraine win rather than tip the scales in Putin’s favor.
European allies also joined the criticism.
Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski confronted Musk on X, questioning whether the billionaire was using satellite communications as a political instrument.
“Hey, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?” Sikorski wrote, warning that European customers were watching.
Musk points to US military and Trump
Musk responded by distinguishing between commercial Starlink and Starshield, the military-grade satellite service.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government,” Musk wrote on X.
He said decisions about operational limits were ultimately made by the US military and the president.
Musk maintained that commercial Starlink service could be used for civilian and defensive purposes but should not support offensive military operations.
A senior US official, however, told Axios that the Trump administration had not been involved in imposing the restrictions. Ukrainian officials remained suspicious that the move was connected to Washington’s pressure on Kyiv to halt strikes against Russian oil facilities.
The conflicting accounts left unanswered who authorized the restrictions, and why they were introduced without warning.
Partial restoration leaves Ukrainian interceptors at risk
Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov reported Wednesday evening that Starlink connectivity was being restored at speeds of up to 160 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour), although restrictions on the military-grade Starshield system remained in place.
Two Ukrainian officials told RFE/RL that connectivity had improved at speeds below that threshold, but the limits continued to complicate efforts to intercept Russia’s increasingly frequent jet-powered drones.
One Ukrainian source said the operating speed would need to reach at least 450 kilometers per hour (280 miles per hour) to effectively counter the faster Russian drones.
