articles.title: In Ukraine, civilian casualties were already rising. Restrictions on Starlink will only worsen the death toll
articles.body:
In Ukraine the situation was already jittery enough. Donald Trump has been inventing ceasefires and buying Russian diesel to shore up his flagging popularity, while a sinister new wave of faster, jet-powered drones are breaking through Kyiv’s stretched air defences. Casualties are rising as the weather turns.
Overnight, Russia bombed three power plants that supply Kyiv, aiming to cut off heating and electricity to the city. According to the president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for a second night in a row no warning came from Ukraine’s western allies of the incoming ballistic missiles – and so no air raid alert was issued.
Then, on Tuesday night, and without warning, Ukraine’s military found that Elon Musk’s Starlink mobile internet system, on which it heavily relies, had stopped working on its drones flying faster than 160km/h (100mph).
Or at least that was the official limit: in practice, drones flying over 80km/h could no longer communicate.
The immediate assumption in Kyiv is that the White House is once again trying to bully Ukraine into accepting an unattractive deal with Russia.
However, on Tuesday Trump did say that no intelligence-sharing had been paused, and similar comments were made by Mark Rutte, the secretary general of Nato on Wednesday. It is possible the lack of ballistic warning is coincidental.
Even Serhii Beskrestnov, Zelenskyy’s high-profile military technology adviser, has expressed public doubts about whether the US had paused the sharing of missile detection. “Friends, this is not the first time that the launch of an S-400 has not been detected,” he posted on Monday. “We should not jump to conclusions.”
However, there has now been an absence of incoming warnings for two days in a row. The second of these was in tandem with the unexpected throttling of Starlink, a system supplied by Musk with the approval of the US military.
So it is hardly reassuring against the backdrop of White House threats, which have emerged every time a flailing Trump has tried to end the war in Ukraine.
The last time Trump paused intelligence-sharing – which is, in effect, valuable information about Russian positions and movements – was in March 2025, shortly after Zelenskyy’s infamous dusting down in the Oval Office.
“You don’t have the cards,” Trump said, as he took another away. Ukraine rapidly lost a chunk of territory it had occupied in Russia’s Kursk region before sharing was restored.
A confirmed pause this time would mark a serious breach when Ukraine is more than holding off its larger neighbour on the frontline, even as the situation on the home front is worsening.
Russia has bombed two bridges in Kyiv, gas stations, city centre buildings and out-of-town warehouses, showing little restraint as it aims to harm Ukrainian civilians while it struggles to win the conventional war.
The effect of a more permanent halt to Starlink for Ukrainian drones or anything military that moves faster than 50mph is a little more complex. Starlink is how Ukraine directs many of its mid-strike (or mid-range) drones accurately towards their targets into occupied areas behind enemy lines, critical for helping the defenders maintain the rough balance on the front.
Yet, ironically, Starlink is not used for the long-range missions that target the Russian oil refineries about which Trump is so concerned, because it has long been disabled by the company inside Russia’s internationally recognised borders.
“There’s no meaningful effect on deep-strike operations,” one Ukrainian soldier said, while conceding there could be as much as a 30-fold drop in mid-strike operations because the alternatives are 30 times more expensive. Commanders are “replanning everything”, the soldier added, and aiming to find ways to carry on missions using different technologies and techniques.
Starlink is also, more importantly – as Beskrestnov emphasised on Wednesday – used by air-defence interceptors in the most effective system to down Russia’s deadly new jet-powered Shahed drones. These are at least twice as fast as traditional piston-engined Shaheds, and Ukraine’s rate of interception had dropped to 60% in September, before recovering to 75% according to the country’s air force.
The reality, then, is that the Starlink manoeuvre may not have much impact on oil prices, and only a limited effect on Ukraine’s frontline position, while putting the country’s civilians in greater danger.
As the Ukrainian human rights activist Oleksandra Matviichuk put it: “Without that protection, Russian drones will strike residential buildings, hospitals and schools like targets in a shooting gallery.”
Meanwhile, diplomatically, the situation is more finely poised. It was already the case that the Trump White House had proved to be a difficult and unreliable partner. What Zelenskyy, on a visit to London on Wednesday, needs from the likes of the UK prime minster, Andy Burnham, is pressure on the US to ensure the Starlink pause and whatever is happening with intelligence-sharing does not metastasise into a deeper crisis.

articles.title: What is Starshield, SpaceX’s military-grade Starlink system, and how will its restriction affect Ukraine?
articles.body:
The development – and its dire consequences for Ukraine – has put the spotlight on Starlink -SpaceX’s commercial satellite internet service – and Starshield, a powerful military version developed by Elon Musk’s company for the Pentagon.
Here’s what we know about the two SpaceX systems, how they are controlled and why Zelenskyy has framed the shift as a betrayal by Donald Trump and the US.
What has happened to Ukraine’s connection?
On Tuesday night, Ukraine’s military reported the Starlink satellite communications system, produced by SpaceX but managed by the US government, was no longer working on terminals moving at speeds greater than 100mph (160km/h).
Kyiv installs SpaceX Starlink receptors in many of its drones as part of an onboard guidance system. Kyiv said the change was imposed without any explanation from the US.
How does the restriction affect Ukraine?
The restriction had two immediate consequences: It effectively rendered most of the drones used by Ukraine to strike behind the frontlines inoperable and it hampered air defence systems that stop Russian drones bombarding Kyiv.
Ukraine uses Starlink systems to direct many mid-range drones towards their targets – a critical frontline offensive capability. Russian Shaheds fly at speeds close to 200mph, so the new restriction means Ukrainian interceptor drones have no chance to chase them down.
Starlink is not used for long-range Ukrainian missions that have successfully targeted Russian oil refineries in recent months.
A Ukrainian air defence unit intercepts a Shahed drone during an attack on Kyiv. Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/AP
What is Starshield?
Starshield is a SpaceX business unit that develops military and intelligence satellite systems for the Pentagon. Starshield’s service is separate from Starlink’s commercial broadband service, but the distinction is sometimes blurry.
Starlink cannot be used for offensive military action, SpaceX says, only defensive activities or for use by civilian clients.
Starshield, however, allows those capabilities and uses enhanced encryption to transmit sensitive information. In addition, Starshield provides users with the ability to integrate sensors on object like drones. Starshield’s secure communications rely on Starlink, the vast network of 11,000 satellites that Musk and SpaceX have sent into space since 2019.
Who made the decision to restrict access, Musk or the Pentagon?
Musk said the Ukrainian military was linked to Starshield, because Starlink is not licensed to clients who are using weapons. He added that any Starshield disruptions being experienced by Ukraine would be the responsibility of the US government, not SpaceX. “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk said, referring to Donald Trump.
A Ukrainian serviceman prepares a Starlink satellite at his positions at the frontline. Photograph: Reuters
The White House has not confirmed or denied Musk’s assertion. But the Trump administration has been pressuring Ukraine to limit its strikes on energy targets inside Russia.
What has the reaction been?
Zelenskyy said he felt personally betrayed by Trump, in an interview with Piers Morgan, saying Kyiv was “losing a strong partner”. As for what it meant for Ukraine and its people, Zelenskyy said: “This decision will bring a lot of human losses … of course, people will die.”
In the US, Democrats denounced the Trump administration. “Trump’s making a choice – and it directly aids Putin’s slaughter of Ukrainian civilians,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Democrats said in a post on X, describing the restrictions as “unconscionable”.
Republican senator Tom Tillis voiced his concern on X: “Supporting Ukrainian sovereignty – or at the very least, allowing for it – should not be a gray area for the US government or for American corporations.”

articles.title: US reportedly weighs dropping 'Mother of All Bombs' on Iran
articles.body:
The U.S. is considering using its largest non-nuclear bomb against Iran if President Donald Trump revives the dormant war, CNN reported Thursday.
The military plans to use the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB) bomb, nicknamed the "Mother Of All Bombs," to target Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites, the news outlet reported, quoting officials familiar with the matter.
Trump seeks to boost his low approval ratings ahead of November midterm elections, with polls showing the unpopular war in Iran and resulting fuel and other price increases are hurting his Republican Party.
Diplomatic efforts to end the conflict, which erupted with U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran in February, have stalled since the summer.
But officials doubt the bomb's efficacy if deployed, particularly its ability to destroy suspected underground nuclear sites in the Islamic republic.
"The MOAB is a massive information operations weapon that is effective for large-area clearance but not much else," a source familiar with the plans told CNN.
"It is not designed as a deep penetration warhead."
The U.S. and Israel said the war was necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons – a goal Tehran has long denied pursuing.
Concerns also exist about potential civilian casualties from such a large weapon.
Washington has in recent weeks dialed back military operations in favor of economic pressure.
Agence France-Presse (AFP) has contacted the Pentagon for comment.
In 2017, the U.S. military in Afghanistan dropped the MOAB to target Daesh hideouts in a complex of tunnels and bunkers, killing more than 90 terrorists.

articles.title: US has warned Ukraine data sharing will cease in event of new strikes on Russia – The Washington Post
articles.body:
US has warned Ukraine data sharing will cease in event of new strikes on Russia – The Washington Post
US intelligence officials warned the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington that the US would immediately halt all intelligence sharing in the event of new strikes against Russian energy facilities.
Source: The Washington Post, citing an informed source
Details: According to the WP's interlocutor, the warnings from the US were sweeping.
"The warnings were so widespread that anyone with a Ukrainian-sounding last name got a call," the source noted.
On Tuesday, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that Ukrainian generals had received threats from Donald Trump's administration regarding a halt to intelligence sharing.
Trump himself claimed on Tuesday 13 October that information sharing would continue.
"We are helping them, and we are sharing intel. We want the war to end," the US president stated.
Anxiety regarding a cessation of intelligence sharing arose after Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv overnight into Tuesday and Wednesday without prior warning for Ukrainian air defence systems.
"A Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. Once again, no early warning from our partners," Zelenskyy commented regarding the strikes.
The president reported that on the night of 13-14 October, the Russians launched 39 ballistic missiles and over 120 strike drones. Russian missiles hit energy facilities in Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast and Kharkiv.
Background:
- On 11 October, Trump published a post on his social media Truth Social announcing an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine, which allegedly took effect immediately. He said that both sides had consented to cease strikes on energy infrastructure, although neither party had been informed of this.
- Barak Ravid, a journalist at American news portal Axios, stated that Zelenskyy had been unaware of the "energy ceasefire" between Ukraine and Russia announced by Trump, but added that Ukraine supports it.
- On the nights of 12-13 and 13-14 October, Russian forces launched massive attacks on Ukraine's energy facilities.
- Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, commenting on overnight Russian strikes on Ukrainian cities, said Kremlin ruler Vladimir Putin has rejected the US-proposed "energy ceasefire". Zelenskyy later called the Russian strikes entirely deliberate.

articles.title: 'Mother of all bombs': US potential Iran strike plans include largest non-nuclear weapon - report
articles.body:
The United States military has developed strike plans against Iran that include using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb (MOAB), colloquially known as the "mother of all bombs," the largest non-nuclear weapon in the US arsenal, CNN reported on Thursday.
According to CNN, multiple US officials said that the plans called for the MOAB to be used against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites, including Pickaxe Mountain.
Another source said that the phrasing used in the plan was that the attack would come “prior to US retrograde in CENTCOM AOR (area of responsibility),” meaning that the US might strike Iran and then immediately pull its forces out of the region.
Several of US President Donald Trump's advisors have also told CNN that, despite Trump's claims that he would not take further action against Iran before the US midterms, it remains unclear whether he will change his mind before Election Day.
The potential deployment of the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal would mark a significant escalation in the conflict, although officials familiar with military planning discussions told CNN that questions remain over its effectiveness in achieving Washington's strategic objectives.
MOAB unlikely to penetrate Iranian nuclear sites
According to several sources, the MOAB likely would be unable to penetrate deep below the ground, where Iranian nuclear facilities, such as Pickaxe Mountain, are believed to be.
“The MOAB is a massive information operation type weapon that is great for huge area clearance but not much else,” one source familiar with military planning discussions around Iran told CNN. “It is definitely not designed as a deep penetration warhead.”
The source said the MOAB's main tactical advantage in this scenario would be its psychological effect on Iran.
“POTUS has unfortunately put himself in a situation where he is almost compelled to do something and, without the ammunition designed to penetrate that level… you have to look at psychological effects for which the MOAB is well-equipped,” the source said.
When asked about the plan, a White House official told CNN that “President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon,” adding that they do not comment on sensitive military plans.
A Pentagon official told CNN that it "plans for a wide range of operational scenarios to execute Presidential and Secretary‑level direction and to ensure mission success in any operational environment.”
Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump Says Leakers ‘Should Be Shot’ and Rails Against Media at Rally
articles.body:
President Donald Trump suggested on Wednesday that people who leak sensitive information about the government to the media “should be shot,” calling them the “scum of the earth.”
“In my opinion, leakers should be shot,” Trump said Wednesday during a rally in Bullhead City, Arizona. “In the old days, we used to shoot leakers, you know, when they leak what time you’re going to attack a country.”
Trump’s remark came as he described a planned raid on Iran that he said had to be delayed after somebody “leaked the time we were leaving, the time we were arriving.” He appeared to be referring to Operation Midnight Hammer in June last year, when the U.S., in a surprise attack, struck three of Iran’s most critical nuclear sites as Tehran was in a 12-day war with Israel.
In the wake of the June attack, a leaked Defense Intelligence Agency preliminary report found that Iran’s nuclear sites had not been as damaged as the Trump Administration first claimed them to be and that Iran could still enrich uranium. Reports also said Iran may have also moved enriched material from the facilities before the attack.
“Somebody leaked—some sleazebag,” the President said. “They ought to go to jail and be shot. For the rest of their life, They should be in jail. But they leaked that we were leaving at 12:07 from Missouri, and it was in the New York Times, CNN.”
Moments later, Trump pointed to the journalists covering his rally and said they were “almost as bad” as leakers. “They leak false information,” the President said. “That makes them a leaker, right?”
Trump’s long-held view that leakers are bad—most of the time
Leakers have incensed Trump even before he was President. In a 2010 clip previewing the radio show of Fox News’ Brian Kilmeade, Trump assailed WikiLeaks, which, at the time, had just released hundreds of thousands of classified U.S. military and diplomatic documents provided by Army private Chelsea Manning. “I think it’s disgraceful,” he told Kilmeade. “I think there should be like death penalty or something.”
As a civilian flirting with the U.S.’s top job, he frequently lashed out at former National Security Agency intelligence contractor Edward Snowden on social media and in public remarks. Snowden’s leaks in 2013 revealed NSA programs that sparked a global debate about government surveillance. Trump, in reaction to the leaks, said that he was a “spy” who “should be executed.”
As President, when the New York Times reported in 2017 that his campaign had repeated contacts with senior Russian intelligence officials in the year before the 2016 presidential election, Trump took to then-Twitter to lament how “leaking, and even illegal classified leaking, has been a big problem in Washington for years” and raged that such leakers “will be caught.”
When a whistleblower came forward in 2019 with a complaint alleging that Trump was "using the power of his office to solicit interference from a foreign country" in the 2020 U.S. election, Trump told the staff of the U.S. mission to the U.N. that he wanted to know who gave the whistleblower information. “That’s close to a spy,” he said. “You know what we used to do in the old days when we were smart, right, with spies and treason, right? We used to handle them a little differently than we do now.”
But Trump has welcomed leaks that benefit him politically. Days before the 2016 presidential election, at a rally in Wilmington, Ohio, he celebrated how WikiLeaks released private emails from John Podesta, the campaign chair of his Democratic opponent Hillary Clinton, as well as emails from the Democratic National Committee. “Boy, I love reading those WikiLeaks!” Trump said. He also mused about Russia having hacked into Clinton’s email, and urged them to publish what they may have found. Trump even said that he could be a fan of Snowden if he released former President Barack Obama’s birth records at a time when conspiracy theories largely fanned by Trump hounded the Democratic former President.
Trump Administration tries to crack down on leaks
The second Trump Administration has since stepped up to limit leaks to the press. When reports of the U.S.’s dwindling ammunition stockpiles amid the war with Iran emerged, the Pentagon subjected dozens of civilian employees and military officers to polygraph tests to identify the source of the leak. Trump had called for the leakers to face long-term jail sentences.
Journalists from the Wall Street Journal and the Washington Post received subpoenas after reporting on national security issues. But the news organizations pushed back against those summons, and the Justice Department withdrew them. In January, the FBI raided a Post reporter’s home, as part of an investigation into a government contractor accused of mishandling sensitive national security information.
The Justice Department has also charged alleged leakers: in April, the department announced it arrested a former Army employee, alleging that she transmitted classified national defense information to unauthorized recipients, including a journalist.
The Defense Department also threatened to withhold Pentagon access to journalists unless they signed an agreement not to publish unauthorized material. Much of the Pentagon press corps declined, and a federal judge sided with the press in March, striking several parts of the department’s press access policy.
Trump has wanted others “shot” too
It’s also not the first time that Trump has floated having certain people shot .
Three years ago, at a California lunch with Republicans, Trump said he was in favor of shooting store robbers and looters, painting himself as tough on crime before the 2024 elections. “They actually go and take everything out of the store, and then you see these guys selling stuff five miles away or selling it from behind cars. It's a horrible thing. When the police are allowed to do their job—and that means, in some cases, shoot them—this will stop immediately.”
The President has also previously pitched shooting migrants to keep them from entering the country. According to the book Border Wars: Inside Trump's Assault on Immigration, by New York Times reporters Michael D. Shear and Julie Hirschfeld Davis, Trump in March 2019 detailed extreme methods to keep them out, privately suggesting to aides that soldiers shoot migrants who cross the border in the legs. But he was told it would not be allowed. Trump addressed the allegations on social media, saying: “I may be tough on Border Security, but not that tough.”
He’s also suggested doing the same to protesters: during the George Floyd protests in the spring of 2020, Trump was reportedly enraged, and, according to his first-term Defense Secretary Mark Esper, the President also considered ordering the military to shoot the racial justice protesters in the legs.
Last week, the President approved what would be the U.S. Army’s first execution of a soldier via firing squad since World War II, and has even shown enthusiasm for livestreaming it. Trump, however, has since changed his tune, amid a chorus of negative feedback.
“There are two thoughts: don’t show it and show it,” Trump told reporters on Saturday. “‘Cause you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did. So I’ll make a decision, ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we’ll make a decision.”

articles.title: King Charles Welcomes Zelensky as Britain Steps Up Military Support for Ukraine
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky met King Charles III at Buckingham Palace on Wednesday, Oct. 14, before holding talks with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, as London pledged faster air defense missile deliveries and tougher sanctions against Russia amid strained US-Ukraine relations.
King Charles received Zelensky for a private audience at Buckingham Palace, underscoring Britain’s continued support for Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I thank His Majesty King Charles III for the audience,” Zelensky said afterward, expressing appreciation for the monarch’s unwavering support and Britain’s assistance to Ukraine.
Britain pledges more missiles and sanctions
Following the royal audience, Burnham welcomed Zelensky to Downing Street with a ceremonial guard of honor involving the Irish Guards.
“We are behind you and that will not change,” Burnham told the Ukrainian president.
Britain announced plans to accelerate a £45 million (approximately $60 million) package of Lightweight Multirole Missiles to strengthen Ukraine’s defenses against Russian drones, including increasingly fast jet-powered models.
The government will bring forward £10 million (approximately $13 million) to meet urgent winter requirements.
London also pledged additional sanctions against Moscow, including restrictions targeting maritime services supporting Russian liquefied natural gas exports.
Burnham said his government would continue providing military and financial support while pressing international partners to increase pressure on Russia.
General Staff Reports 222 Clashes on Wednesday as Russia Continues Pressing Pokrovsk Axis
Burnham seeks to repair US-Ukraine ties
Before meeting Zelensky, Burnham told Parliament he would seek to “repair bridges” between Trump and the Ukrainian president to restore American support.
Despite criticizing Washington’s recent decisions, Zelensky emphasized that Kyiv remained committed to its US partnership.
“We count on our partnership with the United States,” he told Burnham.
“We just want to be very honest, very clear, be strong partners.”
In a separate interview with Piers Morgan, Zelensky said he believed the overnight Starlink restrictions were not caused by technical problems.
“We are professionals. If you are losing the speed of Starlink, we understand what’s going on. So they switched off. That’s their decision,” he said.
He warned that Starlink restrictions weakened Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian drones, while separate disruptions in US intelligence-sharing left Ukraine without advance warnings of incoming Russian ballistic missiles, putting civilian lives at greater risk.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: 850 Shaheds came as Starlink limits hit defense
articles.body:
- Zelenskyy said Russia launched over 850 Shaheds between Oct. 14 and 9 a.m. Oct. 15, during a SpaceX speed cap on Ukraine’s Starlink terminals.
- The 160 km/h Starshield limit, imposed overnight Oct. 13–14, cripples interceptor drones needed against Russian jet-powered Shaheds flying up to 600 km/h.
Russia launched more than 850 Shahed attack drones at Ukraine in roughly a day and a half, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Oct. 15, an onslaught that came as a new speed cap on SpaceX’s Starlink network curtailed the interceptor drones Ukraine uses to shoot them down.
Zelenskyy said the count covered the period from the start of Oct. 14 until 9 a.m. on Oct. 15. He said attacks came in constant waves and that Ukrainian airspace was not free of drones for a single hour. Russian strikes killed three people in Kropyvnytskyi and three more in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Ukrainian media reported.
“From the start of yesterday until 9 a.m. today, there have already been more than 850 Shaheds, and this is precisely at a time of an artificial speed restriction on our defensive capabilities. Some of the Shaheds were shot down. But unfortunately, there were also dozens of hits,” Zelenskyy said, in remarks translated from Ukrainian.
The restriction he referred to took effect overnight on Oct. 13–14, when SpaceX capped Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink used by Ukraine’s armed forces, at 160 km/h (about 100 mph) for terminals in motion. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said SpaceX imposed the limit unilaterally and without warning, and that any terminal moving faster than that loses its connection, disrupting interceptor and mid-range drone missions as well as frontline reconnaissance, logistics and signal relays.
Under the cap, the restriction falls most heavily on Ukraine’s air defense. Russia’s jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones can fly at up to 600 km/h (about 370 mph), so interceptors that must chase them down need far more speed than 160 km/h. Starlink has been blocked over Russian territory since February 2026 under a whitelist of approved terminals, and Ukraine’s long-range strikes on Russian targets rely on other communications. The capped terminals instead serve tactical drones and uncrewed ground vehicles operating over Ukraine and the occupied territories, which means the limit cuts into Ukraine’s defense.
Service was later restored below the 160 km/h threshold, and Mykhailo Fedorov said attack and interceptor drones should be able to fly again, while adding that Ukraine now needs the Starshield speed limit removed altogether.
Elon Musk said on X that the military version of Starlink is controlled by the U.S. military and, ultimately, the U.S. president, the Associated Press reported, while the White House told Kyiv it does not control SpaceX, according to Axios. Zelenskyy told the Financial Times on Oct. 15 that the restriction was a deliberate decision on the American side rather than a technical fault, though he said he did not know whether SpaceX or the U.S. government made the call.
Zelenskyy also accused Moscow of escalating its strikes after seeing sanctions eased and attempts to pressure Kyiv, and urged Americans to side with Ukraine’s defense instead of the aggressor.
The Defense Ministry said it is in contact with the United States, SpaceX and NATO partners and is setting up backup communication channels, but neither SpaceX nor the U.S. Department of War has said whether or when the 160 km/h cap will be lifted.

articles.title: Iran and US on brink of war as Russian mediation falters
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran and US on brink of all-out war as Russia fails to break diplomatic deadlock
Diplomatic efforts to ease tensions between Iran and the United States remain deadlocked despite continued exchanges of messages and mediation attempts, raising fears of a renewed military confrontation as both sides step up their threats and preparations.
Qatar and Pakistan have continued efforts to bring Tehran and Washington back to the negotiating table, but little progress has been made as tensions escalate in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iranian attacks on vessels attempting to use non-Iranian shipping routes have increased.
The diplomatic stalemate comes amid growing US threats and reports of a possible Israeli attack on Iran ahead of Israel's parliamentary elections on 27 October.
Iran, meanwhile, has placed its military on heightened alert, conducting new missile tests in recent days and threatening to unveil additional weapons.
Tehran has also warned Washington and regional governments that another round of war could trigger retaliation across a wider geographical area, including potential ground incursions.
The renewed fighting between Yemen's Houthi movement and Saudi Arabia has further complicated the regional situation, with observers linking the escalation to the wider confrontation between Iran and the US and Israel.
Russia's mediation efforts falter
Russia entered the diplomatic efforts around a week ago, with the Kremlin announcing that President Vladimir Putin had conveyed Tehran's proposals for ending the war with the United States to US President Donald Trump.
According to Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, Putin discussed his forthcoming telephone conversation with Trump during a meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Turkmenistan last week, on the sidelines of a summit of Commonwealth of Independent States leaders.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said on Monday that Pezeshkian had clearly outlined Tehran's position to Putin, including its seven-day proposal for resolving the conflict and other issues surrounding the negotiations.
However, Baghaei stopped short of describing Russia as a formal mediator.
"Technically speaking, in the strict sense of the word, Pakistan and Qatar are still playing the role of actual mediators between Iran and the United States," he said.
He added that Tehran welcomed diplomatic efforts by friendly countries, noting that consultations with Moscow on the nuclear issue and other matters were longstanding.
Iranian analyst Ali Gholhaki told The New Arab that Russian diplomacy was proceeding with "weak and lacklustre steps".
He argued that Moscow was attempting to link efforts to resolve the Iran-US conflict with negotiations over the Russia-Ukraine war, hoping that both disputes could be addressed simultaneously.
This, he suggested, explained Russia's more active diplomatic involvement.
Gholhaki said Iran had demonstrated flexibility, but warned that the current regional military positioning suggested another war was considerably more likely than a diplomatic settlement.
He said a new wave of military escalation could erupt at any moment, although Washington appeared reluctant to become embroiled in a full-scale war before the US congressional midterm elections in November.
According to Gholhaki, the Trump administration would prefer to postpone any expansion of the military confrontation until after the vote.
What could another Iran-US war look like?
Iranian military analyst Mehdi Bakhtiari told TNA that another war was a strong possibility, although he expected any confrontation to be relatively short and extremely intense.
He argued that Washington might attempt another military campaign to secure concessions from Tehran and overcome the strategic difficulties it had encountered in its confrontation with Iran.
Bakhtiari said the US and Israel had already fought two wars against Iran, inflicting substantial damage and losses but failing, in his assessment, to achieve their strategic objectives.
Instead, he argued, they had encountered new challenges, particularly the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz and the resulting rise in global energy and fuel prices.
He suggested that another military campaign could differ significantly from previous confrontations, with attacks potentially concentrating on Iranian nuclear facilities and the country's southern regions.
A central objective, he said, would likely be securing the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
Bakhtiari also warned that Iran had prepared new military strategies for such a scenario.
These could include intensified attacks on US naval vessels, particularly destroyers, following incidents in recent weeks in which Iranian forces had fired towards American warships.
He also raised the possibility of Iranian attacks against a larger number of US military bases across the region, particularly in the United Arab Emirates.
According to Bakhtiari, Iranian military planners believe that targeting US interests in the UAE could significantly increase the costs of further escalation for Washington.
He said Iran's military establishment had spent recent weeks rebuilding its missile and air defence capabilities in preparation for a potential confrontation at sea.
Bakhtiari added that both Iran's political elite and wider public increasingly regarded another round of fighting as likely.
Deep divisions over terms for peace
Masoud Foroughi, former editor-in-chief of the conservative Iranian newspaper Farhikhtegan, said the approaching US and Israeli elections were closely connected to calculations about the military confrontation with Iran.
Speaking to TNA, he argued that the war had not ended in the conventional sense but had instead changed its form and geographical scope.
From Tehran's perspective, he said, the conflict would end only when Washington accepted that military force could not fundamentally alter Iran's political system or its behaviour.
Washington, by contrast, was seeking what he described as Iran's complete surrender, whether through military pressure or diplomacy.
Foroughi said the gap between the two sides' demands was so wide that negotiations under current conditions were unlikely to bridge it.
He compared the situation to two parties standing 50 kilometres apart without any means of communication, arguing that even a distance of one kilometre would be too great for them to hear one another.
As a result, he said, the outcome would continue to depend largely on developments on the ground and each side's political, economic and social ability to withstand pressure.
Foroughi argued that the increasingly aggressive rhetoric from Washington and Tehran was intended to influence each other's strategic calculations.
Regardless of whether Trump intended to launch another direct military campaign before the November elections, he said, the administration was seeking to maintain sufficient pressure to force Iran to reconsider its position.
He concluded that diplomacy would only become effective when the costs of continuing the war became sufficiently high to compel Washington to halt its military campaign.

articles.title: What is the 'mother of all bombs' the US could use against Iran?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
What is the 'mother of all bombs' the US is considering to use against Iran?
The United States is considering using its most powerful non-nuclear bomb against Iran as President Donald Trump weighs renewed military strikes, raising questions about its devastating impact and whether it could penetrate Tehran's heavily fortified nuclear facilities.
According to a CNN report on Thursday, US military planners have drawn up options involving the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, commonly known as the "mother of all bombs" or MOAB, to target Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites.
The plans reportedly include possible strikes on Pickaxe Mountain, an underground facility near Natanz where Washington and Israel believe Iran has stored components of its nuclear programme.
The reported plans come as Trump faces mounting pressure to end the war with Iran, with negotiations stalled and the US president seeking a way to bring the conflict to a close without appearing to concede defeat.
No decision to deploy the bomb has been announced, and the White House has said Trump is keeping all options available.
Here is what to know about the weapon, its destructive capabilities and why the US is considering using it against Iran.
What is the 'mother of all bombs'?
The GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB) is the most powerful conventional bomb in the US military's arsenal.
Weighing approximately 9,800 kilograms (21,600 pounds) and measuring more than nine metres in length, the GPS-guided weapon was developed by the US Air Force in 2003 ahead of the American invasion of Iraq.
Unlike conventional bombs designed to penetrate fortified underground structures, the MOAB is an air-blast weapon that detonates above the ground, generating an enormous explosion across a wide area.
During testing in March 2003, the explosion produced a mushroom cloud visible from approximately 20 miles away.
The weapon was originally designed to destroy large concentrations of troops, military equipment and above-ground fortifications, although its potential targets later expanded to include caves and tunnels.
How destructive is the bomb?
The MOAB is capable of devastating large areas through an immense blast wave that can destroy buildings, military installations and other structures.
The weapon can devastate an area equivalent to approximately nine city blocks, according to the CNN report, although the actual extent of destruction depends on the terrain, surrounding structures and other conditions.
Despite its enormous size, the MOAB is not a nuclear weapon and does not produce the radioactive fallout associated with a nuclear explosion.
The bomb is GPS-guided and is delivered from a military transport aircraft rather than a conventional fighter jet. During its first combat deployment, it was dropped from an American MC-130 aircraft.
Its enormous size and destructive capabilities have also made it a tool of psychological warfare, with US military officials originally hoping that the threat of its use would intimidate enemy forces into surrendering.
Has the 'mother of all bombs' been used before?
Yes. The United States first deployed the MOAB in combat in April 2017, during Trump's first presidential term.
The bomb was dropped on a network of tunnels used by Islamic State (IS) militants in Afghanistan's eastern Nangarhar province, near the border with Pakistan.
The US military said the strike targeted underground tunnels and caves used by IS fighters to move between positions and launch attacks against Afghan and US forces.
Afghan officials reported that 36 IS fighters were killed and three underground tunnels destroyed, along with weapons and ammunition.
US and Afghan officials said at the time that no civilians were killed, although the strike attracted criticism over the use of such an enormous weapon.
Former Afghan President Hamid Karzai condemned the bombing, accusing Washington of using Afghanistan as a testing ground for destructive weapons.
Trump praised the operation at the time, describing it as "another successful job".
The 2017 strike remains the only publicly acknowledged combat use of the MOAB.
Why is Trump considering using it against Iran?
The reported plans come amid uncertainty over how Washington intends to end the conflict after more than six months of US military operations against Iran.
According to CNN, some Trump administration officials have discussed launching a final round of strikes before withdrawing American forces from the region, potentially allowing the president to present the operation as a military victory.
One source familiar with the plans said the proposed attacks could take place before a US military withdrawal from the region covered by Central Command.
The MOAB's psychological impact could also be a factor, with officials suggesting that its deployment could demonstrate overwhelming American military power and increase pressure on Tehran.
However, sources familiar with the discussions have questioned whether such an operation would achieve Washington's strategic objectives or bring the conflict any closer to an end.
Trump has publicly suggested he would refrain from additional military action before November's US midterm elections, although advisers reportedly remain uncertain whether he will maintain that position.
Could the bomb destroy Iran's underground nuclear facilities?
Military officials have expressed serious doubts about whether the MOAB could destroy Iran's most heavily fortified nuclear facilities.
Unlike specialised bunker-busting weapons, the MOAB is designed to unleash a massive explosion across the surface rather than penetrate deeply underground.
Pickaxe Mountain, for example, is believed to be protected by substantial layers of granite, potentially shielding its underground facilities from the bomb's effects.
The US possesses another weapon specifically designed for such targets: the GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator (MOP), which can penetrate hardened underground structures before detonating.
American B-2 bombers deployed 14 of these penetrator bombs during US strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities in June 2025, according to a US Department of Defense report.
The difference highlights a central question surrounding the reported plans: whether deploying the MOAB would inflict meaningful damage on Iran's nuclear programme or primarily serve as a show of force.
What would be the consequences of using it against Iran?
Deploying the MOAB against Iran would represent a significant escalation in the conflict, particularly if the weapon were used against energy infrastructure or facilities near populated areas.
Its enormous blast could cause widespread destruction, while damage to electricity supplies, industrial installations and other essential infrastructure could have consequences far beyond the immediate target.
The International Committee of the Red Cross has warned that explosive weapons with wide-area effects are particularly dangerous in populated areas because their impact can extend beyond intended military targets.
Such attacks can kill and injure civilians, destroy homes and disrupt services essential for survival, including water, electricity and healthcare.
The US military's use of the MOAB would also raise serious questions under international humanitarian law, which requires attacks to distinguish between military objectives and civilians, prohibits disproportionate civilian harm and obliges forces to take feasible precautions to protect civilians.

articles.title: Meink: Operational Prototypes for MMA Drones Coming in 2028
articles.body:
The Air Force will field operational prototypes for an autonomous drone to replace its MQ-9 Reaper in 2028, Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said Oct. 14.
“We’re going to be fielding operational prototypes by ’28, and we’re just awarding the contract now,” Meink said during a panel discussion with Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, other service secretaries, and senior Pentagon officials at the annual AUSA conference in Washington. “That’s the speed of what we’re fielding capability, and into production—large-scale production—starting in ’29. That is the goal.”
An Air Force spokesperson confirmed to Air & Space Forces Magazine that Meink was referring to the Massed Modular Aircraft, the planned successor to the Reaper.
“The autonomous fighters are already in production,” Meink said, in reference to the Air Force’s Collaborative Combat Aircraft program. General Atomics’ FQ-42A Vengeance and Anduril Industries’ FQ-44A Fury have been selected for production and are undergoing testing with the Air Force’s Experimental Operations Unit at Creech Air Force Base, Nev.
“Now we’re looking at essentially the autonomous strike platform, the autonomous bomber,” Meink said, referring to MMA. The aircraft is envisioned as a multimission aircraft, like the MQ-9, that can conduct strike missions as well as intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance. In contrast, CCAs are currently focused on an air-to-air role paired with crewed fighters.
Meink previously announced at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference that the Air Force would field 100 MMAs by 2029 and 500 by 2032.
Air & Space Forces Magazine reported Sept. 30 that the Air Force and Pentagon’s Defense Innovation Unit had narrowed the field for MMA down to seven companies. An Air Force spokesperson declined to confirm any selections, but Meink said Oct. 14 that “we just awarded those contracts … in collaboration with DIU.” He did not name the specific companies or say how many finalists there are.
Sources have told Air & Space Force Magazine the seven companies still in contention are Anduril, Chaos Industries, General Atomics, Grid Aero, Otto Aerospace, Shield AI, and Swarm Aero. They will develop their MMA candidates and submit a proposal to build a prototype.
The Air Force and DIU want each MMA drone to cost $10 million for the base aircraft, not counting the sensors, weapons, or other equipment it may carry. That’s half the $20 million target price the Air Force envisions for CCAs. MMAs will also use open architecture so they could be more easily upgraded with new sensor packages or weapons capabilities.
But while MMAs will have some autonomous capabilities, they won’t be built with all the latest cutting-edge technology in a bid to keep their price down below that of CCAs. They will likely be powered by turboprop engines, for example.
MMA drones are intended to be able to fly about 4,000 miles, twice the range of CCAs, and carry a heavier payload than CCAs. But they will be slower than CCAs.
The MMA effort is part of the broader push by the Pentagon and the Air Force to field more autonomous systems at a lower cost than crewed platforms, or even the drones that are in service today. The goal is to build “combat mass” to counter China’s growing military, which Meink said is going through “the largest weapons buildup probably in the history of the world,” and to respond to the proliferation of autonomous systems in conflicts of today, and the Pentagon’s view, tomorrow.
“There’s no question that there’s a shift coming,” Meink said. “It’s adaptability, scalability, and affordability. The only way we’re going to meet the threat is with autonomous systems.”
Meink said the Pentagon will work with Congress to secure the funding needed for MMA. The Trump administration’s $1.5 trillion fiscal 2027 budget request for the Department of Defense is currently stalled on Capitol Hill. With midterm elections approaching next month, Democrats could take control of one or both chambers, which could lead to congressional gridlock, particularly surrounding the Pentagon’s request for a massive budget increase—and plans to continue that—amid the war with Iran. The DOD plans to devote tens of billions to autonomous warfare just this fiscal year.
Meink acknowledged the uncertainty surrounding the Pentagon’s budget, but expressed confidence the Air Force would be able to hit its targets for MMA.
“It is heavily dependent upon the resources we get from the Hill, but I think we are not only going to deliver significant combat capability, but we’re going to deliver quickly and efficiently,” Meink said.
“We’ve got to make sure this stuff is affordable,” Meink added, referring to efforts across the Air Force and Space Force. “We’ve got to make sure we’re buying it efficiently. And depending on how you do the comparisons, we’re talking five to 10 times cheaper to field some combat power with these autonomous systems compared to not. So it’s critically important. The good news is, in my mind, there’s no question that the leadership we have in the Air Force, in the Space Force, both military and civilian, is ready to do that. And you see that with the results already. We are integrating autonomous fighters into experimental ops units out at Creech right now, from a year from when they first flew to when we were integrating them into experimental ops units. That’s unheard of. And it only took two years to build the first one.”
The goal for MMA is similarly ambitious.
“It’s in the scalability and the producibility,” Meink said. “In many ways, cost goes with schedule. If something is super expensive, there’s a reason for it, which means it’s probably going to take a long time to build, so we’re really focusing on rapid production and scalability, which means we have to get the cost down on these systems as well.”
Meink’s comments came during a panel focused on the Pentagon’s Project Agincourt, a drive to accelerate the fielding of autonomous systems and create a new four-star Autonomous Warfare Command, or AUTOWARCOM, which Hegseth announced during a speech late last month.
“The folks who acquire it need to be right there up with the warfighter at the same time who understand how to iterate it and change on and innovate on it,” Hegseth said.
Adversaries such as Russia and Iran have fielded one-way drone attacks to wreak havoc in Ukraine and across the Middle East. Ukraine has used autonomous systems to great effect to defend against Russia’s invasion. Kyiv’s ongoing and thus far successful Operation Vivaldi offensive has relied heavily on the innovative use of drones, including dropping uncrewed ground vehicles behind enemy lines.
“That’s a different battlefield,” Hegseth said. “We’ve learned a lot from Ukraine, but you can’t use everything that’s in Ukraine because of all the Chinese components involved in it. So you’ve got to be able to ensure that we take the best of that and the lessons learned … and then push it through [with] an AUTOWARCOM commander with four stars who has the ability to drive that change. So we’ve done a lot with acquisitions and a lot with industry from day one to modernize, realizing this is the future of warfare.”

articles.title: Why Ukrainian strikes on data centers are a real problem for Russia — and beyond
articles.body:
Russia's President Vladimir Putin chairs a meeting with members of the government via videoconference in Moscow on June 23, 2026. | Gavriil Grigorov/POOL/AFP via Getty Images
Ukraine’s strikes on data centers inside Russia aimed to disrupt military planning and communication services. There were also reports of another kind of disruption: to customers waiting for their dinner from food-delivery apps.
Kyiv’s drone strikes on three Yandex data centers in Sasovo, Kaluga and Vladimir saw delays and interruptions for thousands of businesses and households that rely on Yandex's cloud infrastructure, including e-commerce, digital payment platforms and apps of food delivery and car services. Ukrainian drones on Wednesday targeted a major Sberbank data center in Russia’s Saratov region, though a senior company executive said it hadn’t affected operations.
After the strikes on Russian data centers, Kyiv noted that Moscow has already repeatedly targeted its digital infrastructure. “Ukrainians wanted to show Russians that two can play this game,” a senior official familiar with the operation told POLITICO, granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.
Advertisement
The attacks and counter-attacks point to a new frontline in war: the infrastructure powering the digital economy.
The attacks on the buildings that supply compute power are akin to striking a power plant supplying the electricity, heating and fuel that both militaries and civilians depend on. It may weaken an enemy's war effort but can also bring everyday life to a standstill.
Experts say the cost of rebuilding in Russia will be particularly high as the centers require scarce materials that must be imported. “Obtaining a large amount of equipment to replace what was destroyed is not going to be easy,” said Oleg Shakirov, a cyber policy and international security researcher, noting that most hardware needs to be imported and that is complicated by high global demand and sanctions on Russia.
“To be honest, no one really knows what’s the actual damage. Since two data centers are still offline, we can assume that it’s significant,” said Shakirov.
Joseph Jarnecki, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, warned that normalizing strikes to data centers could have a new set of dangerous consequences.
“These strikes likely breach International Humanitarian Law and it’s a big risk when global populations increasingly rely on digital services,” he told POLITICO.
Advertisement
When servers become targets
Data centers have entered the crosshairs of other recent armed conflicts. During the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran earlier this year, drone strikes hit three Amazon Web Services (AWS) facilities in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain.
Since data centers can serve civilian and military purposes simultaneously, the legal status of targeting them is far from straightforward.
Kubo Mačák, an expert on international humanitarian law, said a data center must meet two conditions to qualify as a military objective under the Geneva Conventions: it must make an effective contribution to military operations and destroying it must offer a “definite military advantage.”
A delivery robot from Russian tech giant Yandex moves through Moscow. | Alexander Nemenov/AFP via Getty Images
“If you know that they are storing military intelligence or that they're using the data center to power military artificial intelligence tools,” Mačák said, there could be grounds to consider it a military objective.
Following the most recent strikes of the Yandex data centers, users on social media platform X reported a sudden drop in automated bot activity, including from accounts associated with pro-Russian, pro-Trump and Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) narratives.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy seized on the reports to boast that the strikes had made social media less toxic, even as independent researchers and national research institutes found no evidence they specifically disrupted any Russian disinformation campaigns.
Advertisement
Mačák said that even if a data center is being used to “let's say, run some trolls or these bot farms to interfere with elections abroad … that would not be sufficient.” In other words, hosting propaganda bots does not, by itself, make a data center a lawful military target.
The dual-use quandary has often focused on the targeting of energy infrastructure, which has been frequent in the Russia-Ukraine war. On Saturday, U.S. President Donald Trump urged Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil refineries, blaming the attacks for rising fuel prices. He has since called for both sides to halt attacks on energy infrastructure, although the existence of any ceasefire agreement remains disputed.
As data centers become increasingly central to national economies, they will become more consequential targets. A senior NATO official granted anonymity to discuss the matter told POLITICO that data centers are already considered potential targets and that the alliance is factoring their vulnerability into its planning.
NATO allies recognize that their data centers could come under attack in a conflict, the official said: “We would get it in a fight.”
Veronika Melkozerova in Kyiv contributed to this report.

articles.title: Zelenskyy says Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries – FT
articles.body:
Zelenskyy says Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries – FT
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries after Kyiv observed the "energy ceasefire" announced by US President Donald Trump, only to face intensified Russian attacks and slower Starlink satellite communications.
Source: Financial Times
Details: "The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We're done," Zelenskyy said in a forthright interview with the FT in London. He also sharply criticised Washington's eagerness to strike business deals with Moscow and Trump's apparent affinity for Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
Asked to explain the relationship between the two leaders, Zelenskyy said Trump has an instinctive affinity for autocrats and extremely wealthy people.
"He [Trump] speaks about it openly and loudly that he loves such people and he respects such people. Because for him people who can be leaders 20 years, 30 years, 40 years, it means they can be very strong," Zelenskyy said.
The FT noted that Washington has increased pressure on Kyiv to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries, arguing that a moratorium on the attacks, together with an agreement to purchase hundreds of thousands of tonnes of Russian diesel fuel, is necessary to bring down fuel prices in the US.
Zelenskyy said he had suspended strikes on energy facilities for three days to accommodate the US request. However, Moscow continued to attack Ukraine's energy infrastructure and kill civilians, with more than 100 people killed in the past week.
The president also said that, despite Ukraine suspending its strikes, its forces had been left without US early-warning systems for incoming ballistic missiles. Starlink satellite communications, operated by Elon Musk's company, had also been slowed across the country, making battlefield operations and medium-range strikes against Russian military facilities more difficult.
The FT wrote that the deterioration in relations between Kyiv and Washington marks the most serious crisis between Ukraine and its most important security partner since the Oval Office spat in February 2025.
"Zelenskyy stressed that Ukraine's relationship with the US as an 'honest' and 'strategic' partner was essential in the fight against Russia, comparing it to Kyiv's relationship with the UK," the FT noted.
Asked whether Ukraine would stop striking oil refineries even if Russia continued its attacks, in an effort to repair relations with the White House, Zelenskyy said he would agree to do so only if the US supplied him with more American-made Patriot interceptors.
He believes that halting strikes on oil refineries could simply encourage the US and Russia to strike further deals, potentially providing additional funding for Putin's war machine.
"The question will be when will the next deal be? Maybe it will be gas. Definitely it will be gas," Zelenskyy said.
He added that the US suspension of intelligence sharing and disruption of Starlink services has become "dangerous" for Ukraine.
"We will find a way out . . . but it's better not to give him [Putin] the new life or the new will to fight," Zelenskyy concluded.
Background:
- On 11 October, Trump published a post on his social media Truth Social announcing an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine, which allegedly took effect immediately. He said that both sides had consented to cease strikes on energy infrastructure, although neither party had been informed of this.
- Barak Ravid, a journalist at American news portal Axios, stated that Zelenskyy had been unaware of the "energy ceasefire" between Ukraine and Russia announced by Trump, but added that Ukraine supports it.
- Later, Zelenskyy reported a Russian strike on CHP-5 [a combined heat and power plant] in Kharkiv and a power station in Kyiv following Trump's statement.
- On 13 October Zelenskyy stressed that Ukraine has refrained from striking Russian oil refineries and energy facilities for two days in response to a proposal by Trump. Russia, meanwhile, has attacked Ukrainian energy facilities and critical infrastructure.

articles.title: Ukraine accuses US of aiding Russia by withholding strike warnings and slowing Starlink
articles.body:
Ukraine has accused the United States of indirectly aiding Russia by failing to provide early warnings of incoming Russian missile strikes and restricting Starlink satellite internet systems vital to Kiev's battlefield drone operations.
The diplomatic fallout follows two consecutive nights of ballistic missile attacks against the capital, Kiev, where air-raid sirens failed to sound before impacts occurred, killing 15 people nationwide and damaging power plants in Kharkiv, Zhytomyr, Sumy, and Chernihiv.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy denounced the intelligence blackout as "completely unjust", warning that Moscow showed "ostentatious disrespect towards the United States" by breaching a supposed energy ceasefire announced by US President Donald Trump.
Zelenskyy also appealed directly to US billionaire Elon Musk to restore full connectivity for Starlink terminals.
In an interview with British journalist Piers Morgan, Zelenskyy said: "I hope that it's a mistake, maybe huge technical problem. I don't know, but we are asking to do it, to switch (it) on."
He also responded affirmatively when asked if he felt "betrayed" following Washington’s diesel pact with Moscow: "It's painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side."
Starlink restrictions
Ukrainian defence officials reported that satellite terminals were throttled when drones exceeded 160 km/h—and in some instances 80 km/h—crippling the military's ability to intercept Shahed drones or target Russian-held positions.
Musk stated that any disruptions were the direct responsibility of the US government rather than SpaceX, drawing a clear distinction between civilian Starlink equipment and military Starshield hardware.
"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk wrote on X, referring to Trump.
Ukrainian Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov subsequently noted that connectivity up to 160 km/h was being restored, though he insisted that "removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defence."
Meanwhile, in Moscow, Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev confirmed that contracts to supply diesel to the US would be finalised within days.

articles.title: Musk Tells Zelensky to ‘Go’ as Ukraine Questions US Support
articles.body:
Tech billionaire Elon Musk called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky “to go” on Thursday, as Kyiv raised concerns that US restrictions on satellite communications and intelligence sharing were weakening Ukraine’s defenses against Russian attacks.
“And so the slaughter continues,” Musk wrote on X. “Time for Zelensky to go.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The dispute escalated after Ukraine reported restrictions on military Starlink services, which Ukrainian forces rely on for battlefield communications and drone operations.
And so the slaughter continues …
Time for Zelensky to go https://t.co/tMBThajxhH
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 15, 2026
Zelensky warned that the restrictions could lead to significant casualties as Russia intensified attacks on Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.
“It’s a big mistake,” he said. “This decision will bring a lot of human losses… People will die.”
He urged Musk, whose SpaceX operates Starlink, to restore the service, saying he hoped the disruption was the result of a technical problem.
Musk said on Wednesday that Starshield is owned and controlled by the US government, which determines restrictions on its use.
He distinguished it from Starlink, a commercial satellite network used by Ukraine for communications, and said it should not be used for offensive military operations.
The satellite dispute comes amid concerns that reduced US intelligence sharing could leave Ukraine more vulnerable to Russian missile attacks.
Trump Weighs Easing Shadow Fleet Sanctions to Lower Oil Shipping Costs
Ukrainian officials told CNN that the loss of intelligence could give Russian forces an advantage on the battlefield. A European official also questioned Washington’s explanation that weather had caused gaps in missile-warning information.
For two consecutive nights, air raid alerts in Kyiv came only after Russian ballistic missiles were already approaching or striking the capital.
On Oct. 12-13, Russia launched successive ballistic missile attacks, hitting civilian infrastructure and a major power plant. Zelensky said Ukraine had received no advance warning of the launches from Western partners.
The Trump administration has previously warned it could suspend intelligence sharing and halt European purchases of US weapons for Ukraine if Kyiv refused to stop deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
The growing dispute has also spilled into relations between Kyiv and Washington over energy policy.
Zelensky said he felt “betrayed” after US President Donald Trump announced a diesel supply deal with heavily sanctioned Russia.
Trump, facing key midterm elections next month, has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for contributing to fuel shortages and rising prices at US gas stations.

articles.title: Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian refineries after Zelensky condemns withdrawal of US intelligence
articles.body:
Ukraine has resumed its attacks on Russian refineries with a strike at an installation in the Ryazan region, the regional governor said on Thursday, after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky voiced his anger at a "dangerous" withdrawal of US intelligence.
Since US President Donald Trump's surprise announcement of an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on Sunday, Kyiv had refrained from attacking Russian refineries, which the US leader had blamed for raising diesel prices on global markets.
But Zelensky had voiced increasing frustration with Russia's continued attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, which he said on Wednesday had left 600,000 people without power. He warned that Ukraine would not suspend its own attacks indefinitely if Russia did not reciprocate and also criticized what he said was Trump's favoritism toward Russia.
In an interview with the Financial Times published on Thursday, he said Ukraine's patience had run out.
"The block (on attacking refineries) is out. We’re done,” he told the newspaper.
Pavel Malkov, the governor of Ryazan, said in a post on Telegram that a major Ukrainian drone attack on the region had sparked a fire at an oil refinery.
"The material damage is now being assessed. Emergency services are working at the scene," he said.
In his interview, Zelensky criticized Washington’s eagerness to strike business deals with Moscow and Trump’s apparent admiration for Russia’s Vladimir Putin.
Trump calls for Ukraine to replace Zelensky after announcing Russia diesel deal
Trump on Saturday called for Ukraine to replace Zelensky and railed against Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil infrastructure, one day after announcing a diesel supply deal with Russia, aiming to lower fuel prices that have soared since the US-Israeli war with Iran began in February.
Despite Ukraine's suspension of refinery attacks, Ukrainian officials complained that they had not received any US early-warning alerts in recent days for incoming Russian ballistic missiles.
They also said the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications service had been slowed across the country, hampering frontline operations and medium-range strikes against Russian military sites.
Musk said on Wednesday in a post on X/Twitter that Starshield - the military version of Starlink - was owned and controlled by the US government, which decided on any limits on speed.
Zelensky has said that Ukrainian military officials were warned by their US counterparts that Washington would block intelligence unless they halted strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
In the FT interview, Zelensky said the suspension was presented to Kyiv as a technical glitch, but he dismissed the idea that failures of the Starlink satellite system might have been caused by a fault.
“It was not a technical problem, it was the will,” he told the FT.
Zelensky demands US interceptors in exchange for halting strikes on refineries
Asked whether Ukraine would be open to halting energy strikes as a way of repairing relations with the White House, he told the newspaper he could only agree if, in return, he was given more US-made Patriot interceptors, calling it the “minimum” that would be acceptable.
"We didn't destroy any relationship," he said, claiming it wasn't up to him to repair US-Ukraine relations.
Ukraine claims to have damaged six Russian military aircraft
Ukraine's military said on Thursday it had damaged six Russian Su-34M military aircraft in an overnight strike on the Borisoglebsk airfield in Russia's Voronezh region.
In a Telegram statement, Ukraine's military general staff said it had confirmed damage of varying degrees to all six aircraft.
The Su-34M is a large fighter-bomber, costing tens of millions of US dollars apiece and frequently used by Russia to drop devastating glide bombs onto Ukrainian cities near the frontline.
Ukraine said on Telegram that it used its Neptune coastal missile system in the attack.
Reuters could not independently verify the battlefield reports.
Kremlin condemns Ukraine refinery strikes as ceasefire violation
The Kremlin said on Thursday that Ukraine's targeting of Russian energy infrastructure ran counter to US peace efforts, after a Ukrainian drone struck a refinery in Russia's Ryazan region overnight.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Russia did not perceive that Ukraine had ever complied with an energy ceasefire announced last week by Trump. Ukraine says it paused such strikes for three days but resumed them after Russia continued to attack its own energy sector.
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

articles.title: ‘We’re done’: Zelensky says Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries
articles.body:
‘We’re done’: Zelensky says Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries.
“The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” Ukraine’s president said in an interview with the Financial Times.
He said Ukraine had not struck energy facilities in Russia for three days, in keeping with a request from the United States. Moscow, meanwhile, continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure, killing more than 100 civilians over the past week.
Zelensky said that although Ukraine stopped striking oil refineries, it received no American warnings about Russian ballistic missile attacks. He also said Starlink terminal operations had been restricted.
He confirmed that American officials had warned Ukraine that if Kyiv did not stop striking oil refineries, the United States would stop sharing intelligence. Zelensky also rejected the idea that a malfunction had caused the Starlink problems. “It was not a technical problem, it was the will,” he said.
Asked whether Ukraine could stop striking oil refineries to improve relations with Washington, even if Russia continued its own attacks, Zelensky said he could agree to that in exchange for additional shipments of missiles for Patriot systems. That, he said, was the “minimum” he had asked for.
Donald Trump said October 11 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to a truce in the energy sector. Zelensky soon said the Ukrainian Armed Forces had “received all relevant orders” in connection with the truce. Ukraine then stopped striking Russian oil refineries, while Russia’s Defense Ministry reported that Russian forces had struck communications and energy infrastructure in Kyiv.
According to Axios, Trump is counting on Zelensky to observe the energy truce and stop striking Russian oil refineries. “Trump is really mad. He feels Zelensky is taking the U.S. for granted,” a White House source told the outlet.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
