articles.title: It’s not all about strikes against Russia — why U.S. intelligence is important for Ukraine
articles.body:
It’s not all about strikes against Russia — why U.S. intelligence is important for Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
U.S. intelligence is critically important for Ukraine’s air defense and strikes. An expert called its provision and the sale of weapons levers of pressure on Trump.
American intelligence is needed by Ukraine both to defend against Russian missiles and to strike military targets on enemy territory. Over the past few days, Ukraine has not received warnings about the enemy preparing missile attacks. Will the United States put Ukraine in an intelligence “vice” and what other levers of pressure does Trump have — UNN journalists discussed these issues with Oleksii Buriachenko, president of the International Institute for Security Studies.
Why American intelligence is important for Ukraine
According to the expert, American satellite intelligence helps Ukraine detect missile threats and use weapons that operate according to U.S. communications standards. In the expert’s view, this concerns not only American systems but also some weapons supplied by other NATO countries. At the same time, European states have their own capabilities, particularly France and the United Kingdom, but they do not cover the full range of U.S. capabilities.
We use U.S. satellite intelligence in two areas: both for defense and for moving the war onto the territory of the aggressor state. That is why it is critical for us to be able to detect missile launches in time and accordingly configure air defense systems for our own protection
Oleksii Buriachenko also emphasized that European partners are already partially compensating for the need for intelligence, but there is currently no full replacement for American capabilities. Therefore, if the transfer of information to Ukraine is halted, it will have to adapt to new conditions.
The issue is not compensation, but the fact that we work simultaneously with American satellite intelligence and with our European partners. However, the specific nature of NATO and American weaponry is that it is primarily designed to work with American satellite intelligence. Therefore, as of now, Ukraine will not be able to emerge from this situation without losses if the United States really decides to stop providing us with satellite intelligence
Can Trump use intelligence as an instrument of pressure
The political scientist recalled that Donald Trump had previously restricted Ukraine’s access to American intelligence for several days. According to him, at that time it was more difficult for Ukrainian air defense systems to respond to massive Russian attacks. However, in his assessment, the current situation is different because Ukraine has partially diversified its sources of intelligence information.
If we are talking about the current situation, we have no confirmed information that Trump is doing this or will do so. At least in the public sphere, he clearly stated that the United States continues to provide intelligence to Ukraine. In other words, there is no delay. The military says that this delay may be related to the fact that Russia has modified its missiles for the S-400, which had already caused us problems
Oleksii Buriachenko also believes that the domestic political situation in the United States may influence the American president’s decisions regarding Ukraine. However, in the political scientist’s view, the possibility of restricting the transfer of intelligence and the sale of American weapons nevertheless remains one of Washington’s instruments of influence.
Elections are the main reason behind this entire story. The configuration may turn out completely differently. If major criticism of Trump in the public sphere over the diesel deal gains momentum, he may, on the contrary, do something else beneficial for Ukraine. But the opposite may also happen: if Trump decides to force through the terms he agreed on with the Russian Federation, he may resolve this issue by putting pressure on Ukraine. He has instruments of pressure — intelligence and the sale of American weapons
In addition, the expert noted that Ukraine’s dependence on U.S. permits for the sale of American weapons remains a separate problem, even if those weapons were purchased by third countries. He emphasized that without official authorization from Washington, Ukraine will not be able to buy such equipment from other states, and therefore called preserving access to intelligence and the ability to purchase American weapons important tactical objectives for Ukraine.
For Ukraine, it is important now that, under any circumstances, it retain access to intelligence and the ability to purchase American weapons. The United States and President Trump have their own political and economic goals. Sometimes they coincide with ours, and sometimes they do not

articles.title: Houthis threaten escalation after strike on Saudi oil giant Aramco
articles.body:
Houthis threaten escalation after strike on Saudi oil giant Aramco
Yemen's Houthi rebels said Wednesday they had targeted facilities belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco after officials in Riyadh reported a strike on a building in an area housing the energy giant's headquarters. The Iran-back militia also claimed missile strikes on the capital Riyadh and vowed to continue attacking Saudi airports and oil facilities.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Yemen's Houthis vowed on Wednesday to press on with attacks on airports and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia, a day after a strike that sources said caused extensive damage to the headquarters of oil giant Saudi Aramco.
The Houthis said the threatened locations were legitimate targets and described their attacks as retaliation for Saudi strikes on Yemen – threatening to escalate a conflict reignited by the US-Iran confrontation in the Gulf.
Saudi Arabia has faced widening Houthi strikes over the past week, including an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday that killed 13 people.
Read moreSaudi Arabia threatens 'decisive' response after Riyadh airport strike kills at least 12
Tuesday night's attack on Saudi Aramco's base in the eastern city of Dhahran caused a fire that spread across several floors, three people with knowledge of the matter told Reuters. The Saudi energy ministry had said the strike caused a limited fire.
Operations at Aramco were continuing normally, with employees working from home, according to two of the sources. Aramco did not immediately reply to a Reuters request for comment.
Yahya Saree, a Houthi military spokesman, said the Iran-backed group had conducted "a high-quality military operation targeting Aramco in Dhahran", as well as strikes targeting Riyadh airport and a refinery in the capital.
He added the attacks were carried out with missiles and drones, and that operations "will continue in the coming days, targeting Saudi enemy airports and oil facilities".
Saudi-led forces say they intercept missile
The escalating conflict has dealt a blow to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's ambitious plans to transform and diversify the Saudi economy and reduce its reliance on oil.
The Houthis say they have been retaliating for the kingdom's backing of Yemeni government forces in the Yemen war that restarted last month.
The Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis towards Riyadh on Wednesday, and several loud booms were heard in the Saudi capital.
Saudi authorities earlier issued an alert for a possible aerial threat in Riyadh on Wednesday before the warning was lifted, a witness said. It wasn't immediately clear what caused the booms and there was no immediate comment from the authorities on their source.
The Saudi government media office didn't immediately respond to a request for comment about the cause of the booms.
Read moreBlasts rock Riyadh as Houthis target Saudi airports, oil facilities
In their statement on Wednesday, the Houthis said they had launched ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones at the Saudi Aramco facilities in Dhahran, Riyadh airport and an Aramco refinery in Riyadh.
In a broad threat, they urged "international shipping companies", civilians and workers to evacuate Saudi airports and oil facilities.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The Dhahran complex hosts a major operations centre for Aramco, which oversees a vast network of onshore and offshore oil rigs, pipelines, refineries and export terminals.
Riyadh’s international airport has come under attack four times, including Saturday's attack which was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in a decade.
Authorities have closed the airport until October 17, and airlines have canceled flights to Saudi Arabia.
Yemen hospitals overwhelmed, Red Cross warns
Fearing the rise of Iranian influence and the prospect of chaos on its borders, Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen's civil war in support of the government in 2015 after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa.
The UN brokered a 2022 truce between the warring sides in Yemen that kept a fragile peace until this year.
Saudi Arabia resumed its military campaign in Yemen in support of the internationally recognised government in a bid to reverse the Houthis' sudden gains last month, when they swept down the Red Sea coast to the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The Red Cross said on Wednesday that hospitals across Yemen are struggling to cope with a sharp rise in war casualties as fighting intensified along multiple front lines.
The UN World Food Programme warned that life-saving assistance had been cut off to the government-held city of Taiz, which was encircled by Houthi fighters earlier this month.
"WFP and its partners cannot access more than 600,000 people in Taiz who depend on humanitarian assistance, including more than 200,000 women and children," WFP said in a statement.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters, AFP)

articles.title: Musk blames Trump for throttling ‘military Starlink’ in Ukraine
articles.body:
Musk blames Trump for throttling ‘military Starlink’ in Ukraine
Elon Musk has denied instructing his company SpaceX to abruptly restrict Starlink and Starshield satellite communications services used by Ukrainian forces to operate drones.
Ukrainian officials and frontline commanders said terminals suddenly stopped working overnight Tuesday into Wednesday when drones flew faster than 100 mph, disrupting some combat missions. The problems with Starshield, the military-grade counterpart to SpaceX’s Starlink service, occurred as US President Donald Trump was pressuring Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he blamed for surging energy prices.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk wrote on X on Wednesday in response to criticism from Ukraine. He had earlier suggested that the disruption might have been “a mistake” and said he was working to restore connectivity.
Musk also said that Starlink should be used only for civilian and defensive purposes, arguing that using it for offensive operations would be “inappropriate for a commercial company.”
Although Trump has not commented directly on the restrictions, a senior US official told Axios that his administration had nothing to do with the disruption of Starlink services.
In an interview with NPR on Tuesday, Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky confirmed reports that the US had threatened to stop sharing intelligence with Kiev unless Ukraine halted attacks on Russian energy facilities.
Ukrainian officials also said they had received no advance warning from their Western partners before Russian missile strikes on Kiev on two consecutive nights, Monday and Tuesday. According to media reports, US officials attributed the failure to detect the missile launches to bad weather, an explanation their Ukrainian counterparts reportedly found hard to believe.
Asked by British talk show host Piers Morgan on Wednesday whether he had been “betrayed” by the Trump administration, Zelensky replied, “Yes.”
“It’s a pity that we are losing a strong partner,” he added.
Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mikhail Fyodorov said Wednesday evening that Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 100 mph was being restored, but urged the removal of speed restrictions on Starshield altogether.
Ukrainian media reported on Thursday that the operation of Starshield systems had been fully restored. Sources within the country’s Ministry of Defense said military units confirmed that communications were back online while officials continue to investigate the reasons for the restrictions.
Russia has argued that Ukraine would use a ceasefire without preconditions to regroup and replenish its forces. “We want not a ceasefire but a lasting peace, and we are ready to do everything possible to achieve it,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Monday.

articles.title: UK Allocates £45 Million for LMM Missiles for Ukraine’s Air Defense
articles.body:
The United Kingdom will accelerate deliveries of LMM missiles to Ukraine for air defense and is preparing additional packages of military, financial, and sanctions support.
The UK government announced this ahead of a meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and UK Prime Minister Andrew Burnham.
One of the new measures is supplying air defense missiles to Ukraine worth £45 million. The UK plans to accelerate deliveries of Lightweight Multirole Missiles (LMM), which Ukraine’s Defense Forces use for air defense.
The UK government specifically highlighted the use of LMM missiles against Russian jet-powered drones.
The prime minister has instructed ministers to prepare additional sanctions against Russia, along with military aid and financial support packages, to be presented in the coming weeks. The UK has also called on international partners to increase pressure on Moscow.
Under the new £45 million package, the UK will accelerate deliveries of £10 million worth of missiles to meet Ukraine’s most urgent air defense needs this winter.
Overall, the UK has already committed £1.6 billion to supply Ukraine with more than 5,000 LMM missiles over four years. The contract provides for their production at Thales’ facility in Belfast.
The UK continued to increase deliveries of these weapons in 2026. In June, Militarnyi reported on a new British package that included LMM missiles and 150,000 drones.
The increased military support comes with expanded British sanctions pressure on Russia. The government confirmed it intends to fully implement a ban on maritime services for exporting Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG).
The restrictions cover, in particular, British companies’ involvement in the maritime transport of Russian LNG, as well as related financial and brokerage services.
They aim to restrict Russia’s access to British shipping, insurance, and financial services that support maritime transport.
In June, Militarnyi reported on new British sanctions targeting Russia’s defense industry and shadow fleet. The sanctions list also included LNG carriers involved in transporting Russian LNG.

articles.title: German air force fires IRIS-T SLM for first time in Crete
articles.body:
- The German Air Force completed operational certification of the IRIS-T SLM air defense system with its first live firing at NATO’s Crete range.
- Swedish and German Patriot units and German Stinger crews joined the tactical exercise that followed the certification shot, Diehl Defence said.
The German Air Force has fired its new IRIS-T SLM air defense system for the first time at the NATO Missile Firing Installation on Crete, completing the operational certification the system needed before it can be relied on in German service, manufacturer Diehl Defence said this week.
Air Defence Missile Group 61, the unit based at Todendorf on Germany’s Baltic coast that operates the system, trained at the NATO range in October on linking the full fire unit together: the TRML-4D radar, the Common Tactical Operations Center command post and the launcher with its IRIS-T SLM interceptors. After the certification shot, the IRIS-T SLM was folded into a wider tactical exercise alongside German and Swedish Patriot batteries and German Stinger short-range missiles on the LeFlaSys light air defense vehicle.
“Without the soldiers of Air Defence Missile Group 61, this first firing of the IRIS-T SLM in Crete would not have been possible,” said Lt. Col. Björn Klarl, the group’s commander.
Diehl did not disclose what targets were engaged, how many missiles were fired or the results of individual intercepts.
“The successful system certification firing confirms that IRIS-T SLM delivers reliable performance and a very high hit rate in operation,” said Helmut Rauch, CEO of Diehl Defence.
The system can engage targets out to 60 km (37 miles) and up to 20 km (12 miles) in altitude, according to Diehl, and is designed to protect cities and critical infrastructure against cruise missiles and drones as well as aircraft and helicopters. It sits below Patriot in Germany’s layered air defense, covering medium-range threats while Patriot handles ballistic missiles and longer-range targets.
Ukraine has used IRIS-T SLM in combat since October 2022, when Germany delivered the first fire unit to Kyiv, and the system has since become one of the main tools Ukrainian forces use against Russian cruise missiles and Shahed-type attack drones. Rauch said ten nations now rely on the system, and Sweden, whose Patriot crews took part in the Crete exercise, decided to buy IRIS-T SLM in 2025.
Germany was slower to field the system at home. Berlin ordered six fire units in 2023, and the first was delivered in August 2024, but its entry into service was held up because an ammunition loading crane had not been certified to German standards, Defence Industry Europe reported. The Bundeswehr says Air Defence Missile Group 61 formally put the system into service only in February 2026.
The NAMFI range near Chania was set up under a 1964 agreement among several NATO members and has hosted live missile firings by allied air defense units since 1968, with crews from Nike Hercules and HAWK through to Patriot training there over the decades.

articles.title: US weighs relief for sanctioned shadow fleet tankers, days after freeing Russian diesel
articles.body:
The Trump administration is weighing looser sanctions on shadow fleet tankers that have hauled oil from Russia, Iran, and Venezuela, a US official said on 14 October, Reuters reported. An industry research group expects the change to do little for freight rates.
With Reuters calling high fuel prices a risk for Trump before the 3 November midterms, Washington has already eased sanctions on Russian oil and diesel this year and is now looking at the ships blacklisted for hauling sanctioned cargoes. In March, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said a waiver on Russian oil at sea would bring Moscow no significant financial benefit, yet Russia’s seaborne oil income jumped by $890 million in the week to 15 March, Bloomberg data showed.
“Legal oil” on blacklisted ships
The talks center on letting “legal oil” sail on previously sanctioned vessels, the official said. Only crude or fuel free of US sanctions would qualify, not Russian or Iranian oil. Washington wants more crude and refined products moving out of the Gulf, the official added. Companies would need US Treasury approval to use the ships.
Ukraine is going back to hitting Russian oil after its Trump-pressured pause, during which Kyiv got no US warnings of incoming ballistic missiles
Research group Energy Aspects said US Energy Secretary Chris Wright, in a video to the World Petroleum Congress in Riyadh, tied the easing to record freight rates. Those rates hit records after the Iran and Ukraine wars drove up inflation and left US crude too costly for Asian refiners, Reuters said. Energy Aspects itself expects the easing to do little for freight rates, since most tankers sanctioned over Russian or Venezuelan links have kept trading for the past three months.
The Energy Department said any relief would do nothing to help Russia ship its oil or refined products. Treasury referred questions to the Energy Department. Yet Reuters noted that both departments could face pressure to let these vessels carry Russian diesel, given Trump’s push to get it onto world markets fast.
Britain is pushing the other way. UK finance minister John Healey urged counterparts at International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok on 15 October to keep tough sanctions on Russia, “especially a tighter ban on shipping services” that keep Putin’s shadow fleet operating.
Diesel license criticism and an unconfirmed ceasefire
On 9 October, the US Treasury issued a license clearing Russian-origin diesel trade until 7 April 2027. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told reporters it was a weak decision unworthy of Ukraine’s partners. Democratic Senators Jeanne Shaheen, Chuck Schumer, and Elizabeth Warren called it a “total betrayal of Ukraine.” Republican Senator Thom Tillis said there is “a legitimate case for saying the president’s not following the law.”
“He thinks Ukraine is a weak link and that it needs to be squeezed into giving in”: diplomat on why Trump pressures Kyiv, not Moscow
Trump then pressed Kyiv to spare Russian refineries and declared an “energy ceasefire” on 11 October. A White House official told Axios it covers only oil refineries. Neither side confirmed a similar announcement Trump made in mid-September, AAP reported.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters on 13 October that contacts on the ceasefire were continuing and referred further questions to Trump, Russian newspaper Vedomosti reported. He claimed the diesel deal was “a very mutually beneficial item of Russian-American cooperation” that serves the interests of Russia, the US, and world energy markets, Russian newspaper Kommersant reported.
Read also
- America has sided with Russia against Ukraine. Europe should stop pretending and build a coalition against Russia, China, and even the US
- “It finances an economy geared toward total war”—Ukraine’s third president on the Russian diesel Washington just cleared
- Bipartisan US senators say Trump’s Russian diesel deal conflicts with 2022 ban, as he presses Kyiv to spare Russian refineries

articles.title: US military weighs use of 'mother of all bombs' on Iran: CNN
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US military weighs use of 'mother of all bombs' in potential future strikes on Iran, CNN says
The US military has developed strike plans that could include using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, also known as the "mother of all bombs", against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites if President Donald Trump orders renewed combat operations, CNN reported on Thursday citing US officials familiar with the matter.
The potential deployment of the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal would mark a significant development in the war, although officials familiar with military planning discussions told CNN questions remain over its effectiveness in achieving Washington's strategic objectives.
Reuters could not immediately verify the report.
Iran, meanwhile, has placed its military on heightened alert, conducting new missile tests in recent days and threatening to unveil additional weapons.
Tehran has also warned Washington and regional governments that another round of war could trigger retaliation across a wider geographical area, including potential ground incursions.
The US Department of War recently reported that the death toll of US personnel in its war on Iran is 21 killed and 865 wounded in an acknowledgement that losses faced during the conflict were greater than previously admitted.

articles.title: The end of UNIFIL: What next for south Lebanon?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
The end of UNIFIL: What next for south Lebanon?
Beirut, Lebanon - As the UN's longest-serving presence on the Blue Line between Lebanon and Israel counts down to its exit, a European replacement is being floated as the answer.
The real choice facing Beirut, however, is between a security arrangement written in Washington and one it builds itself.
For 48 years, the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) has been deployed across the country's southern border villages.
It never deterred the wars fought across the Blue Line - a 120-kilometre (75-mile) temporary demarcation boundary established by the United Nations on 7 June 2000 to confirm the withdrawal of Israeli forces from southern Lebanon.
What they did, consistently, was watch, record, and report, and in a region where every side contests every account, that act of witnessing carried weight of its own.
Few in Lebanon expect the UN body's exit to change the balance of force. “UNIFIL was merely an eyewitness,” retired Brigadier General Saeed Qazah, a military expert, told The New Arab.
Operating under Chapter VI of its mandate, it could only record violations and report them to the UN. Its absence, he argued, “will not change the military reality on the ground as much as it will leave a logistical and economic vacuum”.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun's push for an extension was blocked by a US-Israeli veto, and he had welcomed a French-Italian idea for a European Union force to take UNIFIL's place. On Monday, the contours of that EU role took a more concrete shape.
European Union foreign ministers agreed to establish a new support mission in Lebanon to advise and train the country's military and internal security forces. It would have an initial mandate of three years.
But the European option still lacks the mandate, consent, and the American backing it would need.
UNIFIL's real successor is being negotiated elsewhere, and what awaits Lebanon after December is less a handover than a test of whether the state can do alone what it has long outsourced.
A European force without a shape
The new European mission "will advise and assist the Lebanese Armed Forces and Internal Security Forces to strengthen territorial control, border security, and internal security," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said in a statement on Monday.
Over 10 EU members are reportedly willing to contribute people and resources to it, but more operational planning is required before it is launched. An EU official told Reuters this week that the mission hoped to deploy personnel in the coming months.
But retired Brigadier General Saeed Qazah sees a deeper flaw.
“UNIFIL could not prevent the Lebanese-Israeli conflict or control the land and the border, and European forces will have no effective role there either,” he said.
Enforcing peace would require a Chapter VII mandate, which a Russian and Chinese veto would block. “No country is willing to send its soldiers to fight or sacrifice their lives on behalf of the Lebanese army,” he added.
Consent is the other wall. Political analyst Ali Sbeiti says Israel refuses to give Paris any role, given their disputes over regional files and the Gaza war. Qazah agrees that no foreign force can deploy on the border without the approval of both Lebanon, Israel, and a UN resolution.
The one exception, he said, “is a mission limited to training and logistical support for the Lebanese army, away from the border. The only feasible European mission, in other words, is the one that does least of what UNIFIL did”.
UNIFIL's real successor is being negotiated elsewhere
Writer and political analyst Nader Hijaz points to the "third party" under discussion in talks between Beirut and Israel, a body that would verify implementation of the framework agreement.
“That is, in practice, the field replacement for UNIFIL,” he said. Whether it would merely monitor or hold broad powers, such as searching homes and seizing weapons, is unresolved, and a deal has been deferred until after Israel's elections.
On one point, Hijaz is categorical. “Washington will never accept any force that is not under direct American command,” he told The New Arab. The US and Israel, he said, are open to a specific Italian role but not a French one.
Sbeiti adds that the Europeans lack the nerve to act in the south without explicit American blessing. The successor, in short, is being decided in a US-brokered process, on a timetable set by Israeli politics.
Beirut and Hezbollah's calculations
The Lebanese state and army would welcome almost any arrangement that averts a vacuum, and President Joseph Aoun immediately expressed backing for the EU’s announcement this week of a security support mission.
Hijaz notes that military cooperation with France and Italy is already established, and Sbeiti describes an official welcome for any friendly presence, even as a mere eyewitness.
Hezbollah, however, is harder to read. Its secretary-general, Naim Qassem, has called the US-sponsored framework agreement a red line and a surrender of sovereignty, holding up instead the US-Iranian memorandum signed in Islamabad.
Qazah expects the party to reject any foreign force, since it does not want a witness to its breaches, “just as Israel does not want neutral forces bearing witness to its violations”.
Sbeiti, however, disagrees. “Hezbollah can no longer block a plan the state backs, and has no fundamental problem with France, given shared understandings between Paris, the party and Tehran,” he told The New Arab. “The main knot remains with the American and Israeli sides,” he noted.
Hijjaz, meanwhile, says the party's stance will hinge on whether a force operates south of the Litani or beyond it, and whether it pursues the group's weapons. Either way, the decisive veto lies outside Lebanon.
What south Lebanon loses
The mission is exiting in its worst hour. It has recorded a sharp escalation between Israel and Hezbollah, with hundreds of projectiles on some days. It still fields more than 7,400 troops from 46 countries, its backbone European, and seven peacekeepers have been killed in hostile attacks in 2026 alone.
Ceasefires have collapsed in succession, from April's arrangements to the US-sponsored Trilateral Framework in June, and Israeli forces still hold positions inside Lebanon that Beirut says block the army's full deployment.
Washington led the push to end the mission, favouring arrangements outside the Security Council, as in Gaza. Prime Minister Nawaf Salam warned of a vacuum, arguing the UN offers a neutrality no other actor can match, and more than two-thirds of parliament petitioned for UNIFIL to be strengthened, not withdrawn.
Since 1978, and especially after its reinforcement following the 2006 war, UNIFIL has been an economic engine for the border villages.
At its peak, Qazah said, more than 15,000 soldiers in a narrow area drove spending, services, and procurement. Their departure will cut “a vital economic artery” in a region already devastated by Israeli strikes.
Three roads after December
The first is direct military coordination between the Lebanese and Israeli armies, favoured by Washington and Israel and signalled by US envoys' talk of opening crossings once the weapons file is closed. Lebanon rejects it as security normalisation.
The second is a multinational force with European troops under American command, which depends on a wider regional deal and US-Iranian understandings and Israel's elections.
The third is self-reliance: Qazah argues the government can declare the border villages a military zone under National Defence Law No. 102 of 1938, placing all security forces under army command and allowing curfews, closures and searches.
A European coalition will remain ink on paper without a UN mandate, the consent of both parties and an American guarantee against escalation. None of these is in Beirut's gift. The world is not handing the south to a new guardian; it is handing it back to the Lebanese state. Lebanon can assert its sovereignty through its own army or risk a vacuum that turns the border strip into an open front once more.
For Qazah, the choice is already clear. Imposing security, he said, is the exclusive responsibility of Lebanon's political leadership, which must give the army firm orders “to impose security by military force, not by begging for it or imposing it by consensus”.
Alaa Sarhal is a Lebanese journalist
This article is published in collaboration with Egab
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: What is Starshield, SpaceX's military version of Starlink?
articles.body:
What is Starshield, SpaceX's military version of Starlink?
Elon Musk’s SpaceX restricted “military-grade” Starlink services overnight into Wednesday, hampering Ukrainian drone strike missions and air defences, Ukraine reported. In response, Musk said that the US government was behind any slowdown in Ukraine's Starshield system.
The claims drew renewed attention to the distinction between Starlink – SpaceX’s commercial satellite internet service – and Starshield, a military version developed for the Pentagon. While Musk has said the two systems are separate, in many cases they share the same underlying satellite technology.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government,” Musk said on Wednesday in a post on X, adding that any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military or the president.
“Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”
What is Starlink?
Starlink is a satellite internet network of more than 11,000 satellites that beam broadband service directly to user terminals about the size of a folded newspaper. Its roughly 13 million subscribers range from households and hikers to shipping companies and major airlines. It is the main profit engine of SpaceX.
Since launching its first Starlink satellites in 2019 aboard reusable SpaceX rockets, the company has built a vast low-Earth-orbit constellation that blankets much of the planet, delivering faster connections than traditional communications satellites, which typically operate much farther from Earth and in far smaller numbers.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Starlink gave Ukraine a critical communications advantage early in the war, reshaping how militaries operate on the battlefield. But Musk has restricted Starlink for certain military uses while highlighting Starshield, a more secure network developed for government and military missions.
What is Starshield?
Starshield is a SpaceX business unit that develops military and intelligence satellite systems for the Pentagon.
While its missions are separate from Starlink’s commercial broadband service, the distinction is not always clear-cut: Starshield’s secure communications services use enhanced encryption and dedicated terminals, but rely on the vast Starlink constellation as their backbone.
Watch moreStarlink restriction 'no surprise' after Musk condemned Ukraine strikes on Russian data centres
Starshield leverages the technology, engineering and operational experiences of Starlink, according to SpaceX. In addition to secure communications, the company says the militarised version can also provide users with Earth observation and the ability to integrate sensors or other payloads.
The Pentagon, Starshield’s largest customer, has spent billions of dollars on both Starlink and Starshield services. It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft for missile-warning missions and a spy constellation for the National Reconnaissance Office, Reuters reported in 2024.
Questions over the relationship between Starlink and Starshield have persisted since Russia threatened Western satellites supporting Ukraine in 2022. SpaceX unveiled Starshield later that year, but the secrecy surrounding national security space programmes has left the precise boundaries between the two systems opaque.
Those distinctions became a point of contention earlier this year when the Pentagon clashed with SpaceX over higher prices for satellite services used by military drones during the Iran conflict, Reuters reported. SpaceX argued that some customers paying roughly $5,000 per terminal for Starlink should instead have been using a Starshield service costing about $25,000 per terminal.
Britain has also adopted Starshield. Under that arrangement, the service uses the same satellite constellation, ground stations and terrestrial infrastructure as Starlink, but operates through dedicated terminals and separate network gateways, Britain’s defence ministry has told Reuters.
Other US partners are evaluating the system as well. New Zealand is doing a trial of Starshield to assess its usefulness for military operations, the New Zealand Defence Force previously told Reuters.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

articles.title: After Trump, Musk tells Ukraine’s president to go. Zelenskyy says he won’t resign and will never accept Ukrainian land as Russian
articles.body:
Tech billionaire Elon Musk wrote on X on 15 October: “And so the slaughter continues … Time for Zelensky to go.” Four days earlier, he had posted that Zelenskyy had gone too far, after US President Donald Trump said it was time for Ukraine to get a new president. Asked by Morgan on 14 October whether he would resign, Zelenskyy said he would not: “It’s my responsibility.”
Musk’s post comes as Washington squeezes Kyiv instead of Moscow: Ukraine’s military satellite links slowed, US missile warnings went missing, and the US threatened to cut intelligence unless Kyiv stops hitting Russian refineries.
Land and elections
Zelenskyy said elections could not be held under constant Russian attack: “From the point of security, you can’t do elections.”
Of any future president, he said: “I’m sure the new man or woman will defend our country.” He also reminded Trump that Crimea and parts of Donbas were already occupied when he took office, under another president, long before the full-scale invasion.
“I’m a realist, and I understand that people are more important than one kilometer or two kilometers. It’s not about kilometers. It’s about land and homes,” he told Morgan.
Zelenskyy has said Ukraine is ready for elections if a full 60-day ceasefire is in place. Numerous sources told The Atlantic that Trump sees Zelenskyy as the main obstacle to a peace deal and related business deals with Russia. One Trump adviser said he is also an obstacle to Trump’s hopes for the Nobel Peace Prize.
Starlink
Ukrainian forces reported restrictions on Starshield, the SpaceX satellite system they use for battlefield communications and drone operations, and Zelenskyy warned the decision would cost lives. On 14 October, Musk said Starshield is owned and controlled by the US government, which sets its limits, and that commercial Starlink cannot be used for offensive military action. Zelenskyy told the FT he did not know whether the decision was SpaceX’s or the US government’s, adding: “I think it’s about SpaceX.” A senior US official told Axios the Trump administration had nothing to do with the restrictions.
Intelligence and refineries
On two consecutive nights, air raid alerts in Kyiv sounded only after Russian ballistic missiles were already approaching or striking the capital. Zelenskyy said Ukraine received no warning from partners of the launches on 12 and 13 October, which hit civilian infrastructure and a major power plant. A Ukrainian official told CNN the loss of intelligence “will give Russians a real leverage on a frontline.” A European official questioned Washington’s explanation that weather caused the gaps in missile warnings. Trump denied halting intelligence sharing.
Washington had warned it could suspend intelligence sharing if Ukraine kept striking Russian refineries, Axios reported. A US official disputed that any explicit threat was made. Sources told CNN the US had also threatened to halt European purchases of US weapons for Ukraine. Zelenskyy told the FT the warning came through military channels.
To lower energy costs before next month’s midterm elections, Trump has pressed Kyiv to stop refinery strikes, CNN reported. Zelenskyy said he felt betrayed after Trump announced a diesel supply deal with Russia. On 14 October in London, he told the FT that Ukraine would resume strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Read also
- “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government”: Musk says Trump, not SpaceX, is behind cut hitting Ukraine
- Fears that Ukraine will lose Starlink are back after Musk backed Trump against Zelenskyy. Adviser says profit makes cutoff unlikely
- Energy truce with strings attached: Kyiv reportedly told to spare Russian refineries or lose US intelligence and arms

articles.title: Axios: White House denies role in Starlink restrictions in Ukraine
articles.body:
A senior official in the U.S. presidential administration told Axios the White House had nothing to do with restricting Starlink’s operation in Ukraine.
Axios’s sources said the Trump administration plans to contact SpaceX to find out what happened with Starlink in Ukraine.
Ukraine’s Defense Ministry earlier announced that it had run into restrictions on Starshield, the military version of Starlink used by Ukrainian forces. Ukrainian servicemen and officials said the restrictions disrupted some missions.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk announced that U.S. authorities own and control the Starshield systems. “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” he wrote on the social media platform X.
The White House has not officially commented on the reports of restrictions on Starlink’s operation in Ukraine.
The restriction on Starlink’s operation was reported amid a crisis in relations between U.S. President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Ukraine also said it had stopped receiving warnings from American allies about the launch of Russian ballistic missiles. Western media, citing government sources, reported that the U.S. told Ukraine it would withhold intelligence sharing unless Kyiv stopped striking Russian oil refineries.

articles.title: ‘We’re Done’: Zelensky Says Ukraine Will Resume Strikes on Russian Oil Refineries
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries after Washington pressured Ukraine to halt attacks, warning that the US has endangered Ukrainian lives by restricting access to intelligence and Starlink satellite communications.
“The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” Zelensky told the Financial Times in an interview in London.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Zelensky said Ukrainian military officials had been warned by their US counterparts that Washington would restrict intelligence sharing if Kyiv continued striking Russian energy facilities.
The comments mark a further deterioration in relations between Zelensky and US President Donald Trump, who has pushed Ukraine to stop attacks on Russian oil infrastructure as Washington seeks to lower fuel prices.
Last week, Trump announced an agreement for Russia to supply diesel to US and global markets, drawing criticism from US lawmakers and European allies.
Zelensky described the deal as a “simple victory” for the Kremlin in an interview with British broadcaster Piers Morgan on Wednesday.
“It’s a pity that we are losing a strong partner,” Zelensky said.
He also accused Trump of taking Russia’s side in the war, arguing that Washington should remain neutral rather than favor Moscow.
“This is our country, our body, our home, our children,” Zelensky said. “That’s why it’s painful when Trump chooses one side.”
ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, October 14, 2026
“If you’re in the middle, you have to stay in the middle. Not on the wrong side,” he added. “This is not the right side of history.”
Starlink restrictions raise alarm in Kyiv
The dispute escalated after Ukraine reported restrictions on military Starlink services, which Ukrainian forces rely on for battlefield communications and drone operations.
Zelensky warned that the restrictions could lead to significant casualties as Russia intensified attacks on Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.
“It’s a big mistake,” he said. “This decision will bring a lot of human losses… People will die.”
He urged Elon Musk, whose SpaceX operates Starlink, to restore the service, saying he hoped the disruption was the result of a technical problem.
Musk said on Wednesday that Starshield, the military-grade satellite system, is owned and controlled by the US government, which determines restrictions on its use.
He added that Starlink is a commercial service intended for civilian and defensive purposes and should not be used for offensive military operations.
The reported Starlink restrictions came amid concerns that a reduction in US intelligence sharing could weaken Ukraine’s ability to detect incoming Russian missile attacks and protect its cities.
Ukrainian officials told CNN that the loss of intelligence could give Russian forces an advantage on the battlefield, while a European official questioned Washington’s explanation that weather had caused gaps in missile-warning information.
For two consecutive nights, the air raid warnings that normally give Kyiv residents precious time to seek shelter came only after Russian ballistic missiles were already approaching or striking the Ukrainian capital.
On Monday and Tuesday, Oct. 12-13, Russia launched successive ballistic missile attacks, striking civilian infrastructure and a major power plant. Ukraine received no advance warning of the launches from Western partners, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
The Trump administration has previously warned that it could suspend intelligence sharing and halt European purchases of US weapons for Ukraine if Kyiv refused to stop deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
Russia intensifies attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure
The dispute comes as Russian forces continue attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities. Zelensky said Russian strikes had left more than 600,000 people without electricity.
Moscow has also intensified aerial attacks as battlefield advances remain limited, with both sides targeting energy infrastructure.
Zelensky has sought to strengthen European support amid uncertainty over Washington’s commitment. During his visit to London on Wednesday, he met British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and King Charles III.

articles.title: The Guardian view on Trump’s deal with Putin: grim and grubby, but not gamechanging | Editorial
articles.body:
When Donald Trump pledged to end the war in Ukraine within 24 hours of re-entering the White House last year, no one with any depth of insight into the conflict believed him. But Mr Trump took his own words seriously enough to feel the lack of a ceasefire as an affront to his self-image as a master dealmaker. After a period when it seemed that Kyiv’s European allies had steered the US president away from pro‑Kremlin partisanship, he has reverted to the grotesque view that Ukrainian capitulation is a necessary precondition for peace.
These are the perilous circumstances in which President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met Andy Burnham on Wednesday in Downing Street. In recent days, the US president has called for a change of government in Ukraine. He claimed that a partial ceasefire had been agreed, while Russia escalated its bombardments. According to Mr Zelenskyy, the latest missile strikes have come without the intelligence warnings from the US that have, in the past, facilitated self-defence. There have been reports of Ukrainian soldiers losing access to the Starlink satellite network, controlled by Elon Musk, the US tech oligarch. This raises suspicion of coordinated pressure to tip the scales in Russia’s favour after many months when Mr Putin’s forces have failed to deliver significant advances and his country’s economy has been suffering from the effect of Ukrainian missile and drone counterstrikes.
Mr Trump is unhappy with Ukraine targeting Russian oil refineries. He claims that this is the cause of high energy prices afflicting American consumers and threatening Republican prospects in next month’s midterm elections. The domestic imperative to keep pump prices down led Mr Trump to do a grubby deal to import diesel from Russia, in flagrant breach of international sanctions.
The real driver of global energy prices is not Ukraine defending itself from Russian attack, but Mr Trump’s failing war against Iran. However, the US president is incapable of admitting any fault. Blaming Mr Zelenskyy enables him to deny his own culpability and, with malevolent encouragement from Mr Putin, to revive the preposterous notion that Ukrainian intransigence rather than Russian aggression is the reason why his promise to broker a peace deal remains unfulfilled.
Disrupting Mr Trump’s pro-Russian delusions is not easy, but it has been done before. It is not a gratifying diplomatic task to indulge the monstrous vanity of the US president by trying to impress upon him a view of his country’s national interest, that Mr Putin is not an ally of his country or his personal friend, which is self-evident to any rational observer.
Mr Burnham rightly resists invitations to denounce the US president in public. He recognises that Ukraine’s cause and, by extension, also the cause of European democracy more widely, is better served by making the case in private. The best response to Mr Trump’s perfidy is for Mr Zelenskyy’s friends to reaffirm their support, as Mr Burnham has done, thereby signalling that Ukraine will not be beaten by deals between the Kremlin and the White House.
Russia is failing to achieve its war aims because the invasion was conceived in delusional hatred for the very idea of independent Ukrainian nationhood, which routinely underestimates that country’s will to resist. That is a flaw in Mr Putin’s plans that no amount of collusion with Mr Trump can fix.

articles.title: EU Disburses Another €2.86B to Cover Ukraine’s ‘Most Urgent Needs’ – Drones and Missiles
articles.body:
The European Union (EU) has disbursed another €2.86 billion ($3.1 billion) to Ukraine for air defense, particularly drones and missiles, as the country nears its fifth winter of Russia’s aggression.
The European Commission confirmed the payment on Wednesday, Oct. 14, made under the defense component of the €90 billion (approx. $100 billion) Ukraine Support Loan. The funds will also cover radars, electronic warfare systems and ammunition.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Amid intensified Russian attacks on our cities and critical infrastructure, this support is vital,” Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said in a statement on Telegram.
“More drones, air defense systems, missiles, and ammunition mean stronger protection for our people and greater capabilities for our defenders on the front line,” he added, noting that Kyiv is working with European partners to secure the rest of the defense funding without further delays.
Funds arrive as Russia escalates its air campaign
The disbursement follows one of Russia’s heaviest strikes on Ukraine’s energy system this autumn.
Overnight on Oct. 13-14, Ukraine’s Defense Forces recorded roughly 39 missiles and 128 launched by Russia, which left at least 600,000 people without power according to President Volodymyr Zelensky.
“As Russia stalls on the frontlines, it continues to escalate its aerial attacks – cruelly targeting Ukrainian civilians and infrastructure,” President of the European Commission Ursula von Der Leyen said.
Russian Strikes Destroy Epicentr K’s Last Major Logistics Hub
The defense payments are expected to reach Ukraine in the upcoming weeks.
What remains for 2026
Ukraine still has €29.64 billion (roughly $33 billion) in EU financial support available for the rest of the year, according to the Commission.
That includes €25.24 billion ($28 billion) under the Ukraine Support Loan, split between €12.54 billion (approx. $14 billion) for Ukraine’s defense industry and €12.7 billion (about $14 billion) in budget support, plus €4.4 billion (about $5 billion) left under the earlier Ukraine Facility.
Budget payments depend on Kyiv meeting conditions set out in the Ukraine Plan and a memorandum of understanding with the EU.
Ukraine had received €1.2 billion (roughly $1.3 billion) just a week earlier, on Oct. 7, bringing total funding received under the program to nearly €13 billion ($14.5 billion) according to Koretskyi.
Mid-September, Koretskyi warned Ukraine risks losing a substantial amount of $29.5 billion in planned international financing if the parliament misses deadlines for required legislation.
The government has moved its deadline for 42 required decisions to Oct. 15 as it prepares for winter pressure on the budget.
According to the European Commission, the Ukraine Support Loan was adopted in February 2026, and it provides up to €90 billion (approx. $100 billion) over 2026-27, with an indicative €60 billion ($67 billion) for defense and €30 billion ($33 billion) for the budget.
The Council approved this year’s allocation on April 23 after Ukraine submitted its financing strategy.
Since 2022, the EU and its member states have provided €231.5 billion ($258 billion) in total support to Ukraine, including €3.8 billion ($4.2 billion) from proceeds of immobilized Russian assets.

articles.title: WATCH aftermath of Ukrainian drone attack on Russian oil refinery
articles.body:
WATCH aftermath of Ukrainian drone attack on Russian oil refinery
Videos online have captured a fire that broke out at an oil refinery in Russia’s Ryazan Region following a major overnight Ukrainian drone raid.
The Russian Defense Ministry said air defenses and military aircraft shot down four Flamingo cruise missiles and 69 fixed-wing drones between 4 AM and 7 AM local time on Thursday. The blaze was caused by the debris of a fallen UAV, it added.
The attack came as Ukraine continued its strikes on Russian oil infrastructure for a second consecutive day, with two oil refineries – in Ryazan and Saratov Regions – being targeted by UAVs on Wednesday, according to Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak.
The Russian military has warned that it will respond in kind to the strikes by Ukraine. Novak earlier said that Kiev had shown no signs of moving towards an energy truce, which US President Donald Trump is trying to broker.
On Thursday, Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky said Kiev will resume attacks on Russian oil refineries after a three-day pause he introduced under pressure from Trump.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said later in the day that “in fact, there was no moratorium on the part of Ukraine. Strikes on our oil refineries and energy facilities continued throughout this whole period. Therefore, there is nothing new here.”
The Trump administration’s “active attempts” to settle the Ukraine conflict “are being crushed by the unwillingness of the Kiev regime and Zelensky, in particular, to agree to peace,” Peskov added.

articles.title: Estonian PM: The faster Russian refineries are blown to smithereens, the better
articles.body:
Estonian PM: The faster Russian refineries are blown to smithereens, the better
Estonia continues to insist that Russian oil refineries and energy facilities should be destroyed because they fund Russia's war against Ukraine.
Source: Prime Minister of Estonia Kristen Michal ahead of a European Council meeting on 15 October, as reported by European Pravda's Brussels correspondent
Details: Michal repeated an argument he has made before: that Russian oil refineries must be destroyed because sales of energy finance the war.
Quote: "I have said publicly in Estonia that the faster all the Russian refineries and ability to sell energy will be blown to smithereens, the better. Because Russia is funding the war with that."
Details: Michal stressed that Estonia relies on the US as a partner and NATO ally that assists with security matters.
"We rely on them. And also sometimes even good friends need a remind[er of] what is right," the Estonian minister said.
Michal mentioned that Estonia shares a border with Russia and has the support of the three nuclear powers within NATO: the US, UK and France.
Quote: "We have had shadow fleet cutting our cables, different kind of pipelines. We have had Russian fighter jets in our airspace. We have even had to shoot down different drones in our airspace. They all came. Help came from NATO… So, basing on that, I must say that NATO is working well and the US is a partner in NATO. Trump has assured us and everybody else last time in Ankara that he is following NATO and also Article 5."
Background:
- The European Council is meeting in Brussels on 15-16 October. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is expected to attend on 16 October.
- No additional decisions regarding financial aid for Ukraine are planned to be made at the meeting, and the question of using frozen Russian assets is not on the leaders' formal agenda, although the topic may be raised during the discussions.
- European Pravda previously reported that the European Council plans to call for stricter visa requirements for Russian citizens.
- The European Council will also "express regret over the agreement reached between US President Donald Trump and Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin on the supply of Russian diesel".

articles.title: Iran sets out defense modernization plans as officials stress deterrence and domestic arms productio
articles.body:
Iran sets out defense modernization plans as officials stress deterrence and domestic arms productio
TEHRAN — Iran is seeking to accelerate the modernization of its armed forces, expand domestic weapons production and strengthen its defense-industrial infrastructure, according to plans presented by defense minister nominee Mehrdad Akhlaqi, as senior military officials stress the importance of deterrence and preparedness amid continued tensions with the United States and Israel.
Addressing the Iranian Parliament, Akhlaqi outlined six-month and 22-month implementation programs designed to build on existing defense initiatives while adapting them to changing technological and operational requirements. His priorities include expanding the production and supply of military equipment, upgrading advanced weapons systems, developing missile and air defense capabilities, and reinforcing cyber infrastructure.
The proposed agenda places particular emphasis on domestic scientific and industrial capacity, with greater participation by private companies and knowledge-based firms expected to help accelerate research, improve production capabilities and meet the Armed Forces’ requirements.
The plans come as senior commanders of Iran’s Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) have reiterated their emphasis on indigenous defense capabilities, describing sustained weapons production and technological development as essential to military preparedness and deterrence.
In a separate meeting with Akhlaqi, IRGC Commander Major General Ahmad Vahidi stressed the strategic importance of maintaining Iran’s defense production chains and expanding cooperation between the Armed Forces’ operational and industrial sectors.
Together, the statements outline a defense agenda centered on technological development, domestic manufacturing, and military readiness, while reflecting Tehran’s stated position that its capabilities are intended to deter aggression and enable a forceful response to any renewed attack.
A timetable for military modernization
Presenting his plans to parliament, Akhlaqi said the Defense Ministry would continue existing programs with appropriate revisions while introducing six-month and 22-month implementation frameworks to advance its objectives.
He identified the production and supply of weapons required by the Armed Forces as a central priority, emphasizing the need to mobilize the country’s industrial, scientific and technological resources.
The nominee also highlighted targeted research projects capable of producing practical results in the near term. He said cooperation with domestic industries, private-sector companies and knowledge-based firms could accelerate technological development, increase production capacity and improve the military’s ability to respond to operational requirements.
Maintaining combat readiness, Akhlaqi said, would require the continuous upgrading of advanced weapons and equipment, the expansion of intelligent systems and investment in emerging fields of warfare.
He called for defense planning and force architecture to evolve alongside technological advances and regular assessments of operational needs. The broader objective, according to his presentation, is to align military requirements with the country’s scientific and industrial capabilities while improving the efficiency of defense-related investment.
Missile capabilities are another priority. Akhlaqi said Iran’s missile capacity should be strengthened in line with the level of regional threats.
His proposed program also includes strengthening air defense, developing ground combat capabilities, pursuing the development of a heavy multirole fighter aircraft and reinforcing cyber infrastructure.
The nominee called for the reconstruction and modernization of defense facilities and infrastructure, stressing that commanders’ assessments should be consolidated to establish priorities and guide the allocation of resources.
IRGC head stresses domestic production and industrial coordination
In a meeting with Akhlaqi, IRGC Commander Major General Ahmad Vahidi emphasized the contribution of specialists and employees in Iran’s defense industries during ‘the US-Israeli wars of aggression.’
Vahidi said domestic knowledge, the determination of technical specialists and the continuity of defense equipment production were essential to maintaining the Armed Forces’ readiness and countering potential threats.
He called for the fuller use of national scientific and industrial capabilities, arguing that closer coordination between operational units and defense manufacturers could strengthen military preparedness and deterrence.
Vahidi also stressed the need to develop strategic technologies, reinforce production infrastructure and mobilize domestic expertise to address both current and future defense requirements.
Akhlaqi, for his part, said the Defense Ministry was prepared to prioritize support for the Armed Forces while ensuring the continuity of production chains and advancing technological development, particularly in strategic weaponry.
He also highlighted the potential for expanded cooperation between the ministry’s industrial sectors and corresponding IRGC divisions in the design, manufacture, supply, and maintenance of military equipment.
IRGC Navy commander issues warning over Strait of Hormuz
IRGC Navy Commander Rear Admiral Ali Ozmaei, in his first televised interview, challenged US forces to approach the waterway if Washington believed the strait was open and secure.
“If the Americans think the Strait of Hormuz is open, let them come closer. We are impatient to sink American warships,” Ozmaei said.
He stated that a US warship worth $13 billion had been rendered ineffective and had moved approximately 700 kilometers away from the strait because it did not dare approach the waterway.
“We are waiting for US warships to approach the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz so we can sink them. We are counting down every moment until this happens,” he added.
Ozmaei also accused the United States and its regional partners of imposing a media blackout to prevent international audiences from learning about vessels penalized for violating rules governing passage through the strait.
He said the IRGC Navy had released footage of two incidents involving vessels that had violated the rules and faced consequences.
IRGC spokesman says Iran has acquired more advanced weapons
IRGC spokesperson Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi has separately said Iran has acquired substantially more advanced weapons since the 40-day war of aggression imposed by the United States and Israel, arguing that the country’s military capabilities have continued to develop since the conflict.
Mohebbi described a renewed US attack as an illogical course of action but said the possibility could not be ruled out. He suggested that the Trump administration might seek a military or political achievement ahead of the US midterm elections.
He warned that Iran was prepared to respond forcefully to any renewed aggression.
“This time, the consequences for the US will be far more painful,” Mohebbi said.
According to the IRGC spokesperson, Iran relied mainly on older-generation weapons during the 40-day conflict but has since gained access to considerably more advanced weaponry.
Mohebbi also criticized US media coverage of foreign military campaigns, arguing that mainstream outlets were concealing the realities and consequences of military aggression from the American public.
He rejected allegations by US officials that divisions within Iran’s leadership were undermining coordination among the country’s authorities. Describing those allegations as “completely false,” he said they were intended to justify Washington’s failures during the war.
The spokesperson’s remarks reinforce the message conveyed by Akhlaqi’s proposed plans: that military modernization and the development of domestic weapons production remain central priorities following the conflict.
A World War, in the view of the global public
Brigadier General Yadollah Javani, deputy for political affairs of the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC), also underscored the full combat readiness of the Iranian Armed Forces to counter potential threats, saying any miscalculation by the enemy will prompt a crushing response.
Speaking at the Administrative Council of the northern province of Golestan on Wednesday, General Javani addressed the regional and global consequences of the US-Israeli aggression, stating that the war imposed on Iran is not labeled a world war, but global public opinion considers it one.
He explained that the US-Israeli war on Iran had the same nature and characteristics as World Wars I and II, which impacted the global order, the geometry of power, and the shifting power equation—creating new realities.
Referring to Iran's evolving capabilities, he said new technologies, weaponry, and equipment have bolstered the country's defense—a reason the US was forced to move its aircraft carriers some 700 to 800 kilometers away. "Today, the Persian Gulf region—which previously hosted over 100 military vessels and warships—is free of foreign military forces."
Iran will dictate terms for ending the war
The advisor to the chief commander of the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC), Brigadier General Ramezan Sharif, has also argued that Iran’s geopolitical position and military response would ultimately compel the United States to accept conditions set by the Islamic Republic to end the war.
Speaking in Mashhad on Wednesday in a book unveiling ceremony in Razavi Khorasan Province, Sharif said there was no prospect of a US victory in a war against Iran.
He praised the performance of the Iranian Armed Forces in confronting US-Israeli aggression and said Washington had mobilized its regional and European resources to weaken the Islamic Republic.
According to Sharif, those efforts had failed to achieve their objectives.
He also argued that the United States and Israel had miscalculated the consequences of targeting Iran’s senior leadership and military commanders, believing that such actions could bring about the collapse of the Islamic Republic or overturn the Islamic Revolution, which is approaching its 48th anniversary.
Sharif said the two countries had assumed direct responsibility for the confrontation after their regional allies proved unable to carry out the objectives expected of them. He portrayed Iran’s response as a demonstration of the country’s strategic resilience and its ability to challenge a militarily superior adversary.
The IRGC adviser further stated that Iran’s defense operations had neutralized US capabilities at 17 bases surrounding the country, and the outcome was one that Washington had not anticipated.

articles.title: Russian nuclear submarine conducts live-fire drill in Pacific (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Russian nuclear submarine conducts live-fire drill in Pacific (VIDEO)
The Russian Navy has successfully conducted a live-fire exercise in the Pacific, using a nuclear-powered submarine to strike sea and land targets with cruise missiles.
The Yasen M-class attack submarine Novosibirsk launched the weapons while submerged during a scheduled drill, the Russian Defense Ministry announced on Wednesday.
According to the report, an Onyx cruise missile struck a simulated enemy warship at a distance of 170 km.
A Kalibr cruise missile was used to hit a land target at the Kura testing range on Kamchatka Peninsula, more than 1,200 km from the launch position.
The 130-meter-long Novosibirsk is the first submarine of the upgraded Yasen-M class to be built in series production.
Construction began in 2013, and the vessel was launched in 2019. It joined Russia’s Pacific Fleet in 2022 alongside the Knyaz Oleg nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine.

articles.title: As Russia Intensifies Air Attacks, EU Allocates $3.3 Billion for Ukraine’s Drones and Air Defenses
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
As Russia Intensifies Air Attacks, EU Allocates $3.3 Billion for Ukraine’s Drones and Air Defenses
The European Commission has allocated €2.86 billion ($3.3 billion) to Ukraine for the purchase of drones, air defense systems, missiles, and other urgently needed military equipment as Russia continues its aerial attacks on Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.
According to a statement published by the European Commission on October 14, the funding forms part of the defense component of the EU's €90 billion (around $107 billion) loan to Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The newly allocated funds will be used to procure unmanned aerial systems, air defense equipment, missiles, radar systems, electronic warfare capabilities, and ammunition to address Ukraine's immediate battlefield requirements.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen emphasized the importance of maintaining military assistance to Ukraine as Russian forces continue targeting civilian infrastructure.
“As Russia stalls on the frontlines, it continues to escalate its aerial attacks - cruelly targeting Ukrainian civilians and infrastructure. Europe's steadfast support matters more than ever to help Ukraine protect its skies and save lives. With today's €2.86 billion disbursement, we keep addressing Ukraine's most urgent operational needs, including drones and missiles vital to its defense,” von der Leyen said.
The Commission noted that the urgent delivery of military equipment is particularly important as Ukraine prepares for another winter amid Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion.
According to the statement, the assistance is intended to strengthen the Ukrainian Armed Forces' ability to protect civilians and urban areas from Russian attacks, particularly through improved air defense capabilities.
Overall, since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, the European Union and its member states have provided Ukraine with a combined €231.5 billion (approximately $259.1 billion) in assistance. That amount includes €3.8 billion (about $4.3 billion) financed through proceeds generated by frozen Russian assets, according to the European Commission.
The announcement also comes as the EU advances Ukraine's accession process, with two additional negotiating clusters formally opened during an Intergovernmental Conference in Luxembourg on October 13.
According to Transparency International Ukraine, the decision was announced at a press conference following the meeting. The newly opened areas include Cluster 2, covering the internal market, and Cluster 3, focusing on competitiveness and economic growth.

articles.title: The Armed Forces of Ukraine explained how restrictions on Starlink's operation are already affecting the performance of combat missions
articles.body:
The Armed Forces of Ukraine explained how restrictions on Starlink's operation are already affecting the performance of combat missions
Kyiv • UNN
SpaceX has restricted the speed of Starshield terminals, causing drones to lose connection in flight. The Ministry of Defense has appealed to the United States, SpaceX, and NATO.
On the night of October 14, SpaceX imposed restrictions without warning on the Starshield military satellite communications system, causing Ukrainian drones to begin losing connectivity during flights. Some Ukrainian Armed Forces units have already had to cancel some combat missions. Defense Express reports this, citing sources in the military and Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense, UNN writes.
Details
According to the publication, SpaceX set a speed limit for Starshield terminals at 160 km/h. After this threshold is exceeded, the terminal loses connectivity. At the same time, the military is recording disruptions even at significantly lower speeds—approximately 72 to 161 km/h.
In particular, when drones fly at speeds of 110–120 km/h, the connection may disappear for 10–20 seconds. Although the drones continue moving, such interruptions significantly complicate controlling them.
The restrictions threaten attack drones and interceptors
The greatest problems arise with high-speed drones, in particular Middle Strike-type drones, which need to reach high speed immediately after launch. Due to the unstable connection, some aircraft may lose the ability to carry out their missions.
The restrictions have also affected interceptor drones. At the same time, the forced reduction in flight speed makes Ukrainian UAVs more vulnerable to Russian countermeasures.
According to a Defense Express source, on October 14 alone, one of the unmanned systems units was forced to cancel some missions because of problems with Starlink.
Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense confirmed to journalists that the restrictions had been introduced and said it was already in contact with the United States, SpaceX, and NATO partners. The American company has so far provided no official explanations for the reasons behind the changes.

articles.title: Ukraine Says Missile Strike Destroyed 6 Russian Warplanes at Voronezh Airfield
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Navy said Thursday that it destroyed six Russian Su-34M fighter-bombers in an overnight missile strike on the Borisoglebsk military airfield in southwestern Russia’s Voronezh region.
The Navy said the attack was carried out using its Neptune coastal missile system. It also reported damage to equipment supporting flight operations, a fire and secondary explosions.
Ukrainian monitoring channels published satellite images purportedly showing damage to an aircraft parking area. The reported destruction of the six warplanes could not be independently verified.
Russian authorities did not acknowledge a strike on the airfield.
Voronezh region Governor Alexander Gusev said air defenses intercepted 33 drones and “several jet-powered aerial targets.” Falling debris damaged outbuildings at several private homes and a car in the regional capital, Voronezh, he said.
Residents of Borisoglebsk reported explosions and a large fire, with smoke visible from several parts of the city.
The military airfield lies about 6 kilometers (3.7 miles) east of Borisoglebsk.
Russia uses Su-34 fighter-bombers to launch guided glide bombs at Ukrainian positions and populated areas. The Su-34M is an upgraded version of the aircraft.
In September, Ukraine’s military said it had destroyed a Russian MiG-29 fighter jet near the Millerovo airfield in the Rostov region and a Ka-27 helicopter near the Yeysk airfield in the Krasnodar region.
Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces had previously reported striking four aircraft at the Shagol airfield in the Chelyabinsk region: two Su-57 fighters, a Su-34 and another Sukhoi aircraft of an unidentified model. Those targets were about 1,700 kilometers (1,056 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
This article was translated with the help of artificial intelligence and was reviewed by a Moscow Times editor before publication. Learn more about our newsroom's AI policy here.
Read this article in Russian at The Moscow Times' Russian service.
