articles.title: A North Korean Missile Already Supplied to Russia Just Got a Much Longer Reach
articles.body:
- Category
- World
A North Korean Missile Already Supplied to Russia Just Got a Much Longer Reach
North Korea launched a KN-30 ballistic missile more than 910 kilometers during an October 12 test, demonstrating substantially greater range than in the weapon’s earliest known trials.
The same missile type has previously been transferred to Russia and could potentially be used in strikes against Ukraine, according to Militarnyi on October 14.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
North Korea’s state-run KCNA released images from the launch but did not publicly identify the missile or disclose its range.
Based on photographs of the five-axle mobile launcher, the secretary general of the Korea Defense and Security Forum identified the weapon as the Hwasong-11Da-2.5, also known in Western reporting as the KN-30.
The KN-30 is a solid-fueled short-range ballistic missile and an enlarged member of North Korea’s Hwasong-11 family. Pyongyang has claimed that the weapon can carry a 2.5-ton warhead, although that figure has not been independently confirmed.
At least two ballistic missiles were launched toward the Sea of Japan on October 12. Japan’s Defense Ministry said one traveled roughly 220 kilometers, while the second flew more than 910 kilometers and reached an altitude of about 70 kilometers.
KCNA said the test was intended to verify improvements made to key components of the missile system. North Korea did not specify which components had been upgraded, leaving open the question of whether the longer flight reflected changes to propulsion, guidance, payload configuration, or another part of the weapon.
The reported 910-kilometer flight is particularly notable compared with earlier KN-30 tests. When North Korea first tested the missile in March 2021, Pyongyang claimed a range of 600 kilometers, while Japanese and South Korean military assessments placed the actual distance at roughly 420 to 450 kilometers.
The KN-30 was first publicly displayed during a military parade in Pyongyang on January 14, 2021. It is launched from a mobile transporter on a five-axle wheeled chassis and uses a solid-fuel motor, allowing it to be prepared and fired more quickly than liquid-fueled ballistic missiles.
Russia has already received KN-30 missiles from North Korea. Their presence in Russian stocks has raised concern that Moscow could add the weapon to the growing inventory of North Korean ballistic missiles used or available for strikes against Ukraine.
Earlier, reports emerged that more than 50% of the identified electronic components in North Korean Hwasong-11 (KN-23) ballistic missiles recovered in Ukraine were found to be fake.

articles.title: South Korea tests vehicle-mounted laser against drones
articles.body:
- Hanwha Systems said its Cheongwang laser and a 30-kilowatt vehicle-mounted laser destroyed all three target drones during a South Korean Army exercise.
- South Korea began fielding Cheongwang in December 2024, and Hanwha puts the cost of each laser shot at about $1.50.
South Korea’s Cheongwang laser air defense weapon and a 30-kilowatt vehicle-mounted laser shot down all three target drones flown against them during a South Korean Army exercise on Oct. 14, manufacturer Hanwha Systems said.
The demonstration took place during the Army TIGER+ Future Warfare Integrated Combat Exercise hosted by Republic of Korea Army headquarters, in front of about 500 attendees including the army chief of staff, military officials, academics and industry representatives. Hanwha did not say how far away the drones were, what types were used, how long each engagement took, or how the three targets were divided between the two lasers.
Cheongwang, which means “light of the sky,” is the official name of the Laser Air Defense Weapon Block-I, developed by Hanwha Systems with South Korea’s Agency for Defense Development. Instead of firing missiles or shells, the system focuses a high-energy beam on a drone until its structure or electronics fail, and it keeps firing as long as it has electrical power. Hanwha puts the cost at about $1.50 per shot, in line with the roughly 2,000 won figure South Korea’s arms procurement agency has used since 2024.
South Korea began fielding Block-I in December 2024 and calls it the first operationally deployed laser weapon in the world. About five units have since been installed at major state facilities, including the Ministry of National Defense building in Seoul, and the system is rated in the 20-kilowatt class, Korea JoongAng Daily reported. The same report said engineers have since built a domestic laser oscillator, the core component that generates the beam, to replace a German-made part.
The program grew out of a December 2022 incident in which five North Korean drones crossed into South Korean airspace, one of them reaching the northern edge of Seoul, and fighter jets and attack helicopters failed to shoot any of them down. South Korea started developing the laser in 2019 with a budget of 87.1 billion won, and officials have kept its engagement range classified. The procurement agency has also acknowledged that Block-I struggles in rain and fog, a common limit for laser weapons, and plans a more powerful Block-II.
Hanwha said Cheongwang also destroyed four drones and two larger unmanned aircraft in a row on Sept. 16 at the 2026 Defense Drone Technology Exhibition organized by South Korea’s defense ministry.
“Laser weapons are core assets that will fundamentally change the game of air defense,” said Joohun Shin, head of the Laser Systems Business Center at Hanwha Systems.
Hanwha is developing a 50-kilowatt laser armored vehicle with its own money, aimed at export customers, and displayed it at the MSPO defense exhibition in Kielce, Poland, which opened Sept. 8. The company has not named any foreign buyer, and it did not provide specifications for the 30-kilowatt vehicle-mounted laser used in the Oct. 14 demonstration or say whether the South Korean Army plans to buy it.

articles.title: French police hit student protesters with ‘violent charge’ – RT reports (VIDEO)
articles.body:
French police hit student protesters with ‘violent charge’ – RT reports (VIDEO)
French police have launched violence charges against student protesters in Paris, arresting young demonstrators as security forces crack down on schoolchildren protesting against staff shortages and underfunding in education, RT correspondent Nadege Abderazzak has reported.
The protests began in late September at a high school in Créteil, a Paris suburb, where teachers and students protested severe staff shortages and deteriorating facilities. The movement quickly spread across France, with thousands of students demanding better education funding and an end to cuts in public services. Demonstrators have also challenged government spending priorities, calling for money to be spent on schools rather than weapons.
Reporting from Paris on Wednesday, Abderazzak described police charging at demonstrators and arresting a young protester. “We’re witnessing a very violent charge by the security forces who have just arrested a young individual,” she said, pointing to the detainee lying on the ground.
Abderazzak said that tensions had persisted for two hours, with an estimated 300 to 400 protesters facing three to five times as many police officers and gendarmes. The march had begun at Paris City Hall, she said, noting that two demonstrations had been authorized by the Paris Police Prefecture.
Since the protests erupted last month, the unrest has repeatedly escalated into confrontations, with police deploying tear gas, water cannon, and stun grenades against demonstrators. Thousands have reportedly been detained and hundreds injured nationwide since late September, including minors. A 15-year-old boy reportedly lost a hand after picking up a police grenade.
By early October, protests had disrupted more than 1,000 educational institutions, with over 160,000 demonstrators taking to the streets on Tuesday, according to authorities. Protesters have challenged France’s spending priorities, demanding: “Allocate money to education, not to buying arms,” according to media reports.
The police crackdown has drawn international criticism, including from Iran, which condemned the use of force against students, while French authorities have defended their response and pledged additional school staff.
The protests come as President Emmanuel Macron’s government cuts public spending while pouring billions into militarization and military aid to Ukraine. France has boosted its 2026 defense budget by €6.7 billion to €57.1 billion, with another €36 billion earmarked for military spending through 2030.
Meanwhile, France’s budget deficit is expected to hit 5.4% of GDP this year, with public debt climbing to 119.3%. Despite the mounting financial strain, Paris has pledged to keep supplying Kiev with weapons, including missiles and air defense systems.
Watch RT's full report:

articles.title: SpaceX curbing Ukrainian drone strikes – officials
articles.body:
Ukrainians blast SpaceX limits on Starlink
Elon Musk’s SpaceX has disrupted Ukrainian drone missions by abruptly restricting the military’s high-speed access to the Starlink satellite network, according to officials in Kiev and frontline commanders. The complaints come as US President Donald Trump has ramped up pressure on Vladimir Zelensky to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries and hold a long-overdue presidential election.
The development was reported on Wednesday by Sergey Beskrestnov, Zelensky’s technology adviser, who claimed that SpaceX had imposed a speed limit of 100 miles per hour (160 km/h) on Starshield, its military-grade satellite communications service, without informing Kiev in advance. 
“Our defense forces were not notified of this restriction, and it has resulted in the disruption of several missions,” he wrote, adding that the move was clearly connected to the “current political situation.”
Later, he added that the curbs imposed on long-range missions are only part of the problem, as the restrictions also impact Ukraine’s interceptor drones, rendering them less potent in tackling Russia’s own strike UAVs.
The disruption was corroborated by four Ukrainian frontline sources cited by Ukrainskaya Pravda. According to the article, one commander provided footage showing two drones losing connectivity above cloud cover and becoming unable to complete their mission.
Ukraine’s 7th Air Assault Corps also confirmed serious operational problems, noting that satellite connections were dropping for 10–20 seconds at speeds of just 110–120 km/h, well below the reported 160 km/h limit. It also warned that slower-flying drones become more vulnerable to Russian air defenses, while aircraft used in mid-range strikes against Russian logistics could become impossible to launch or operate effectively.
Sergey Sternenko, a Ukrainian activist and former Defense Ministry adviser, suggested that SpaceX had acted at the request of the Trump administration. Neither Washington nor Musk has commented on the reports.
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski also weighed in, addressing Musk directly. “Hey, Elon Musk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?” he wrote on X. Poland spends approximately $50 million annually on Starlink services supporting Ukraine, and Sikorski had previously threatened to reconsider those payments after SpaceX announced roaming restrictions affecting Polish customers, a decision which was later rolled back.
Meanwhile, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia had no independent information about the reported restrictions but argued that “it would be better if remarkable technologies such as Starlink were not used for military purposes at all.”
Starlink has become a cornerstone of Ukraine’s military communications since the escalation of its conflict with Russia in 2022, with Kiev’s forces relying on the network for reconnaissance, logistics, and drone control. However, SpaceX has refused to enable the service for strikes deep inside Russia, with Musk reportedly believing that doing so would escalate the conflict.
The reported disruption comes as Trump has ramped up pressure on Kiev to stop attacking Russian oil refineries – something Zelensky said he was ready to agree to on the condition that Moscow stops targeting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. The US president has also eased restrictions on Russian diesel exports following talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, triggering Zelensky’s pushback.
Musk echoed Trump’s criticism of the strikes, writing on X that “Zelensky has gone too far.”
The Trump-Zelensky feud also turned personal, with the US president suggesting that Ukraine needs “a new president.” The Ukrainian leader’s presidential term ended in 2024, and he has refused to call a new election, citing martial law. Russia has since declared him “illegitimate,” arguing that his dubious status is a major obstacle to signing a binding peace deal.

articles.title: Ukrainian troops lost Starlink access for a day. Elon Musk and the Trump White House both deny responsibility.
articles.body:
Ukrainian troops lost Starlink access for a day. Elon Musk and the Trump White House both deny responsibility.
On the morning of October 14, Ukrainian soldiers began reporting restrictions on Starshield, the military version of the Starlink satellite network that is essential for maintaining contact with drones moving at high speed. Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to the Ukrainian president, said “this action can’t be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation,” referring to the conflict between Volodymyr Zelensky and Donald Trump. On the morning of October 15, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said the system was working again. At the same time, no one in the United States has taken responsibility for the outage. Here is a brief summary of the various versions of what happened.
Volodymyr Zelensky, president of Ukraine. It’s their decision. It’s a big mistake. This decision will bring a lot of human losses. People will die if the attacks continue and Starlink doesn’t work. I hope that it’s a mistake, maybe a huge technical problem. We’re asking them to turn it back on. That would be fair.
Elon Musk, head of SpaceX (the satellite operator behind Starlink). Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.
The White House, anonymously. The U.S. presidential administration has nothing to do with the disruptions to Starlink’s operation.
The White House, officially. Declined to answer questions about Starlink. The president and his team remain committed to continuing to play a constructive role in ending the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Thom Tillis, U.S. senator. I’m not holding my breath for Defense Secretary Hegseth to offer transparency, so we’ll be asking the DOD Inspector General to initiate an investigation and report back to Congress and the American People. At best, this was an unacceptable error or lapse, and at worst a conscience decision to clear the field for a Russian attack.

The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. articles.title: Trump ignores Russian strikes on US businesses in Ukraine – CNN
articles.body:
Trump ignores Russian strikes on US businesses in Ukraine – CNN
Despite Russia escalating attacks on facilities in Ukraine connected to American corporations, Trump and his administration are not reacting to this in any way.
Source: CNN
Details: The US president and his administration have stepped up pressure on Ukraine to force it to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries, claiming it harms American consumers.
However, CNN notes that both Donald Trump and administration officials remain silent regarding Russian strikes on American businesses in Ukraine.
The publication emphasises that over the past few months, Russia has intensified its attacks on facilities connected to American corporations and on civilian infrastructure in Ukraine as a whole.
Andy Hunder, president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Ukraine, said that Russian missiles and drones have damaged facilities belonging to some of the most famous American brands, including Coca-Cola, PepsiCo, McDonald's and Oreo.
Hunder notes that although Russia has also tried to interfere with the work of successful American businesses in the past, the direct strikes with drones and missiles, as well as the fact that the Russians continue hitting American businesses in Ukraine, are things that have never happened before.
Quote from Hunder: "It's sending a message that they're targeting American business. We're not seeing any response from the White House. We need this to stop because these are American interests, American money, American investors that are being hit and are being targeted."
Details: CNN recalls that when a Russian drone hit a Coca-Cola plant near Kyiv in early September, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the attack was a "clear signal" for the US.
"The Russians cannot possibly be unaware that this is an American enterprise," Zelenskyy added at the time.
Later that month, a Russian strike drone hit a warehouse belonging to McDonald's. McDonald's Ukraine confirmed in a statement that a warehouse operated by one of its logistics partners in Kyiv Oblast was damaged as a result of a drone attack on 25 September.
PepsiCo acknowledged in a statement at the end of August that a production facility in Mykolaiv Oblast was damaged, but there were no casualties.
Among American businesses on the ground, there is no unity on how much they want to speak publicly about being hit "or disclose the fact that they've been targeted multiple times", a former senior State Department official told CNN.
"Some businesses do want us to raise this," Hunder reiterated, but others "are treading very carefully".
CNN notes that several Democratic US lawmakers have publicly called on the White House to do more to protect American businesses in Ukraine and condemn Moscow's actions.
Ukraine emphasised that these attacks are one of the reasons to strengthen defence support so that they can sufficiently protect American companies on the ground.
The Chamber of Commerce and Industry meets with members of Congress from both parties and asks them to raise this issue before the White House.
Trump spoke publicly when asked in August 2025 about a Russian strike on an American electronics plant, saying he told Russian leader Vladimir Putin that he was "not happy about it".
Quote from CNN: "Still, the relative lack of condemnation on the strikes from the Trump administration stands in contrast to the admonishments to the Ukrainian government about striking Russian energy infrastructure."
Details: In February, the US administration warned Kyiv that its strikes on Russian oil facilities in the Black Sea late last year affected US investments in Kazakhstan.
And in recent weeks, Trump has blamed Ukraine for strikes on Russian fuel facilities and for rising fuel prices.
Hunder told CNN he found it difficult to understand the administration's silence on the issue.
Quote from Hunder: "Any company, any business, wants to have some sort of protection. You would expect your government to stand up in your corner and fight the fight with you, especially if it's a foreign military that is attacking the American companies."
Details: The American Chamber of Commerce sent a message requesting a meeting with representatives of the US president, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, last month to inform them about the state of American business in Ukraine but received no reply.
Background:
- Philip Morris Ukraine reported that part of its factory in Kharkiv was damaged by a Russian missile strike on the night of 29-30 January.
- On 25 September, Russian drones damaged one of the warehouses that, among other things, supported the operation of the McDonald's restaurant chain in Kyiv Oblast.
- The New York Times wrote that Russia had intensified strikes on facilities belonging to US companies in Ukraine in an attempt to undermine its economy.
- Assets belonging to Cargill, Coca-Cola, Boeing, Mondelez, Philip Morris, Flex and Bunge came under attack. Since the beginning of 2026, the attacks have only intensified and within four weeks, facilities of Bunge, Philip Morris and Mondelez were struck.
Your support on Patreon helps us keep the news free and accessible.

articles.title: Yemeni army claims 1,250 Houthis ‘neutralized’ in ‘Dawn of Yemen’ operation
articles.body:
Yemeni government forces said Wednesday that 1,250 Houthi fighters had been “neutralized” during the “Dawn of Yemen” military operation on several fronts, Anadolu reports.
Yemeni Armed Forces spokesman Majed Abdullah al-Nazili said in a statement that government forces conducted 2,309 “precise and direct” strikes using warplanes, drones, field artillery, rocket launchers and sniper units.
He claimed the operations disrupted Houthi defensive lines, command-and-control centers, frontline positions and supply routes, allowing government forces to advance.
The spokesman said more than 460 military vehicles and other pieces of equipment had also been destroyed or damaged.
In the southwestern province of Taiz, government forces continued airstrikes and ambush operations targeting Houthi forces and reinforcements, according to the statement.
Al-Nazili urged residents in Houthi-controlled areas to keep their children away from recruitment campaigns and military positions, and reiterated an amnesty by Presidential Leadership Council Chairman Rashad al-Alimi to fighters who lay down their weapons.
He also accused the Houthis of targeting civilian infrastructure and residential neighborhoods in Taiz.
READ: Pakistan reiterates ‘unwavering’ commitment to Saudi Arabia’s protection under Makkah defense pact
The Yemeni army also said it captured five Houthi commanders west of Taiz province, including senior commander Akram Amer, who holds the rank of major general.
Separately, the Yemeni government launched the “Dawn of Yemen” operation earlier this month to retake Houthi-held areas, including the national capital, Sanaa. Government-aligned forces have since announced advances on several fronts, including around the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait.
The operation has been backed by a Saudi-led coalition, which has intensified air operations against Houthi positions. The coalition said earlier this month that 100 fighter jets took part in one phase of the offensive and later announced that 136 military targets had been destroyed.
The escalation follows renewed fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, including cross-border missile and drone attacks and intensified coalition airstrikes in Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized Sanaa in 2014, forcing the internationally recognized government from the capital. A Saudi-led coalition intervened militarily in support of the government in 2015.

articles.title: Another Starlink facility hit by blaze in EU (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Another Starlink facility hit by blaze in EU (VIDEO)
A blaze has occurred at a Starlink satellite internet service facility near Bulgaria’s capital Sofia, Bulgarian Prime Minister Roumen Radev has said.
The incident follows a fire at a SpaceX station in Poland, which serviced the Ukrainian military, in late September. Ukraine has relied heavily on Starlink during the conflict with Russia for battlefield communications and controlling drones.
Earlier this week, an MP for the opposition Democratic Bulgaria coalition, Ivaylo Mirchev, claimed that masked men had deliberately set a Starlink facility outside Sophia on fire, destroying 11 out of the 17 antennas at the site. He also published a video purporting to have captured the incident.
🚨 Two masked men reportedly set fire to 11 of 17 antennas linked to SpaceX's Starlink network near Sofia, Bulgaria. via WarSurv https://t.co/RgvLK4sasG
— Post Open Source (@CocoPostel) October 14, 2026
Radev confirmed that the blaze had happened when he appeared before the Bulgarian parliament on Wednesday, but declined to say if it was a result of an arson attack.
“An investigation is underway. Just a little more patience, and there will be a result,” the prime minister said, urging other government officials against disclosing any details of the probe until it’s concluded. “If the specific findings are revealed, we will not achieve the outcome we are aiming for,” he added.
Bulgarian Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev told lawmakers that additional measures to protect Starlink stations and similar facilities across the country will be implemented. However, he stressed that they are private sites and that the primary responsibility for their security lies with their owners.
However, Democratic Bulgaria MP Bozhidar Bozhanov wasted no time waiting for the results of the investigation of the blaze to lash out at Moscow. “Why are you afraid to name Russia? Why don’t you act like Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk,” he asked Radev.
The prime minister responded by saying that Bozhanov apparently has “a crystal ball and therefore knows who the perpetrator is.”
Tusk previously called the fire at Wola Krobowska outside Warsaw last month “another act of hybrid warfare.” Polish special services coordinator Tomasz Siemoniak said this week that there was “no doubt that Russian intelligence services are behind this act of sabotage,” but provided no proof to the accusations. Two Turkish nationals have been arrested in Germany in connection with the incident.
Russia has consistently rejected claims of it engaging in any sabotage activities in Europe. Russian President Vladimir Putin and various officials have said that the so-called “Russian threat” is only being promoted by Western politicians to scare their public, distract people from the mounting problems in their own countries and justify growing military spending.
On Wednesday, Ukrainian officials and frontline commanders complained that Starlink terminals had suddenly stopped working when drones flew faster than 100 mph, disrupting some combat missions. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk denied giving any instructions to restrict Kiev’s access to the service, saying that doing so is the prerogative of the American military and US President Donald Trump personally.
The problems occurred as Trump is working to increase pressure on Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he blames for surging global energy prices.
Last month, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that allowing Starlink to be used to facilitate Ukrainian strikes deep into Russian territory would be “a very harmful, potentially dangerous and misconceived step.” Moscow has all the means to respond to such actions, he warned.

articles.title: How to watch the EU leaders’ summit like a pro
articles.body:
BRUSSELS — European leaders came for the budget. They’re staying for everything else.
A two-day European Council starting Thursday was supposed to be all about the money. Instead, leaders of the 27 EU member countries are heading into one of their most crowded summits in years, with a succession of geopolitical crises threatening to hijack the EU’s carefully laid plans.
European Council President António Costa originally wanted the gathering to accelerate negotiations on the bloc’s next seven-year budget, hoping to seal a deal before elections in France, Italy and Poland in 2027 make an already difficult agreement even harder.
Advertisement
But the world had other plans. Soaring energy prices, tensions with China, Russia’s war in Ukraine (and U.S. President Donald Trump’s ambiguity over it), migration and turmoil in the Middle East have all elbowed their way onto the agenda.
The result is a two-day marathon covering virtually every major challenge facing the EU, from keeping European factories competitive to ensuring the world’s most important shipping lanes stay open.
For anyone trying to follow the action without spending 48 hours glued to Brussels, here’s your guide to what matters.
With the usual warning: EU leaders are notorious for letting discussions drag on or reshuffling the agenda — that’s what our liveblog is for.
Thursday at dawn: The pre-match warm-up
Before the summit even starts, Europe’s political families will gather at the crack of dawn.
The European People’s Party meets from 7:30 a.m. at the Sofitel Brussels Europe — the place to be if you can get in, given how many center-right leaders will be at the summit table.
Advertisement
The Socialists gather from 8:30 a.m. at PES headquarters, with Costa, Spain’s Pedro Sánchez and Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen expected.
Renew kicks off at 8 a.m. at the Palais d’Egmont, with French President Emmanuel Macron and top EU diplomat Kaja Kallas among those expected.
Even without leaders in the summit room, the far-right Patriots got a head start Wednesday, with Marine Le Pen delivering a scathing attack on the state of the EU.
Thursday morning: The energy blame game and China
Leaders kick off with discussions on Europe’s struggle for economic competitiveness, starting with energy — potentially the most politically explosive debate.
Governments want immediate relief from soaring energy prices as a result of the war in Iran, and will push the Commission to introduce new measures on top of the wide-ranging but somewhat toothless package it announced back in March.
Expect finger-pointing between capitals and Brussels over who should act, and for climate policies like the upcoming Emissions Trading System on heating and transport to come under fire.
Advertisement
Next comes China. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will brief leaders on efforts to tackle the EU’s enormous trade imbalance with Beijing, following trade chief Maroš Šefčovič’s negotiations with Chinese officials.
Leaders are expected to renew their demand for Brussels to “urgently” tool up with further trade defenses to prevent further deindustrialization of the bloc and to shield further industrial sectors from Chinese competition.
There’s also time for the familiar fight over EU red tape, with calls for Brussels to stop legislating.
The positions are well known: The self-styled “modernists” — essentially the old frugals in disguise — want to contain costs, while countries benefiting from EU spending are determined to defend their allocations, under the less glamorous banner of “friends of cohesion.” Positions on new EU-wide taxes are similarly entrenched.
But the real story is timing.
Advertisement
Governments have watered down a commitment to secure an agreement by December, according to draft conclusions seen by POLITICO. Costa wants a deal before a series of high-stakes elections in 2027 complicate negotiations; capitals fear a deadline could weaken their bargaining power.
Most importantly, Costa is moving into the driving seat as budget talks enter their most politically sensitive stage. Watch for clues about a possible extraordinary summit in late November — and whether December remains a credible deadline or leaders quietly start preparing for negotiations to spill into 2027.
Thursday dinner: Making room for new members
Over dinner, leaders will tackle enlargement and the EU reforms needed to accommodate new members — after all, October’s summit has historically been devoted to the bloc’s hopefuls.
Montenegro is edging closer to completing accession negotiations, while progress elsewhere raises questions about whether the bloc is institutionally and financially ready to grow.
The Commission has outlined proposals to prepare the EU for enlargement, and leaders will discuss how internal reforms should accompany the accession process. Watch for a positive signal to Montenegro and commitments on reforming the bloc itself.
Friday morning: Ukraine’s wish list
The second day begins with Ukraine and an expected appearance by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Declarations of European solidarity are all but guaranteed. The more interesting question is what leaders are actually prepared to do.
Advertisement
Kyiv needs air defense systems, interceptors and financing as Russian attacks intensify. Leaders could discuss tougher action against Moscow’s shadow fleet and visa restrictions for Russians. And while EU financing for Ukraine has already been agreed for 2026, the country’s needs beyond that remain an increasingly pressing issue.
Could this mean reopening the debate on using frozen Russian assets to plug future funding gaps? That remains a question mark — although no immediate breakthrough is expected.
Friday pre-lunch: Defense and three dangerous waterways
Before breaking for lunch, leaders will turn to Russian hybrid attacks, maritime security and the Middle East.
In the Black Sea, recent attacks on civilian shipping threaten Ukraine’s crucial grain export route. Turkey has floated new protected shipping corridors, while countries including Romania and Bulgaria are pushing to give the issue more attention.
Will leaders back concrete measures or stop at condemnation? That’s the question.
Discussions then turn to the Middle East and two other critical shipping routes: the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. The fallout from the Iran–U.S. war, increased Iranian attacks around Hormuz and renewed Houthi threats in the Red Sea have disrupted global trade and energy flows.
Advertisement
The EU’s Aspides naval mission is short of vessels, and Kallas wants governments to contribute more. Watch whether leaders put ships behind their promises.
The broader Middle East discussion will also touch on Iran, Yemen, the West Bank and Lebanon.
Friday lunch: The migration showdown
Spain’s Pedro Sánchez, Italy’s Giorgia Meloni and Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen are worth watching as leaders discuss migration over lunch, following the crisis in Spain’s North African exclave of Ceuta.
Irregular arrivals have been declining, but disagreements remain over border crises, solidarity and tougher migration controls.
And with an election looming in Spain on Nov. 29, this could be Sánchez’s last tango — and a final chance to defend his government’s handling of the crisis while venting his frustration over the lack of European solidarity.
Watch whether the debate produces agreement or another political clash, as happened last time.
Advertisement
Bonus: Two pressers are better than one
With such a packed agenda, leaders won’t wait until the end of the summit for the usual joint press conference by von der Leyen and Costa. An additional one is planned for Thursday, after the budget debate.
On Thursday, watch Costa’s language on the budget deadline and whether von der Leyen offers any concrete measures on energy prices.
On Friday, look for promises of additional support for Ukraine, whether commitments on maritime security come with actual ships and resources — and commentary on how the migration showdown over lunch went.

articles.title: Burnham’s ‘Russia did Brexit’ ruse crumbles
articles.body:
Burnham’s ‘Russia did Brexit’ ruse crumbles
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s attempt to blame Russia for the Brexit vote is a crude attempt to undo the referendum and tie the UK back to Brussels. It’s also imploding dramatically.
In an appearance on the ‘The Rest is Politics’ podcast on Sunday, Burnham said that he sought answers about alleged meddling in the 2016 Brexit referendum after taking office this summer.
“I asked the question coming to Downing Street: Well, was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia? I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was.”
Burnham did not identify who had provided the assessment or present any evidence to back it up. Nor did he say whether the alleged interference actually affected the result of the referendum. However, he insisted that anti-establishment movements in Britain, France, and Germany – where Chancellor Friedrich Merz has claimed that the right-wing AfD are “Russian-backed” – are “instigated via our enemies, namely Russia.”
Haven’t we heard this all before?
On June 23, 2016, Britain voted to leave the EU by a margin of 51.89% to 48.11%. The vote was largely driven by a public desire to reclaim sovereignty, control immigration, and humiliate the country’s political elites, the majority of whom favored continued EU membership.
Six months later, Labour MP Ben Bradshaw announced in parliament that Russia “probably interfered” in the vote. Bradshaw conceded that “we do not have the evidence for that yet, but it is highly probable.” His claims were picked up by media outlets in Britain and the US, where the ‘Russiagate’ hoax was taking root in Washington.
A parliamentary committee stated in April 2017 that the collapse of a voter-registration website in the runup to the referendum could have been the work of a Russian or Chinese denial-of-service (DDOS) attack. In November of that year, City University alleged that 13,000 bot accounts – some of them Russian – were tweeting about Brexit before and after the referendum.
X, then called Twitter, rejected the City University study, stating that it found no evidence linking the bot accounts with Russia; separate research tying Russia to the ‘leave’ campaign was found to be fabricated by an anti-Brexit group funded by liberal billionaire George Soros; and in 2020, a parliamentary report found “no evidence of successful interference in the EU referendum.” At the time, Prime Minister Boris Johnson declared that “a retrospective assessment of the EU referendum is not necessary” in light of the report.
All of this begs the question: ten years after the Brexit vote, why is Burnham conjuring up the specter of “Russian interference” again?
Burnham’s big break
Burnham’s political maneuvering is obvious here. The British PM has repeatedly said that he would like to see the UK rejoin the EU, and two weeks before appearing on ‘The Rest is Politics’, he opened his speech at the UN General Assembly with a reference to Brexit, lamenting that “my country has lived through the disruption it brought.”
Speaking at his Labour Party’s annual conference a week later, Burnham argued that “Brexit has done more harm than good.” The following day he pledged to forge closer relations with Brussels and, if politically feasible, “go all the way” and rejoin the union.
Burnham has refused to say whether he intends to run his next election campaign on a platform of EU membership. However, he has promised to have “a serious dialogue about the different options for our relationship in the long-term” when he meets EU leaders in Brussels next month.
With the UK and EU both embroiled in a proxy war with Russia, there is no more effective way to delegitimize the Brexit vote at the moment than by tying it to Moscow. Burnham made this explicit in an address to Parliament on October 12, arguing that it would be “a dereliction of duty” not to pursue closer relations with the EU, given Russia’s alleged interference in the referendum.
The hoax crumbles
The prime minister’s confidence began to crumble under questioning. Asked by Conservative MP Julian Lewis “exactly how he thinks Russia was able to alter the result of the referendum,” Burnham replied that Moscow’s interference in British elections was “a matter of record,” without elaborating further.
Responding to Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, Burnham claimed that he never implied that the result of the referendum was invalid, before repeating the same “matter of record” line.
Burnham’s lack of evidence became clear when his foreign secretary, Stephen Doughty, appeared on ITV’s ‘Good Morning Britain’ the same day.
“What did Russia do during that Brexit referendum?” host Susanna Reid asked Doughty, who responded that he was “not going to get into the specifics.”
“Why are you not getting into specifics when the Prime Minister has just got into the specifics on the podcast?” Reid pressed.
Asked repeatedly about Russian interference in the Brexit vote, Doughty gave a variation on “Russia attempts to interfere in all of our democratic processes. They’ve been doing this for many, many years” every time.
“This is embarrassing,” co-host Ed Balls interjected. “It’s really bad for politics when you just blatantly don’t answer the question on something so important and go back to a nonsensical line, which is contradicted by what the prime minister just said.”
The final nail in the coffin came from MI5 Director Ken McCallum. McCallum is no stranger to anti-Russian opportunism, having pushed for mass internet surveillance to prevent Russia causing “mayhem on British and European streets.” However, he warned on Tuesday against exaggerating “Russian influence” on Brexit, arguing that debating the influence of “Russian trolls” on the vote “play[s] into our adversaries’ hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall.”
The Burnham playbook
Burnham has a habit of making extraordinary claims without the extraordinary evidence to back them up. After five Londoners were arrested outside RAF Fairford in an apparent terror bust last month, the British PM told the BBC that there are “strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened.”
The five men – plus two more suspects arrested afterwards – have all been released on bail. No explosives were found in their vehicles, and no link between the men and the Iranian government has been established, according to all available information. However, Burnham told the BBC that “we can confirm our belief that we believe Iran to have played a part,” before telling Parliament that the supposed terror plot was “almost certainly” directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
Tehran has described the incident as “a clumsy false-flag operation,” aimed at “advancing an anti-Iran campaign and evading accountability for Britain’s involvement in the US-Israeli military aggression against the Iranian people.”
Likewise, Moscow has repeatedly denied interfering in the Brexit referendum. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov described Burnham’s allegations as “the latest baseless accusations made without any proof.”
One final irony
Burnham’s claim would never have been torn apart in parliament, in the media, and by his own domestic intelligence agency had ‘The Rest is Politics’ host Alastair Campbell pushed back and demanded evidence or elaboration. However, Campbell has a track record of embellishing facts to suit political narratives, with disastrous consequences.
Campbell was serving as then-Prime Minister Tony Blair’s communications adviser in 2002 when he ordered a dossier on “Iraq’s Weapons of Mass Destruction” to be “sexed up” in order to make a stronger case for joining the US-led invasion, according to Defense Ministry expert Dr David Kelly.
An inquiry found that Campbell changed multiple lines within the dossier to make Iraq appear more threatening. Among them was a line stating that Iraqi forces “may be able to deploy” chemical weapons against British troops within 45 minutes of receiving an order, which became “are able to deploy.”
Campbell then compiled a second dossier, now known as the “Dodgy Dossier.” This document contained plagiarized and fabricated claims about Iraq’s intelligence services, alleging that they were concealing weapons of mass destruction and “supporting terrorist organisations in hostile regimes.” None of these claims were true.
The second dossier was published in February 2003. Five weeks later, Parliament held a vote to join the invasion, with Burnham one of 139 Labour MPs voting in favor of the war. Burnham has since said that, if he could go back to 2003, he “wouldn’t have voted for it.”
More than two decades later, Burnham is once again making “dodgy dossier”-tier accusations in service of two foreign conflicts, and in aid of his own political ambitions.

articles.title: Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,880 Troops, 3 Air Defense Systems, and 535 Vehicles in One Day
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,880 Troops, 3 Air Defense Systems, and 535 Vehicles in One Day
Russia lost an estimated 1,880 troops and dozens of pieces of military equipment over the past 24 hours, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on October 15.
The latest figures bring Russia’s estimated personnel losses since the start of its full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022, to approximately 1,559,230.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russian forces also lost two armored combat vehicles, bringing cumulative losses in that category to 25,537, while estimated tank losses remained unchanged at 12,414. Ukraine also reported four multiple-launch rocket systems and three air defense systems lost during the latest reporting period, raising those totals to 2,216 and 1,707, respectively.
Another 1,308 operational-tactical UAVs were added to the tally, bringing estimated cumulative losses to 564,897. Ukraine also recorded four unmanned ground systems lost, raising that category to 2,955, while four additional cruise missiles brought the cumulative figure to 5,130.
Russia’s estimated aviation losses remained unchanged at 443 aircraft and 356 helicopters, while naval losses stayed at 35 ships and boats and two submarines.
Another 535 vehicles and fuel tankers were recorded as lost over the past day, pushing the cumulative total to 163,324. Ukraine also reported two additional pieces of special equipment, bringing that figure to 4,830.
Fighting remained particularly intense, with Ukrainian forces recording 260 combat engagements across the front during the latest reporting period.
Earlier, reports emerged that Ukrainian forces have regained control of another 101 square kilometers (39 square miles) of territory and liberated three villages in the Donetsk region, bringing the total area recovered during Operation Vivaldi to 277 square kilometers (107 square miles).

articles.title: Ukraine to resume refinery strikes amid dispute with US
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said his country would resume hitting Russian oil refineries and adopted a noticeably more defiant tone towards U.S. President Donald Trump in an interview published on Oct. 15 by the Financial Times.
Since Trump returned to power, Washington’s support for Ukraine has fluctuated alongside his unexpected social media remarks, which have often taken Moscow and Kiev by surprise.
Trump last week unilaterally announced an “energy ceasefire” that was never publicly confirmed, and Moscow continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
But after a wave of renewed Russian strikes on facilities on Oct. 14, Zelensky told the FT: “The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done.”
Russia said on Oct. 15 that Ukraine had attacked an oil refinery in Ryazan, south of the capital, Moscow.
Since Russia launched its invasion in 2022, Ukraine has faced repeated strikes on its power infrastructure and gradually expanded what it says are retaliatory strikes into Russian territory, including on refineries.
Trump criticized the attacks, especially after he struck a surprise diesel deal with Moscow and ordered Ukraine to stop targeting Russian refineries.
Zelensky said Ukraine paused the strikes for several days, despite Russian claims, denied by Kiev, that Ukraine attempted to target refineries during that period.
Despite complying, Zelensky said Ukraine saw its access to key U.S. military capabilities and intelligence restricted.
Starshield, the satellite network built on Starlink and used by militaries, was slowed over on Oct. 14.
“It was not a technical problem, it was the will,” Zelensky told the FT.
He also warned of a “dangerous” cutting off of intelligence sharing with Kiev, which relies heavily on early warnings to protect its cities from Russian air attacks.
Fears that Washington could curb intelligence cooperation had already surfaced after a public clash between Trump and Zelensky early in Trump’s presidency.
The Ukrainian presidency has since worked to smooth relations with Washington, trying to adapt to Trump’s fluctuating stances.
In the interview, Zelensky made a pointed comment about the relationship between Trump, and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Trump “speaks about it openly and loudly that he loves such people and he respects such people. Because for him people who can be leaders 20 years, 30 years, 40 years, it means they can be very strong”, he said.
Zelensky also urged the United States not to stand with the aggressor on Oct. 15, calling for “honesty.”
“We need HONESTY from our partners about this war: It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war, and guarantee security,” Zelensky said on social media.

articles.title: Taiwan seeks 462 extended-range air defense missiles for NASAMS
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan is seeking 462 extended-range missiles for 12 US-made National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile Systems (NASAMS) to strengthen its air defenses and protect critical infrastructure.
The first phase of the procurement includes 123 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile Extended Range (AMRAAM-ER) missiles. The US has yet to announce the exact number for the second phase, but Taiwan hopes to acquire 462 across both phases, per Liberty Times.
The AMRAAM-ER has an effective interception range of up to 50 kilometers and a maximum altitude of about 25 kilometers. Its range is roughly 50% greater than that of the AIM-120C-7 missiles previously used by NASAMS, more than three times that of Taiwan’s land-based Sky Sword II missiles, and more than 10 times that of the Stinger missiles used by Taiwan’s Avenger air defense systems.
A military official told Liberty Times on Thursday that the US Air Force awarded Raytheon a contract in April to prepare for large-scale AMRAAM-ER production. The contract covers foreign military sales to countries including Taiwan, Hungary, and the Netherlands.
Taiwan’s Air Force plans to deploy NASAMS as a distributed network, with centralized command and control and launchers positioned at multiple locations. Each of the 12 systems would have three launch vehicles carrying six missiles apiece, for a combined capacity of 216 ready-to-fire missiles.
If Taiwan acquires all 462 planned missiles and fully loads the launchers, 246 would remain in reserve, Liberty Times reported. Those missiles would be stored in protected facilities for reloading after an initial engagement.
NASAMS has also been deployed in Ukraine against Russian aerial attacks. By February 2025, the systems had made about 900 successful interceptions there, with a reported success rate of 94%, according to Norwegian military figures cited by Euromaidan Press. Nearly 60% of the intercepted targets were cruise missiles.

articles.title: Russia Builds Military Communications Network Across Belarus Toward NATO and Ukraine — BELPOL
articles.body:
A new secure military communications system for the Belarusian Ministry of Defense is being deployed across Belarus. It is designed to support the deployment and movement of Russian troops toward the borders of NATO countries.
This is according to the analytical report “The Militarization of Belarus,” presented in Warsaw by the Belarusian association BELPOL and the clandestine Community of Railway Workers of Belarus (CRWB), as reported by Centrum Europy.
The 48-page document was presented the previous day with the participation of Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, leader of Belarus’s democratic forces, as part of the Warsaw Security Forum.
According to the authors, the report was compiled using open sources, materials from the Belarusian underground, and information obtained from Russian generals.
The network under construction is based on radio relay links and directional antennas that allow data to be transmitted over radio channels with minimal risk of interception or eavesdropping.
Specialized equipment is being installed on towers operated by mobile operator MTS, which is 49% owned by Russia and 51% by the Belarusian state.
BELPOL analysts emphasize that the system’s architecture indicates that it is designed to meet Russia’s military needs.
The radio relay network is not being built outward from Minsk to regional centers. Instead, continuous east-to-west routes are being established from the Russian border to the borders of Poland, Lithuania, Latvia, and Ukraine.
One such route is being laid along the M-10 highway between Gomel and Brest.
BELPOL representative Matvei Kupreichik said the geographical distribution of the repeaters points to preparations to provide infrastructure for the Russian army, while the system’s sole command center is located in Russia.
It was previously reported that in the second half of 2025, Russia deployed a network of repeaters in Belarus to control drones attacking northern regions of Ukraine.
Areas stretching from the Kyiv region to Volyn are at risk of strikes by these Russian drones.

articles.title: How Russia plans to revive its ties with Slovakia
articles.body:
BRUSSELS — Slovakia is reviving a dormant cooperation forum with Moscow, putting Russia’s gas and oil supplies, nuclear fuel and the treatment of Russian athletes high on the agenda of their first such meeting in five years, according to a Russian government note obtained by POLITICO.
The note, written by Russian Science and Higher Education Minister Valery Falkov, says Slovak Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár agreed during an Aug. 20 video call to hold a meeting of the Russian-Slovak Intergovernmental Commission in Moscow.
Slovakia’s Prime Minister Robert Fico said Wednesday the meeting is scheduled for Nov. 25. The Russian note — which is dated Sept. 10 — initially set the date of the meeting as Oct. 26-27.
Advertisement
The IGC, which covers economic, scientific and technical cooperation, has been dormant since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The last meeting was the commission’s 21st session, held in Bratislava on Nov. 12, 2021.
The meeting comes as Moscow finds openings in other international arenas. The U.S. has invited Vladimir Putin to December’s G20 summit in Miami, while the International Olympic Committee has provisionally lifted its suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee and urged sports bodies to ease restrictions on Russian athletes.
Asked about the purported agenda for the IGC, the Slovak foreign ministry directed POLITICO to Blanár’s public statements after the Aug. 20 call. “We pursue a policy in all directions and maintain dialogue with all countries that are interested in pragmatic cooperation with us for the benefit of the Slovak Republic’s national interests,” Blanár said at the time.
The Russian foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment.
The renewed push for warmer Slovak-Russian relations follows Fico’s May 9 visit to Moscow, where he met Russia's President Vladimir Putin during Victory Day commemorations. It comes after Viktor Orbán’s defeat in Hungary’s April election, which cost Putin one of his closest partners in Europe and forced him to look elsewhere for EU allies.
Months before losing the election to Péter Magyar, Orbán rebooted the Russian-Hungarian Intergovernmental Commission on Economic Cooperation, which had been suspended for several years after the 2022 invasion. Magyar's government did not confirm to POLITICO whether the commission would go ahead next year.
Advertisement
EU leaders, including Fico, will gather in Brussels on Thursday for a two-day summit focused on issues including energy prices and support for Ukraine, with the country's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expected to join them for a conversation on Friday.
Oil imports and cultural integration
In the August video call, Blanár raised Slovakia’s opposition to the EU’s phaseout of Russian gas imports and asked to discuss supplies at the Moscow meeting, according to the document, which POLITICO could not independently verify but bears the hallmarks of a legitimate Russian ministerial note. Slovak representatives also stressed the importance of continued Russian oil deliveries through the Druzhba pipeline and welcomed regular shipments of nuclear fuel for Slovak power plants, according to the note.
Slovakia remains heavily reliant on Russian oil and gas, and Fico has argued that ending imports would raise costs. When the two leaders met in Moscow on May 9, Putin said Russia would do everything to meet Slovakia’s energy needs.
The agenda for the meeting next month reaches beyond energy, according to the document. The sides plan to explore working groups on culture, tourism, agriculture and environmental protection, and to discuss the status of the Russian Center for Science and Culture in Bratislava.
Falkov also records Blanár’s opposition to what the note calls the “discrimination against Russian athletes” at international competitions, noting the issue is to be discussed at the IGC meeting.
The International Olympic Committee lifted the suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee in July and said its previous recommendations restricting Russian athletes’ participation no longer applied. World Archery lifted restrictions on Russian athletes and officials in August. FIFA President Gianni Infantino has also called for Russia to be allowed back into international football.
Advertisement
The approach echoes Moscow’s recent effort to lock in closer ties with Orbán’s Hungary. Budapest and Moscow in December agreed on a 12-point plan to expand cooperation in areas including energy, trade and culture. The plan was signed by then Hungarian Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó and Russian Health Minister Mikhail Murashko after talks in Moscow in December. The Slovak note points to a similar breadth of ambition.
The Kremlin’s outreach to Fico shows how Moscow can use energy ties to pull individual EU countries away from a united stance on Ukraine. Putin made a similar pitch in Washington last weekend: After a call with the Russian leader, President Donald Trump said Russia would supply diesel to U.S. and global markets to bring down fuel prices. The deal would provide revenue to Moscow while weakening efforts to maintain a united front against the Kremlin.
But there are questions over whether Putin can follow through on his pledge to Trump. Ukraine has been stepping up drone strikes on Russian refineries, aiming to disrupt fuel supplies and cut revenue for Moscow’s war effort. Kyiv said this month that strikes had disabled 51 percent of Russia’s oil-refining capacity.

articles.title: Deadly drone strikes in NATO waters raise stakes for Black Sea trade
articles.body:
Krapets resident and engineer Valeri Baronov, 81, shows the wreckage of a drone, which he claims is Russian, a day after suspected Russian drones struck two cargo ships off Bulgaria. | Nikolay Doychinov/AFP via Getty Images
The Ukraine war’s spillover into the Black Sea is creating a growing European security and commercial risk: Drones are hitting ships and killing sailors, grain routes are under strain, and insurers and investors are weighing the cost of operating through Ukraine’s ports.
Five commercial vessels have been hit in Bulgarian and Romanian waters over the past week alone, leaving at least four people dead, several sailors missing and others injured. In response, Black Sea countries Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey have raised the issue at NATO, asking for more focus toward the region and joint support, according to two alliance diplomats.
“The attack within Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone is absolutely unacceptable. It constitutes a serious breach of maritime and international law and will further jeopardise safe navigation in the Black Sea,” Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said on X after the attacks last week.
Advertisement
Russia has been attacking Ukrainian ports and cities in the area since the start of its full-scale invasion. But the recent strikes have brought the spillover into NATO territory. If they continue, EU leaders will face pressure to protect Black Sea shipping and keep Ukrainian trade moving.
Those questions will be top of mind at Thursday’s European Council summit. According to draft conclusions obtained by POLITICO, leaders are expected to discuss the “immediate restoration of safe passage for grain cargo ships.”
A wider problem
Russia is not the only country using naval drones in the Black Sea. Ukraine has also used them against Russian-linked shipping. In June, a Ukrainian sea drone exploded in Romania’s Constanța port after Kyiv said it had veered off course because of Russian electronic interference.
“The Black Sea situation is quite dangerous because attacks are coming from both [sides],” said an EU shipping representative, who was granted anonymity to speak freely. “You have to worry about both.”
Attribution can also be difficult. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said Wednesday that investigators still have not proven that Russia is behind the strikes — although some have attributed his reticence to his broadly softer approach toward the Kremlin.
Drone operations by both Russia and Ukraine are likely to continue as long as each has the money and production capacity to sustain them, said Cristian Vlas, assistant research manager for Eastern Europe at the think tank ACLED.
Advertisement
Oleksii Goncharenko, a Ukrainian lawmaker and founder of the Black Sea Security Forum, told POLITICO that a “serious diplomatic initiative” was needed, bringing together Ukraine, Russia and a third-party guarantor, such as Turkey, "to restore freedom of navigation in the Black Sea.”
Grain routes under pressure
The security risk is disrupting routes that carry Ukraine’s harvest to market, with consequences for EU transport links. Black Sea ports are Ukraine’s main export gateway, handling around 95 percent of the country’s grain exports, as well as significant volumes of iron ore. Shipping traffic has fallen as the security risk has grown.
Some cargo is being rerouted to the River Danube, but capacity there has been stretched in recent months as drought pushes water levels to record lows. Operators are trying to add rail capacity, but that risks moving the bottleneck westward to Romania.
Moving more Ukrainian grain overland also risks reviving tensions with farmers in neighboring EU countries, Vlas said. Romanian farmers have worried that Ukrainian produce meant only to transit could stay on the domestic market, he added, while transport operators are already juggling competing demands for capacity.
Ukraine’s Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi has warned that millions of tons of unsold grain is piling up, and that farmers who can’t sell won’t be able to afford to resow all their land.
Bulgaria is working with Romania and Turkey on a joint initiative to protect freedom of navigation in the Black Sea, which Radev plans to bring to EU leaders on Thursday.
Advertisement
Following the Black Sea countries' request at NATO, military officials are likely to look into possible options such as shifting counter-drone systems to the region, the two alliance diplomats said. Radev said Sofia will convene his counterparts in Ankara and Bucharest to examine further proposals, while a senior Bulgarian official called for new joint anti-drone systems with Romania, partly financed by the EU.
Investment at risk
The attacks also threaten what had started to look like a renewed bet on Ukraine’s ports. MSC, the world’s largest container line, was among the biggest and newest investors, reportedly acquiring a majority stake in a container terminal at a port near Odesa in May.
Ukraine has also been offering investors a long-term concession at the Chornomorsk terminal near Odesa. This terminal is one of Ukraine's largest planned port public-private partnerships and part of what is expected to be a multibillion-euro reconstruction effort involving European companies.
But people who work in Ukraine’s ports say the case for rebuilding is collapsing.
“No one is ready to invest and rebuild, since you know that tomorrow there will be another missile, another pack of drones,” Oleg Grygoriuk, chairman of Ukraine’s Marine Transport Workers’ Trade Union, said.

articles.title: A Russian drone damaged Cosmogony, Ukraine’s largest painting, in the section depicting the future. Its artist spent nearly two years creating it
articles.body:
Debris from a Russian drone damaged Cosmogony, a painting that set a national record in Ukraine, the Korsaks Museum of Contemporary Ukrainian Art in Lutsk, where the artwork was exhibited, reported on 14 October. A fire destroyed part of the painting’s final section, titled The Future, according to the statement.
Russian drones continue to attack Ukraine. Overnight into 15 October alone, Ukrainian air defense forces downed or suppressed 536 Russian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). In recent days, Lutsk, a city in northwestern Ukraine, has been among the cities damaged by Russian attacks. Russian UAV attacks set fire to an oil depot, a wholesale warehouse, and a shopping center. At the museum, located on the shopping center’s premises, the fire damaged Ukraine’s largest painting, which covers a canvas of more than 2,000 square meters.
Russian attack damages museum in Lutsk
A fire broke out at the Adrenalin City shopping and entertainment complex, where the museum is located, Suspilne Lutsk reported. The blaze damaged the last of the painting’s six sections, according to the report.
“By destroying art and culture, they are also trying to destroy Ukrainians,” Tetiana Repnytska, director of the Museum of Contemporary Ukrainian Art in Lutsk, told Suspilne Lutsk.
Museum staff also had to evacuate more than 300 works by Ukrainian artist Emma Andiievska, which were exhibited alongside Cosmogony, Oles Tomakh, the museum’s chief curator, told Suspilne Lutsk. Some works could not be removed in time, resulting in shattered glass. However, the museum’s other exhibition halls were unaffected, the chief curator said.
The museum is weighing whether to fully restore the damaged fragment or keep the fire’s traces as a reminder of the war, and will decide after consulting the artist, Petro Antyp, and restoration specialists, it said. Repnytska told Suspilne Lutsk that the painting’s authors could also create a new section.
“Despite the shelling, we will continue to develop contemporary Ukrainian art and preserve it,” the museum director said.
Cosmogony—Ukraine’s largest painting
Artist Petro Antyp began working on the painting in November 2022, Suspilne Lutsk reported, and it took almost two years to complete, according to the museum’s website. The painting covers an area of 2,086 square meters.
In September 2024, the project set a national record as Ukraine’s largest painting.
The artwork explores the evolution of the universe, Earth, nature, humanity, society, culture, and science. Its six sections combine myths, legends, scientific theories, and symbols from different cultures, according to the museum’s website.
The project extends beyond the canvas, as the museum presents a multimedia performance that combines light, sound, and art.
Civilians killed and injured in Russia’s latest attack on Lutsk
Around noon on 14 October, a Russian jet-powered Shahed drone attacked Lutsk. Drone debris damaged a wholesale goods warehouse and a residential building, Roman Romaniuk, acting head of the Volyn Regional Military Administration, told Suspilne.
Falling drone debris sparked a large fire at the Yevrohurt wholesale warehouse. A nine-story residential building on Sobornosti Avenue was also damaged, Romaniuk later reported on social media.
Six people were killed in the strike on the warehouse: five were found at the scene, and another person died in the hospital. Eleven more people were injured, Romaniuk said.
Two other people, including a child, were injured in the residential building. Twelve people remained hospitalized, one of whom was in serious condition, according to the report.
