- Ukraine warns of “a new type of humanitarian crisis” as Russia aims at its biggest cities

articles.title: Thales quadruples Belfast missile output
articles.body:
Thales is now building Lightweight Multirole Missiles at its Belfast site at four times the rate it managed in 2022, and has committed £100 million to expanding that capacity further, the company told the UK Defence Journal after the Prime Minister announced accelerated deliveries of the weapon to Ukraine.
Phil Siveter, chief executive of Thales in the UK, said: “We are proud that the Prime Minister continues to see Thales in the UK as a trusted partner of the UK Government. Our Lightweight Multirole Missiles are designed and built at our site in Belfast, which has been supplying complex weapons to the UK for more than 70 years. With the support from Government, we have been able to quadruple our production to meet the global demand, and we are committed to investing £100m to expand this capacity further.
“The work carried out in Northern Ireland helps to sustain 1,100 direct jobs and supports around 700 more across our UK supply chain, giving the UK a sovereign capability it can rely on when it matters.”
Andy Burnham hosted Volodymyr Zelensky in Downing Street on Wednesday, pledging faster deliveries of air defence missiles alongside further military aid and tighter sanctions on Russia, with Britain pressing international partners to restrict Russian liquefied natural gas exports and to lean harder on Moscow over its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
The Prime Minister said: “Our rock-solid support to Ukraine is vital for keeping us safe here in the UK and ensuring those on the frontlines have the equipment they need to push back Russia.”
All of that rests on a single production line in Belfast, a site that has built complex weapons for Britain for more than seventy years, through Shorts and then Thales, and it is the home of the Starstreak family from which LMM descends. Starstreak and LMM share the launcher and much of the surrounding equipment, which is part of why the line has been able to grow quickly.
LMM is a laser beam riding missile weighing around thirteen kilograms, with a range of about six kilometres. It is fired from shoulder launchers, from lightweight multiple launchers on vehicles, and from the Royal Navy’s Wildcat helicopters, where it carries the name Martlet. Against drones it is substantially cheaper than the surface to air missiles that would otherwise be expended on them, which is the characteristic that has driven demand since 2022.
The Belfast expansion is the kind of industrial response the Strategic Defence Review and the Defence Investment Plan have both called for, with onshore capacity that can be surged when a war consumes stock faster than peacetime contracts replace it.

articles.title: Swedish man detained over Kiev sabotage plot – FSB
articles.body:
Swedish man detained over Kiev sabotage plot – FSB
A Swedish national has been detained in Russia, accused of entering the country to carry out sabotage and terrorist attacks against military facilities, the Federal Security Service (FSB) announced on Thursday.
The man was detained in Sebezh District, Pskov Region, after illegally crossing the border from a neighboring country, the agency said. He allegedly intended to use a declared desire to join the Russian armed forces as cover for his mission.
In footage released by the FSB, he identified himself as Freddy Mikael Stalkrantz Lindholm, a 35-year-old from Stockholm. He said he signed a contract with Ukraine’s infamous neo-Nazi Aidar unit in Ternopol and underwent FPV drone training, also instructing others because of his previous experience.
“They used me because they wanted me to make terrorist attacks and diversion in Russia,” he said, referring to his Ukrainian military commanders.
According to the FSB, Lindholm served under contract between February and June 2026 as a drone squad commander in the 24th Separate Assault Battalion, also known as Aidar, a formation designated a terrorist organization in Russia.
The agency also released Ukrainian military documents bearing his name, including an appointment order assigning him to a drone command position in May, pay records, and a June discharge order stating that he failed his probationary period.
An earlier recruitment interview published on the International Legion’s Instagram account shows Lindholm describing how he decided to join the Ukrainian armed forces. Discussing his mental preparation for the deployment, he described taking a life as “the easy part,” but said he also had to prepare himself to give his own.
Investigators have opened a criminal case for illegal border crossing and are considering additional charges connected to terrorist activity and mercenary service.
The Swedish Foreign Ministry told Reuters it was aware of reports of the detention but was not currently involved in the case. Ukraine did not immediately comment.
Kiev has sought more foreign recruits amid manpower shortages, draft evasion, and desertion. Then-Defense Minister Mikhail Fedorov said in March that increasing foreign recruitment was part of his plan to address mobilization problems.
At least 20,000 foreign mercenaries have fought for Kiev since 2022, Russian diplomat Yulia Zhdanova told the OSCE Forum for Security Co-operation on Wednesday, noting that most have come from the US, UK, Canada, and Georgia.
Moscow regards foreigners fighting for Kiev as mercenaries and has repeatedly warned that they are not entitled to prisoner-of-war protections under the Geneva Conventions. The Russian authorities have prosecuted hundreds, many in absentia.

articles.title: Poland considers reinstating conscription
articles.body:
Poland considers reinstating conscription
Poland is mulling reintroducing compulsory military service that was abolished in 2009, Deputy Defense Minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka has said. Her comments came shortly after an opinion poll indicated that over a half of Poles under 24 were against the reinstatement of conscription.
In an interview with RMF FM radio station on Wednesday, Sobkowiak-Czarnecka revealed that “discussions at the Ministry of National Defense today cover all possible scenarios.” The official said that she personally is a proponent of universal conscription modelled after the Israeli draft system, where both men and women are called up for service.
Sobkowiak-Czarnecka argued that the pool of volunteers should first be exhausted before moving toward the reinstatement of the draft. The Polish deputy defense minister acknowledged, however, that she has “colleagues who are absolutely opposed” to the idea of compulsory military service.
Earlier on Wednesday, RMF FM reported that a recent Opinia24 poll indicated that 46% of respondents were in favor of reintroducing conscription, while 38% were against, with the other 16% undecided. The share of those opposing the draft rises to 53% in the 18-24 cohort. Following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, Warsaw has announced plans to expand its military from the current 220,000 personnel to 500,000, including 200,000 reservists, by 2039.
Speaking at a press conference on the sidelines of the Warsaw Security Forum on Tuesday, Polish Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz called on the European Union to shift to “war-mode” military production.
In recent years, Poland has emerged as one of the most rapidly militarizing EU nations, with its military spending reaching around 4.7% of its GDP. The country has also been one of Kiev’s staunchest backers in its conflict with Moscow, providing Ukraine with weapons, including artillery systems, tanks, armored vehicles, warplanes, and ammunition. Some estimates place Poland in first place among all other Western countries in terms of the volume of assistance provided relative to its own GDP. Poland has also served as a key logistical hub for Ukraine-bound arms shipments from other countries.
Neighboring Germany has emerged as Ukraine’s top backer in Europe in absolute terms, according to the Kiel Institute for the World Economy. The German government is likewise aiming to increase the number of active-duty troops to more than 260,000 by 2035, backed by 200,000 reservists. In recent months, several politicians in Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s ruling coalition have floated the idea of reinstating conscription.
A new military service system introduced in early 2026 requires all 18-year-old men to register for potential service. While enlistment remains voluntary for now, parliament can activate compulsory service if recruitment targets are not met or the security situation deteriorates.
The new model has sparked nationwide student protests, with an estimated 45,000 demonstrators taking to the streets in some 100 cities and towns late last month.
Both Poland and Germany have justified their respective military buildups by claiming that Russia is harboring aggressive plans against NATO member states. Moscow has repeatedly dismissed these allegations as “nonsense” and even suggested providing written guarantees that it has no such plans.
President Vladimir Putin has accused
European NATO member states of openly preparing for war with Russia while using bogus claims. Moscow has also repeatedly warned Western nations against supplying ever more sophisticated weaponry to Ukraine, saying that the bloc is becoming increasingly involved in the conflict with Russia, with potentially dire ramifications.

articles.title: Japan Summons Russian Ambassador to Protest Journalist’s Arrest
articles.body:
Tokyo summoned the Russian ambassador on Wednesday to lodge a protest over Moscow’s arrest of a Japanese journalist on suspicion of espionage, with the foreign ministry urging “fair and impartial treatment.”
Russia has arrested several citizens of what it calls “unfriendly” countries in recent years, accusing them of working for Western intelligence services.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Russia’s foreign ministry identified the reporter Tuesday as Yuki Imai from the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, with a spokeswoman saying he was accused of “conducting espionage activities on Russian territory.”
Moscow’s FSB security service said a Japanese national was arrested on the Far East island of Sakhalin – near a disputed cluster of islands – but did not name the individual.
It said the person had worked for Japanese intelligence to collect information about Russia’s defenses.
On Wednesday, the Japanese foreign ministry said European Affairs Bureau official Kimitake Nakamura summoned the Russian ambassador, Nikolay Nozdrev.
Nakamura “lodged a strong protest with the Russian side over the detention of a Japanese national and the issuance of unilateral statements regarding the case,” the ministry said in a statement.
It added that Tokyo had not received any explanation concerning the case.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitri Peskov meanwhile said in a briefing that the security service “is doing its job.”
Ukraine’s Lyman/Vivaldi Offensive Concludes With Solid Terrain Gains, Russian Losses
“If there are spies, they get caught,” he said.
Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said Japan has not been able to contact the individual and did not know about the arrest until the official announcement from Moscow.
Japanese diplomats in Russia have requested “the prompt provision of information” and “humanitarian consideration and fair and impartial treatment,” Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi said.
The Hokkaido Shimbun said in a statement that it was aware of the Russian announcement but was “still confirming the details.”
“Ensuring the safety of the journalist is our top priority, and we are responding accordingly,” the newspaper said.
Territorial dispute
The FSB said it had “opened a criminal case against the Japanese national,” and that he had been placed in pre-trial detention, TASS and RIA Novosti news agencies reported, citing the security service.
Russian media reported he would remain in custody until Dec. 12.
“Attempts by Tokyo to use its correspondents in Russia... to gather information aimed at undermining the security of our state is regrettable,” Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said.
This was “not an isolated case,” she added.
The charges carry up to 20 years in prison.
Media rights group Reporters Without Borders (RSF) called for the journalist’s “rights to be respected and for his release,” saying in a statement on X that the gathering of information is part of journalism.
The FSB published a video showing masked officers storming a hotel room, pushing a man to the floor and handcuffing him.
He was flown to Moscow, where a court ordered he be held in pre-trial detention.
It did not say when the arrest or court hearing occurred.
In 2023, US journalist Evan Gershkovich was arrested in Russia on espionage charges, later sentenced to 16 years in prison before being released in a 2024 prisoner swap.
Moscow and Tokyo have been locked in a territorial dispute for decades over the status of a string of islands in the Pacific Ocean, off the northeast coast of Japan and to the southwest of Russia’s Sakhalin region.
The Kuril Islands – called the Northern Territories in Japan – have been under Russia’s control since the end of World War II, when they were seized by the Soviet Union.
On Wednesday, Japan protested a visit by a Chinese delegation to one of the Northern Territories islands controlled by Moscow and claimed by Tokyo, calling it “absolutely unacceptable.”
The Chinese foreign ministry meanwhile said a delegation visited Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, the capital of Sakhalin Oblast in Russia, which is not on the disputed islands.
They “carried out friendly exchange activities with the local side,” ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said.

articles.title: Houthis renew attacks on King Khalid airport in Riyadh and Aramco facilities
articles.body:
Yemen’s Houthi group has targeted King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh with a ballistic missile, the group’s military spokesman said.
Brigadier General Yahya Saree said the missile scored a “direct and accurate” hit on the airport.
He also said the group had targeted gatherings of Saudi-backed government forces in the Ras al-Ara and Al-Mudharaba areas with three ballistic missiles, claiming the strikes had caused a large number of deaths and injuries and damaged several military vehicles.
The Houthis also targeted Aramco facilities in Dhahran, in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province, and an Aramco refinery in Riyadh, Saree said. The attacks followed threats issued on Tuesday in response to any strike on the Yemeni capital, Sanaa.
READ: Yemen’s Houthi rebels threaten further attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities
He said the operation involved a large number of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones, claiming the strikes had caused destruction and fires at the targeted sites.
Saree said attacks deep inside Saudi Arabia would continue in the coming days, targeting airports and oil facilities.
The Houthis renewed their warning to international shipping companies, as well as civilians and workers at the airports and facilities, urging them to stay away and evacuate immediately, saying the sites had become “legitimate targets”.
READ: Saudi football league postpones 3 matches after Houthi attacks

articles.title: The US is considering using the "mother of all bombs" against Iran - CNN
articles.body:
The US is considering using the "mother of all bombs" against Iran - CNN
Kyiv • UNN
The US military has prepared plans to strike Iran's energy and nuclear facilities, potentially using the MOAB. Advisers have doubts about the strategy.
The U.S. military has developed new plans for strikes against Iran that envisage the possible use of the largest non-nuclear bomb in the U.S. arsenal — the GBU-43/B, known as the "mother of all bombs." Potential targets include Iran’s energy infrastructure and nuclear facilities. CNN reports this, citing U.S. officials familiar with the military plans, UNN reports.
Details
According to CNN sources, one of the plans involves strikes against a significant number of Iran’s energy infrastructure facilities, with the possible use of the MOAB bomb. Another option concerns nuclear facilities, including Pickaxe Mountain, where, according to U.S. and Israeli assessments, Tehran stores components of its nuclear program. President Trump has repeatedly threatened to strike Pickaxe Mountain. He says the U.S. goal is to prevent Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons.
The use of a MOAB in the conflict with Iran would mark a new stage of escalation. At the same time, according to the publication, sources familiar with discussions of the military plans have expressed doubts about whether this weapon would help achieve the strategic goals of U.S. President Donald Trump or change the balance of power in the war.
Although the U.S. military continues to provide Trump with options for potential strikes against important Iranian targets, some officials continue to privately question whether the White House has a strategy that takes these plans into account in a way that would actually bring the war to an end — something only the president has the authority to do. For months, Trump and his advisers have discussed options that could serve as the "final" end to the war, at least from a communications standpoint, recognizing how unpopular the conflict has become among Americans. Although some administration officials have characterized the war as effectively won, Trump has been more cautious in his latest statements, not declaring victory and saying that the U.S. still has unfinished business in the country
At the same time, over the past several weeks, White House advisers have held meetings to discuss various courses of action regarding Iran.
Although Trump publicly announced that he would take no new action until the midterm elections, several advisers privately said they did not know whether this statement was final or could change before Election Day. One source told CNN that Trump had ordered the military to develop additional strike packages against Iranian targets, including a "significant number of energy infrastructure facilities" and the potential use of the Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB). The same source said the wording used was that this attack would take place "before the U.S. regression in the CENTCOM area of responsibility," indicating that the administration could carry out additional strikes, try to declare victory, and quickly withdraw everyone
We will remind you
U.S. President Donald Trump promised that the U.S. would not attack Iran before the midterm congressional elections in November. He also said that Washington was "holding productive talks" with Tehran.

articles.title: The US threatens to completely cut Ukraine off from intelligence after the next attack on Russian oil refineries – WP
articles.body:
The US threatens to completely cut Ukraine off from intelligence after the next attack on Russian oil refineries – WP
Kyiv • UNN
WP reports that the US warned Ukraine of a complete halt to intelligence sharing after new strikes on Russia’s energy facilities. The decision has not yet been made.
U.S. intelligence agencies warned the Ukrainian embassy that the United States would immediately stop sharing any intelligence with Kyiv in the event of further Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities. The Washington Post reports this, citing a source, according to UNN.
Details
According to the publication, Washington made a firm demand to halt attacks on Russia’s energy infrastructure. This concerns not a partial restriction of cooperation, but a possible complete suspension of intelligence sharing.
The newspaper’s source claims that the American warnings were exceptionally broad and reached a wide range of contacts connected to Ukraine.
U.S. warnings reached an unprecedented scale
The warnings were so extensive that everyone whose surname sounded Ukrainian received a call
The report came amid tensions surrounding Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities. Earlier, the Financial Times wrote that representatives of Donald Trump’s administration had also threatened to suspend the PURL mechanism, under which European allies purchase American weapons for the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
It is currently unknown whether Washington has made any decision to restrict intelligence cooperation. The cited report contains no official confirmation that such threats have been implemented.

articles.title: Israeli ad firm helped spyware target Al Jazeera journalists
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israeli ad firm helped spyware target Al Jazeera journalists
Israeli digital advertising agency Discover-Tech spied on internet users through a sprawling network of online ads that it used to track targets and help hack their devices, notably Al-Jazeera offices in Doha, two research groups said on Thursday.
Its services gave Israel's Candiru—a spyware company blacklisted by the US government—as well as other Israeli surveillance firms access to advertising platforms run by Google, Comcast, Russia's Yandex and others, according to separatereports from Canadian cyber watchdog group Citizen Lab and New York advertising security firm Confiant.
The reports show how the online advertising business, long a subject of privacy concerns, can also serve as a channel for sweeping espionage campaigns.
"The way online advertising works today is a systemic security threat," Wolfie Cristl, a senior researcher at Citizen Lab, told Reuters. "For states, the private sector, civil society and everyone else alike."
Discover-Tech's online ads—often for ordinary products such as phones or earpods—reached more than 120,000 websites and 75,000 apps through its various partnerships, Citizen Lab said.
Users who visited sites or used apps with the malicious ads could be identified and tracked by Discover-Tech, which would sometimes also try to extract phone numbers from some smartphone users, the researchers said. Ads only needed to load on a website for the spying to occur.
Some ads would be used to help plant spyware from Candiru on users' devices, both research groups said, though Confiant said that ads it tied to Candiru were a tiny fraction of Discover-Tech's overall volume.
Malicious ads
Confiant cofounder Jerome Dangu said Discover-Tech was pumping out at least 10 million ads per day all around the world and that data-sharing arrangements—called cookie matching—allowed it to track people even beyond the reach of its advertisements.
"Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech," Dangu said.
Discover-Tech, which was founded in 2020, did not return messages left via its contact form. A LinkedIn message and emails sent to its chief executive, Dekel Boni, were not returned.
Reuters' attempts to reach Candiru's owners were not successful. The US Commerce Department blacklisted Candiru in 2021 for allegedly supplying spyware that was used to maliciously target government officials, journalists, activists and academics.
Citizen Lab said a powerful form of Candiru spyware delivered through Discover-Tech's ads had been used to compromise 45 Windows devices at the Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera between 2024 and 2025, something it said it was able to confirm because the media group had shared its network logs with the group. Al Jazeera did not return messages seeking comment.
Dangu of Confiant said that the malicious ads had been shown to users in "hundreds of networks in sensitive categories," including the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency, and the International Criminal Court. He also said that some regions, like the Palestinian territories, were particularly saturated by the Israeli firm's ads.
"You go to almost any site in Palestine—any site—you find a Discover-Tech ad. It gives them a very complete visibility on the digital activities of an entire country," he said.
Citizen Lab also said it had similar evidence showing the malicious ads were shown to people in the United Nations, NATO, the European Commission, and more than a dozen other national governments. Other networks the ads appeared in included chip-related firms such as Nvidia, Sandisk, Broadcom, and Micron, as well as several media organizations in Mexico, Israel, and Europe that were not identified.
In addition to identifying Candiru and a couple of other surveillance vendors, Citizen Lab said it was able to glean some details about where Discover-Tech's users might be based because the firm inadvertently exposed its authentication logs to the internet, showing people logging in from internet protocol addresses in Israel, Europe, and the Gulf.
Measures against Discover-Tech
Discover-Tech is now being frozen out of parts of the online ad market.
Google said in a statement that it had collaborated with Citizen Lab and Confiant's investigation and kicked Discover-Tech off its ad platforms "for systematically violating our policies."
IAB Europe, the European-level association for the digital marketing and advertising ecosystem, said in an email that Discover-Tech had been suspended from its list of globally approved vendors last week after an audit identified policy violations.
Comcast ad tech subsidiary Beeswax removed Discover-Tech from its platform "following recent activity," Comcast said in a statement. Yandex did not return Reuters messages seeking comment.
Advertising-driven surveillance is increasingly being seen as a national security threat. Earlier this year, the Pentagon said it had received reports that US forces deployed to war zones had been targeted using location data harvested by ad tech firms and data brokers. Branches of the military have since disabled ad tracking on some devices.

articles.title: "Partners need to be honest about the war": Zelenskyy pointed to an escalation in Russia's strikes
articles.body:
"Partners need to be honest about the war": Zelenskyy pointed to an escalation in Russia's strikes
Kyiv • UNN
Russia attacked Ukraine with more than 850 "Shahed" drones, leaving people dead and causing destruction. Zelenskyy called on partners to strengthen air defense and support for Ukraine.
Since the beginning of the previous day, Russia has launched more than 850 Shahed-type drones at Ukraine, with fatalities and destruction reported in a number of regions. And it is obvious that Russia deliberately escalated its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine. Against this backdrop, partners need to be honest about the war. President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy said this on October 15, UNN reports.
Details
"Emergency services continue to provide assistance in dozens of our cities and communities, while repair crews and rescuers are working to eliminate the consequences of Russian shelling. In fact, a massive Shahed attack continued throughout the entire day yesterday and overnight today; there were constant waves, and not a single hour was our sky clear of them. From the beginning of yesterday until 9 a.m. today, there had already been more than 850 Shaheds, precisely at a time of artificially imposed limitations on the speed of our defensive capabilities. Some of the Shaheds were shot down. But, unfortunately, there were also dozens of hits," Volodymyr Zelenskyy said
According to him, one of the largest attacks against the Kirovohrad region took place. There was also damage in Kyiv and the region, in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Odesa region, Rivne region, Kharkiv region, Donetsk region, Zaporizhzhia, Kherson region, Mykolaiv region, Vinnytsia region, Zhytomyr region, Khmelnytskyi region, Poltava region, and Ivano-Frankivsk region.
"Three people were killed in Kropyvnytskyi, and three in the Dnipropetrovsk region. My condolences to their families and loved ones," he said.
It is obvious that Russia deliberately escalated its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine. Russia exploits every such moment and must be held accountable for what it does. Strong decisions are needed to end this war. Stable support for Ukraine is needed, first and foremost for the defense of our skies. Partners need to be HONEST about the war: it is important that everyone in America stand not on the side of the aggressor, but on the side of protecting our lives and our efforts to end this war and guarantee security
Reminder
The Kirovohrad region endured Russia's largest-scale attack since the beginning of the full-scale invasion: nearly 360 Russian UAVs were recorded in the region. As a result of strikes on 26 locations, three people were killed and six others were injured.

articles.title: US considers using ‘mother of all bombs’ against Iran, report says
articles.body:
The U.S. military has developed new plans for possible strikes on Iran that include using the so-called "mother of all bombs" against infrastructure and nuclear sites if President Donald Trump orders attacks to resume, either before or after the U.S. midterm elections, CNN reported, citing American officials familiar with the matter.
Deploying the GBU-43/B, the largest non-nuclear bomb in the U.S. arsenal, for the first time in the conflict with Iran would mark a significant escalation.
However, sources familiar with internal U.S. military discussions told CNN that doubts remain over whether the weapon could achieve Trump's stated strategic objectives or significantly alter the course of the war.
One source told CNN that Trump had ordered the military to develop additional strike packages against Iran, including "numerous energy infrastructure targets" and the possible use of the MOAB. The source said the wording used was that the strikes would take place "before the U.S. withdrawal from the area of responsibility of U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM)," suggesting the administration could launch further attacks, seek to declare victory and rapidly withdraw all its forces.
Another source told CNN that military plans to strike Iranian nuclear sites, including Pickaxe Mountain, explicitly call for the use of the MOAB. Trump has repeatedly threatened in recent months to attack Pickaxe Mountain, where the United States and Israel believe Tehran has stored components of its nuclear program.
However, questions remain about the MOAB's effectiveness against Iran's nuclear facilities and other sites buried deep underground. The GPS-guided bomb can destroy an area equivalent to nine city blocks, but some officials believe it is unlikely to penetrate deeply enough to destroy suspected nuclear facilities at Pickaxe Mountain, which is believed to be protected by layers of granite, or other Iranian nuclear sites that remain intact.
The "mother of all bombs" has been used in combat only once, in Afghanistan in 2017. It was developed in the run-up to the Iraq War and first tested in 2003. Following its deployment against tunnels used by ISIS terrorists in Afghanistan nearly a decade ago, a U.S. military spokesman said the bomb contained approximately 11 tons of explosives. Because of its enormous size, it was dropped from the rear of a U.S. Air Force C-130 transport aircraft.
Production of GBU bombs began in the 1990s, with the weapons designed to strike surface targets rather than underground bunkers. They became increasingly common with the introduction of GPS guidance technology, which significantly improved their accuracy. Development of the GBU-43 began in 2002, and the bomb could only be carried by a C-130 Hercules aircraft. Once released from the plane, it is guided to its target by GPS.
First published: 07:23, 10.15.26

articles.title: Air Force Searching for Next-Gen Perimeter Air Defense Radars
articles.body:
The Air Force is looking to replace the three-decade-old radar warning system that protects the coastlines and borders of the United States and a few remote locations.
A Sept. 21 notice from the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center seeks sources for new technology to continue the Air Route Surveillance Radar-4’s mission and potentially improve its technology.
The notice’s details are classified, but AFLCMC updated the original notice Oct. 13, according to Sam.gov.
The number of radars needed to replace the 44-radar network and the price for those replacements has not yet been determined and will come via market research, Air Force Materiel Command spokesperson Mark Wyatt told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
There is also no development timeline publicly available, though responses to the sources sought notice are due by Oct. 21.
Wyatt said AFLCMC is requesting an instrumented range of 250 nautical miles, identical to the current ARSR-4.
ARSR-4 helps operators distinguish aircraft or potential missile threats from other radar “clutter,” which is more prevalent at lower altitudes. While historically the radar has been very effective at this task, newer additions to the cluttered landscape, namely wind farms, can distort the radar’s ability to “see” clearly.
“Wind farms are one of many sources of clutter that any solution would have to address,” Wyatt said. “The Air Force is not prescribing any technique to solve this long-standing challenge for radars.”
Interested industry parties can continue to pair their replacement option with the existing Monopulse Maintenance Surveillance Radar or replace that radar with another solution, Wyatt said.
The MMSR works with the ARSR-4 to “interrogate” aircraft transponders it detects by sending out coded radio frequency pulses that the transponder then responds to.
Using the monopulse method, the MMSR can determine an aircraft’s azimuth from a single pulse received from the transponder, instead of needing multiple hits when sweeping the area.
The MMSR is mounted on the ARSR-4, and they rotate together as they monitor the skies.
ARSR-4 Locations
- Ajo, Ariz.
- Bootlegger Ridge, Mont.
- Bucks Harbor, Maine
- Caribou, Maine
- Cross City, Fla.
- Deming, N.M.
- Eagle Peak, Texas
- Empire, Mich.
- FAA Academy (Training Site), Okla.
- Falls City, Ore.
- Finley, N.D.
- Fort Fisher, N.C.
- Fort Green, Fla.
- Gibbsboro, N.J.
- Jedburg, S.C.
- King Mountain, Texas
- Lake Charles, La.
- Lakeside, Mont.
- Makah, Wash.
- Melbourne, Fla.
- Mica Peak, Wash.
- Mill Valley, Calif.
- Morales, Texas
- Mount Kaala, Hawaii
- Mount Laguna, Calif.
- Key West, Fla.
- Nashwauk, Minn.
- North Truro, Mass.
- Oceana Naval Air Station, Va.
- Oilton, Texas
- Mount Santa Rosa, Guam
- Paso Robles, Calif.
- Rainbow Ridge, Calif.
- Remsen, N.Y.
- Riverhead, N.Y.
- Rocksprings, Texas
- San Clemente Island, Calif.
- Slidell, La.
- Tamiami, Fla.
- Tyndall Air Force Base, Fla.
- Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif.
- Watford City, N.D.
- Whitehouse, Fla.
- Guantanamo Bay Naval Base, Cuba
An Aging Platform
The Air Force purchased most of the existing 44 radars in the 1990s, upgrading the previous 1, 2, and 3 models that have monitored the skies since the late 1950s.
The Raytheon-built ARSR-1 entered service in 1958 and was first used to manage the exploding growth of civil aviation. It had a 170-200 nautical mile range. That early system used the Army/Navy/Fixed Radar Surveillance-20 and later variants of the AN/FPS-66. In the 1960s, Raytheon produced the ARSR-2, which improved maintenance and reliability factors. That radar was the AN/FPS-115.
Both the ARSR-1 and -2 ran on vacuum tubes.
Westinghouse Electric Corporation built the AN/FPS-130, the radar base of the ARSR-3, fielding it in the 1970s and extending detection ranges beyond 240 nautical miles; it was incorporated into joint military-civil air defense networks.
The ARSR-4, also built by Westinghouse and commissioned in the 1990s, was the first radar in the family to offer three-dimensional target tracking. That capability allows users to simultaneously measure a target’s range, azimuth, and altitude. The system also provided advanced look-down/clutter rejection capabilities for military operations.
Northrop Grumman acquired Westinghouse in 1996, rolling the company’s radar and electronic warfare programs into its Electronic Systems sector.
While the ARSR-4s monitor the perimeter of the country, Guam, and Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, for the U.S. interior, the FAA manages a network of Common Air Route Surveillance Radars. The CARSR has an estimated 200 nautical mile range.
The complete CARSR system replacement rollout concluded in 2015. The rollout maintained the legacy sites, towers, and mechanical controls while refitting the internal electronics of the radars.
One ARSR-4 location has a strategically vital area to protect: Watford City, N.D., is 165 miles from Minot Air Force Base, N.D., home of the 91st Missile Wing, and 263 miles from Malmstrom Air Force Base, Mont.—putting hundreds of ICBM silos in its range.
A Larger Network
The ARSR-4 system is one piece of a larger detection system used to track incoming threats.
The Air Force and NORAD used the AN/FPS-117 and AN/Transportable Phased Array System-77, both of which serve as northern warning systems out to 250 nautical miles. These systems are specifically designed for extreme cold weather, such as in their locations in Alaska and northern Canada.
The Space Force operates the AN/Frequency Precision and Quantization-16 Perimeter Acquisition Radar Attack Characterization System, which tracks missiles and precision space objects out to about 2,000 miles. USSF also operates the AN/FPS-108 COBRA DANE to track missiles out to 2,000 miles and high-altitude space objects at 25,000 miles.
The Space Force’s 20th Space Surveillance Squadron at Elgin Air Force Base, Fla., operates the AN/FPS-85 Phased Array Radar, which can track objects beyond 22,000 miles.
NORAD is also currently building and deploying high-frequency systems to detect hypersonic missiles with over-the-horizon radar, modernizing the Northern Warning System and building a polar over-the-horizon radar network.
The Homeland Defense OTHR, which kicked off in 2022, is being funded by both the United States and Canada at an estimated $6-7 billion and $3.1 billion, respectively. Initial Operating Capability is slated for 2028-29, with Full Operational Capability targeted for 2031.
Canada’s Polar OTHR is expected to cost up to $3.5 billion and is a slice of the nation’s estimated $38.6 billion overhaul of its portion of NORAD.
The polar project is currently in the site procurement phase, with operational deployment planned for 2029 and FOC by 2033.
The U.S. Northern Warning System Modernization project “Crossbow” could cost up to $6 billion, and the system rollout is expected to last until 2028, with the project concluding in 2035.
The High-Altitude and Mobile Near-Space Surveillance Systems has a $4.2 billion contract ceiling and is currently in field testing and initial low-altitude deployments. It is expected to achieve full cloud-based command-and-control network integration by 2028.

articles.title: US could drop ‘mother of all bombs’ on Iran – CNN
articles.body:
US could drop ‘mother of all bombs’ on Iran – CNN
The Pentagon is developing plans to use the largest conventional bomb in the US arsenal in its war on Iran, CNN has reported, citing multiple sources in US President Donald Trump’s administration.
If approved, the strike would mark only the second combat use of the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, or MOAB, following its deployment in Afghanistan in 2017 during Trump’s first term.
According to CNN, such an operation would primarily serve as “psychological warfare” against Iranian forces while potentially boosting domestic support for the Trump administration. Sources suggested the weapon, nicknamed the “mother of all bombs,” could be dropped ahead of the US midterm elections in early November.
The MOAB is a massive 9,800 kg (21,600-pound) airburst munition designed to devastate a large area and intimidate enemy forces witnessing the explosion. While capable of destroying relatively unfortified targets, it is not a penetrating “bunker-buster” designed to destroy deeply buried installations, such as those used by Iran for critical military infrastructure.
The “bunker-buster” GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator weighs approximately 14,000 kg (30,000 pounds). However, the MOAB carries at least four times as much explosive material.
“The MOAB is a massive information operation type weapon that is great for huge area clearance but not much else,” one of CNN’s sources said.
“POTUS has unfortunately put himself in a situation where he is almost compelled to do something,” the official added. With the president’s options limited, “you have to look at psychological effects for which the MOAB is well-equipped.”
In 2017, the US dropped a MOAB on a tunnel complex in Afghanistan’s Nangarhar Province, targeting militants identified by American officials as members of ISIS-K, a local offshoot of the now-defunct Islamic State terrorist group. Initial reports put the death toll at 36.
A series of recent US media reports has suggested that military officials are preparing options for renewed large-scale attacks on Iran, which would potentially be timed shortly before or after the midterm elections.
Skeptics argue that the initial US-Israeli assault in February and March failed to crush Iran’s military, while American forces are now in a significantly weaker position, having depleted crucial munitions and lost access to military bases across the Middle East.
Meanwhile, Tehran retains the ability to threaten commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, putting economic pressure on Washington. Iran could also launch large-scale attacks against strategic economic targets in US-allied Gulf states if it faces an imminent defeat.

articles.title: FSB says it detained a Swedish citizen in Russia, accuses him of fighting for Ukraine and plotting sabotage
articles.body:
FSB says it detained a Swedish citizen in Russia, accuses him of fighting for Ukraine and plotting sabotage
Russia’s Federal Security Service says it detained a Swedish citizen in the Pskov region, alleging he fought on the side of Ukraine’s armed forces in the Russia–Ukraine war.
The FSB said in a statement that he had traveled to Russia “under the guise of joining the Russian Armed Forces” to carry out sabotage at military facilities.
The FSB said the Swedish citizen served from February to June 2026 as commander of an unmanned aerial systems squad in the 24th Separate Assault Battalion, an organization Russia has designated as a terrorist organization. “There are documents confirming his participation in combat operations against our country as part of Ukraine’s armed forces,” the agency said.
The FSB has not disclosed his name. Russian authorities have opened a criminal case against him for illegally crossing the Russian border, and the FSB plans to open a second case charging him with organizing the activities of a terrorist organization and mercenarism.
On October 13, the FSB said it had detained Yuki Imai, a Japanese citizen and correspondent for the newspaper Hokkaido Shimbun, in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk on espionage charges. The agency claimed the journalist, acting on assignment from Japanese intelligence, had been gathering data on how many Kuril Islands residents had been mobilized or volunteered to fight in the war in Ukraine.

Discussion continues at the White House over intelligence for Ukraine - media
Kyiv • UNN
Trump is furious about the strikes on Russian oil refineries, but did not issue an order. CIA Director Ratcliffe opposes restricting data sharing.
A discussion is currently underway at the White House regarding the further provision of intelligence to Ukraine. CIA Director Ratcliffe opposes restricting the provision of intelligence. articles.title: EU's new Lebanon security mission explained, and what's next
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
EU's new security mission to Lebanon explained, and what's next
The European Union has agreed to establish a new security mission in Lebanon as the country faces mounting uncertainty over the future of UN peacekeepers amid continued Israeli attacks and its occupation of parts of the south.
Approved on Monday at the request of Lebanese authorities, the mission will operate under the EU's Common Security and Defence Policy, with an initial mandate of three years.
The move comes as the United States opposes extending the mandate of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL), which expires on 31 December 2026, raising concerns about a potential security vacuum along Lebanon's southern border.
While the European mission is intended to strengthen Lebanon's army and security institutions, it will not replace UNIFIL or carry out peacekeeping operations.
So what exactly will the new mission do, when will it begin, and what does it mean for Lebanon's security?
What is the EU's new mission in Lebanon?
The mission is a European initiative designed to strengthen Lebanon's security institutions, improve border management and support the Lebanese state's ability to exercise authority across its territory.
It was established by the Council of the European Union following a formal request from Lebanese authorities and will operate under a unified political mandate.
Unlike a conventional peacekeeping force, the mission will not deploy troops to patrol Lebanese territory or monitor ceasefire violations.
Instead, it will provide technical assistance, specialised training and strategic advice to the Lebanese Armed Forces and Internal Security Forces.
Its work will extend beyond southern Lebanon, with a broader focus on strengthening state institutions and improving security capabilities nationwide.
EU sources told The New Arab that the initiative is separate from ongoing discussions about UNIFIL's future.
When will the mission begin and how long will it last?
The mission could begin operations in late 2026 or early 2027, according to EU sources who spoke to TNA.
However, no final start date has been agreed, and the number of personnel who will participate remains undecided.
The EU is expected to announce further details as decisions are finalised.
The mission has been granted an initial three-year mandate, although the precise arrangements for its deployment and activities have yet to be confirmed.
Unlike UNIFIL, which operates under UN Security Council resolutions, the European mission does not require Security Council approval because it was established through a bilateral agreement between Lebanon and the EU.
What will the European mission actually do?
The mission will have two main components, military and civilian, working under a single political mandate.
The military component will support the Lebanese army through training and advisory assistance in several areas, including border security, maritime operations, intelligence gathering, surveillance and reconnaissance.
It will also help strengthen the army's ability to monitor and control land borders, combat smuggling and improve coordination between security units.
The civilian component will focus on Lebanon's Internal Security Forces, providing specialised training to improve operational capabilities and establish sustainable training programmes.
These will cover areas such as cybercrime investigations, anti-smuggling operations and internal security.
The mission will also help improve security management at Lebanese ports, including the Port of Beirut.
The broader objective is to strengthen Lebanon's state institutions and contribute to long-term stability in line with UN Security Council Resolution 1701.
Will the EU mission replace UNIFIL?
No. European officials have explicitly ruled out the mission replacing UNIFIL or serving as the alternative international force currently under discussion.
The two missions have fundamentally different responsibilities.
UNIFIL was established in 1978 under UN Security Council Resolutions 425 and 426, with its mandate expanded following the 2006 war between Israel and Hezbollah under Resolution 1701.
Its responsibilities include monitoring the cessation of hostilities, supporting the Lebanese army and helping the government extend its authority across southern Lebanon.
UNIFIL peacekeepers maintain a physical presence throughout the south, including along the Blue Line separating Lebanon and Israel.
They conduct patrols, monitor military activity and work alongside Lebanese forces.
The EU mission, by contrast, will not carry out operational deployments, patrol borders or monitor ceasefire violations.
EU sources said the missions would also have different geographical areas of focus, with the European initiative extending beyond southern Lebanon.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas emphasised the distinction during her visit to Beirut last week, while stressing the importance of avoiding a security vacuum if UNIFIL withdraws.
Why is UNIFIL's future under threat?
UNIFIL's mandate is due to expire on 31 December 2026, amid US opposition to extending the peacekeeping operation.
Washington and Israel have criticised UNIFIL's performance, arguing that it failed to prevent Hezbollah from building its military infrastructure in southern Lebanon.
The United States has also pushed for new security arrangements, including direct military coordination between the Lebanese and Israeli armies.
Lebanon has resisted such proposals, instead calling for UNIFIL's mandate to be extended or for a replacement international force to operate under UN authority.
Lebanese MP Najat Aoun Saliba told The New Arab that 14 of the Security Council's 15 members were prepared to support extending UNIFIL's mandate, but Washington remained opposed.
Saliba is among 86 Lebanese MPs who submitted a legal memorandum calling on the Security Council to reconsider Resolution 2790, particularly the timing and mechanism of UNIFIL's withdrawal.
She warned that implementing the resolution under current conditions would be extremely difficult because Israeli forces continue occupying Lebanese territory.
One particular concern involves the transfer of UNIFIL positions and facilities to the Lebanese army.
Saliba argued that where these positions remain under Israeli occupation, transferring them to Israeli forces instead would effectively consolidate that occupation.
What happens to southern Lebanon if UNIFIL leaves?
The potential withdrawal has raised serious concerns about border monitoring, civilian protection and the ability of the Lebanese army to fill the gap.
Saliba warned that more than 10,000 residents of three southern Lebanese villages, Debel, Ain Ebel and Rmeish, could become completely isolated without an alternative to UNIFIL.
The peacekeeping force currently helps maintain a humanitarian corridor serving these communities, which have faced increasing pressure as Israeli occupation expands around their villages.
Residents are also dealing with the weakening presence of Lebanese state institutions and limited access to essential services.
Saliba warned that UNIFIL's departure would leave important border positions along the Blue Line without international observers.
"UNIFIL is responsible for the border points demarcated by the Blue Line," she said.
"If it leaves the south, these points that safeguard Lebanon's borders will be left open and unattended."
She stressed that the central concern was the absence of international monitors to help protect Lebanon's borders.
Could another international force replace UNIFIL?
Discussions are continuing over the possibility of establishing an alternative international force, although no agreement has been reached.
Lebanon wants any replacement to operate under the United Nations, maintaining international oversight of the southern border.
Washington has not ruled out an alternative force, according to Saliba, but the negotiations remain complicated by US and Israeli demands for new security arrangements.
Among the proposals is direct coordination between the Lebanese and Israeli militaries, an arrangement Beirut opposes.
The EU mission will operate independently of these negotiations and will not assume the responsibilities of any future international peacekeeping force.
For Lebanon, the European initiative could provide valuable long-term assistance to its military and security institutions.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Navy says it hit six Su-34 bombers at a Russian airbase with Neptune missiles—the jets that drop glide bombs on Ukrainian towns (updated)
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Navy hit six Su-34M bombers at Russia’s Borisoglebsk military airfield in Voronezh Oblast with Neptune missiles overnight into 15 October, the Navy said. Residents filmed a large fire at the base after a missile alert, and the Navy’s count has not been independently confirmed. The facility is about 400 km from the frontline.
Glide bombs are now central to how Russia’s army fights, used to pin down Ukrainian defenders, including drone teams, before small infantry groups move in. They also hit frontline cities and the civilians who live in them.
Six bombers and flight equipment hit, the Navy says
The Neptune coastal missile system also hit technical equipment that supports flights, the Navy said. It recorded secondary detonations and a fire on the airfield and said details were still being clarified.
The Su-34M can carry several guided and high-explosive aerial bombs at once, along with missiles, the Navy noted. It called the jet one of Russia’s key tools for glide-bomb strikes on Ukrainian positions and frontline towns. In September, a Ukrainian Neptune missile reached a Russian warship at its own pier.
Fire over the airfield late on 14 October
Voronezh Oblast Governor Aleksandr Gusev declared a missile alert across the region shortly before 22:00 local time on 14 October. Within an hour, Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported explosions and a fire, preliminarily at the Borisoglebsk airfield. It later wrote that the airfield had come under missile attack and a fire was burning there. Ukrainian monitoring channel Supernova+ posted footage from the town showing the blaze.
On the morning of 15 October, Gusev claimed that 33 drones and several jet-powered aerial targets had been downed over the oblast overnight. He did not mention the airfield.
A base Ukraine has hit before
The airfield hosts the 783rd training aviation center and units of the 105th composite aviation division of Russia’s Aerospace Forces, which flies Su-34, Su-35S, and Su-30SM jets, Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi reported. In summer 2026, it had no permanently based combat jets, and Russia used it mainly as a stopover to refuel and rearm aircraft striking Ukraine, the outlet said, citing satellite observation.
Ukrainian drones hit the airfield overnight on 8 July, starting a fire, and satellite images later showed its fuel and lubricants depot destroyed. Drones also attacked the base’s pilot training center in July 2025.
The same night, Ryazan Oblast Governor Pavel Malkov reported a fire at an oil refinery in Ryazan. It came as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine was resuming strikes on Russian refineries.
Update: Satellite imagery confirms the strike
New satellite images show damage at Borisoglebsk airbase and six Su-34 bombers positioned in the affected area two days earlier, although the extent of the aircraft losses remains unconfirmed.
The monitoring channel Exilenova+ reports that 4 airframes were completely destroyed, while 2 others sustained significant damage.
